settledReviews.head: c84ba767743ce2c96109a89f234d234485b3a230
settledReviews.title: Check TMPFS and VFS locking contracts
settledReviews.summary:
Publish the three-line TMPFS lock annotation amendment on #14343?

git -C ~/code/gvisor range-diff e438da4be^! c84ba7677^!
settledReviews.body: Dropping the child directory’s .. link uses the parent inode. Using the dentry’s existing pointer lets Nogo verify the filesystem mutex at that call. Both AMD64 and ARM64 analyses passed. Removing the function’s lock precondition made both report the missing mutex at this line.

settledReviews.head: cfdbe9edf497581ae3340e184806b5e3d39b7dbf
settledReviews.title: Check TMPFS and VFS locking contracts
settledReviews.body:
Make checklocks enforce the existing guards for TMPFS file data and VFS registries, mount state, dentries, and epoll state. Express shared filesystem ownership where the checker can follow it, and document the remaining collection and callback boundaries.

Use filesystem receivers for TMPFS path traversal so callers can prove which mutex they hold. Initialize the VFS registries before the VFS is shared, and keep the construction of its anonymous mount checked. Detach the filesystem registry before releasing its entries so release callbacks run outside the registry lock. Read file offsets through Seek in the existing TMPFS test.
settledReviews.summary:
Publish the qualified amendment and reply to Ayush. All 40 VFS and 171 TMPFS tests passed on native AMD64 with no skips. Nogo passed for AMD64 and ARM64. On each architecture it detected the same unguarded vfs.devices write with the exception confined to the helper. Suppressing the entire Init function hid that write.

Proposed inline reply

Yes, those lock pairs aren't needed while this VFS is private. Checklocks already supports `// +checklocksignore` on a function. I confined it to the helper that initializes the guarded fields so the rest of `Init`, including construction of its anonymous mount, stays checked. For a general annotation I'd want to name the exclusively owned receiver or parameter and check that precondition at call sites.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

git range-diff c84ba7677^! cfdbe9edf^!
settledReviews.note: Retired the proposed amendment and reply. Ayush’s long-term suggestion is in a resolved thread, and he approved the existing PR head.

nodes.summary:
Flit now runs with the execution platform’s registered Python. The previous action tried to start a GNU-linked target interpreter on an AMD64 musl worker that lacks its ELF loader. The integrated action used the static execution interpreter and produced the wheel and source distribution. The older combined proposal and wheel-scanner amendment remain on hold.

The large Bazel release action at b5bd72431 and the wheel scanner amendment at d67495aac are withheld after contributor feedback. The existing setuptools release produced identical file contents across workers, but gzip and tar metadata differed. No catalog amendment is needed for the backend-only experiment. The native uv_build backend requires Python 3.8 or newer, which excludes the package’s supported Python 3.7 source installs.

With Flit 3.12 and a fixed SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, both existing release frontends produced byte-identical wheel and source archives on one Linux worker. Each installed offline on actual CPython 3.7.17 with stock-equivalent modules and README. License-Expression preserves Apache-2.0, replacing the legacy License field and classifier. The old setuptools-generated files drop out of the source archive. The overall comparison failed on two other checks. uv left two lockfiles in the stock temporary directory, and Hatchling included a parent .gitignore symlink that uv rejected in this Bazel fixture. The original cross-worker results remain below.

On feab64aff Bazel calls Flit’s two public build hooks with one pinned build dependency. AMD64 and ARM64 scratch actions produced the wheel and source archive previously installed offline on CPython 3.7.17. Make staged the same bytes with Docker disabled. The default registered Python and standalone license check passed. The wheel has three license paths containing two distinct texts, both cataloged. The versioned Buildkite command at 11013b7d6 ran without Docker and staged the same wheel and source archive. The original caller tried Docker 13 times and failed before creating either file. The comparison supplied a fixed version and registry reply. With the Buildkite Bazelisk prerequisite, the plain make artifacts-python command takes DOCKER_BUILD=false from the job environment. GNU Make selected the same build and copy commands as the tested explicit override.

rules_python 2.4.5 selects uv for the target platform and keeps its toolchain executable alias private. Using uv for a cross build would require another execution-platform adapter. Replacing a literal version in pyproject.toml can also silently lose a release override. The uv experiment did not replace the qualified Flit producer.

contributorReview.head: 49c4a3a920d738e4bb92d72b41ddfe3a5a8b8ecb
contributorReview.title: Run clang-tidy through Bazel compile actions
contributorReview.summary: Bazel runs clang-tidy for each configured C++ compilation. The revised action calls clang-tidy directly and declares its frontend diagnostics file. On an AMD64 image containing only /hello, two clean actions produced identical files. An invalid include printed its source line and check name in the Bazel log and failed the build. The previous revision covered 371 AMD64 and 370 ARM64 actions.
contributorReview.body:
A source file can compile with different flags and headers in different
targets. Running clang-tidy once per source in a local execution root
misses those differences and keeps Bazel from scheduling lint remotely.

Run the LLVM toolchain's clang-tidy for each configured compilation of
repository sources. Pass the compile action's arguments, declared
inputs and clang-tidy's matching builtin headers. Share header
discovery with the editor's compilation database and include transitive
generated sources in that database. Keep generated and third-party
sources outside the lint selection.

Declare a serialized Clang frontend diagnostics file for each action.
Clang writes it even on a clean run, so Bazel can invoke clang-tidy
directly without a shell. Read clang-tidy findings in the Bazel action
log. With warnings treated as errors, clang-tidy's exit status replaces
the Python diagnostic parser and thread pool.

worker Linux reported a system-wide limit of 1,821 threads. Request a
large worker to leave room for the ptrace tracers and the guest tasks.

Ayush closed #17204 without merging it. On copy-on-write filesystems such as Btrfs, a write to a mapped page can still fault after fallocate succeeds. The published #15181 head 61470ea41 keeps fault-protected clearing and separately reserves storage for strict disk-backed allocations.

settledReviews.title: Preserve disk-backed reservations across the allocator rebase
settledReviews.summary:
Publish the rebased allocator and update its description? The one-page and recycled-disk controls failed on master. The fix passed 441 package test records. The new benchstat rows report the remaining 4 KiB cost.

git -C ~/code/gvisor range-diff --creation-factor=999 36900f035^! 61470ea41^!
settledReviews.body:
tmpfs uses AllocateAndCommit to reserve space for disk-backed files.
A one-page allocation can pass through the population hint without
backing that page. Clearing a recycled disk-backed page can also
succeed without reserving its storage. In both cases Allocate can
report success before it has fulfilled the caller's request.

Touch the advised mapping to establish its huge-page policy, then
reserve the requested range with fallocate before calling ReaderFunc.
Keep the disk-backed zero check for pages that cannot be written.
Clearing recycled shmem pages already commits them. Use fault-protected
stores so Allocate can release the range and return ENOMEM if a page
cannot be backed.

Use REP STOSQ on amd64 CPUs with ERMS for clears of at least 2 KiB.
This keeps bulk zeroing inside safecopy's fault handler.

BenchmarkAllocateRecycled [1] measures the allocation path for private
anonymous faults and copy-on-write. Hot samples reuse one range. Cold
samples rotate through 256 MiB. On one pinned AMD EPYC 9V74 core, 16
alternating samples per revision gave these changes in time [2].

                              │  70008149c  │             61470ea41              │
                              │   sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base               │
    AllocateRecycled/4K/hot     240.7n ± 1%   250.0n ± 1%  +3.86% (p=0.000 n=16)
    AllocateRecycled/64K/hot    4.032µ ± 0%   4.041µ ± 0%  +0.22% (p=0.004 n=16)
    AllocateRecycled/4K/cold    517.4n ± 1%   534.2n ± 1%  +3.23% (p=0.000 n=16)

settledReviews.head: a5e521f7d2b149674006a4a2c5762db56f75da94
settledReviews.title: Support externally owned buffer chunks
settledReviews.body:
Proposed PR description

Linux accepts writes to `/dev/net/tun` larger than the interface MTU [1]. gVisor rejects them and copies accepted writes into Go heap storage. Removing the limit would allow large heap allocations whose failure cannot be returned to the writer as a syscall error.

MemoryFile, the Sentry's file-backed allocator, can report allocation failure. To use it for TUN packets, a buffer must keep the backing alive while packets are queued or cloned, even after the TUN file is closed. This change provides the buffer support. The TUN write path and its MTU limit are separate changes.

A view can now take ownership of external storage. Clones share the chunk, writes to a shared chunk still detach, and the last reference releases the owner. Both heap and external chunks hold their usable slice directly. `AsSlice`, `Full`, `Capacity`, and `AvailableSize` read the same fields as before.

External bytes are checkpointed by their owner only. Loading the object graph rebuilds the sharing and orders the owner's Go restore callback before a restored buffer can release it. An owner that maps its backing later installs the slice after its mapping succeeds, before buffer users resume. The wait does not make separately restored MemoryFile metadata available during object loading.

On heap-backed buffers, single-view and multi-view ReadAt cost 3.92% and 2.08% more with external storage support. The eight-view AsSlice traversal measured 9.604 ns before and 9.591 ns after (p=0.235, n=18). All three benchmarks measured zero allocations [2].

```text
                 pre-feature      external storage   change in sec/op
ReadAt           8.146n ± 0%      8.466n ± 0%      +3.92% (p=0.000 n=18)
ReadAtMultiView  45.02n ± 2%      45.95n ± 2%      +2.08% (p=0.011 n=18)
```

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/drivers/net/tun.c#L1735
[2]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41773274379/artifacts/13296013890

<!-- codex-thread: 01a0e5cd-f894-7c00-9aa2-26d0e91eec77 -->

Proposed replies

https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15443#discussion_r4462958129

Added the waits on the saved view, chunk, and storage. The regression covers releasing either a restored Buffer or a standalone View from its owner's `afterLoad`. Both cases released storage before its own Go callback on 5af539b23. The wait orders those callbacks. A MemoryFile-backed owner still needs its separately restored metadata before it can release its range.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15443#discussion_r4462958137

The accessors now read `chunk.data` directly again. The external owner supplies the slice once at construction and installs the restored slice before packet I/O resumes. The paired benchmark compares 5af539b23 (public) with the proposed amendment (candidate). All three benchmarks measured zero allocations.

```text
                │    public    │              candidate              │
                │    sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base                │
ReadAt            10.340n ± 0%   8.466n ± 0%  -18.13% (p=0.000 n=18)
ReadAtMultiView    57.64n ± 0%   45.95n ± 2%  -20.28% (p=0.000 n=18)
ViewListAsSlice   25.990n ± 0%   9.591n ± 0%  -63.10% (p=0.000 n=18)
```

Single- and multi-view ReadAt still measured 3.92% and 2.08% above pre-feature. Eight-view traversal measured 9.604 ns pre-feature and 9.591 ns on the amendment. [Paired benchmarks](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41773274379/artifacts/13296013890)

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

nodes.title: Build C and C++ with the declared LLVM toolchains
nodes.summary:
4bee07965 uses the Go offset generator from #16516. An alternative compiler submission on Linux hosts with shell utilities could precede #16516 by declaring @llvm//tools:llvm-nm for the existing script. On an AMD64 host, both generators produced all 10 AMD64 and 11 ARM64 offsets, with every name and value matching the linked ELF. The two arms used identical ELF and stub bytes for each architecture. With implicit $(NM), Bazel previously returned success but both generated Go files contained only a 105-byte header and zero offsets. The comparison covered offset generation. The shell-free build still requires the Go generator.

An AMD64 worker built static runsc and Sentry for AMD64 and ARM64 with LLVM 0.8.24. The linked vDSOs, signal stubs and generated offsets matched what the Sentry embeds. Runsc printed its stamped version natively on AMD64 and under QEMU on ARM64. This run did not boot a Sentry.

Since the earlier approval, only default-toolchain static Go race builds select musl. Explicit C toolchains and custom platforms retain their libc. Three release sidecars are freestanding; the signal stub needs target libc headers. #17114 replaces the LLVM source that fails to build the NVIDIA parser under the new libc++.

A downstream AMD64 client built gVisor’s ARM64 vDSO with the declared LLVM compiler. Changing Gazelle 0.51.3 to read its environment only when used produced the same 7,056-byte ELF as the eight-file gVisor workaround and preserved gVisor’s existing Gazelle exports. The Bzlmod and WORKSPACE runners each matched the original generated script. Both real Gazelle invocations and the environment tests passed. The ELF was checked on AMD64. contributorReview.head: 4bee07965270dc7cb4ed89eb6a3b17968b3e0a90
contributorReview.title: Build C and C++ with the declared LLVM toolchains
contributorReview.body:
The Coral toolchain looks for GCC and target headers under /usr. An
AMD64 worker therefore needs an installed cross-compiler to build the
vDSO and signal handler for an ARM64 Sentry.

Register the toolchains from the LLVM 0.8.24 module already in
MODULE.bazel. Bazel selects the compiler for the execution platform and
the sysroot for the target. Keep GNU17 and C++17 and remove the Coral
repositories, toolchain definitions and patches.

The three runsc sidecars provide their own entry points and use Linux
UAPI headers. Only the signal stub needs target libc headers for its
signal and ucontext types.

The default GNU sysroot lacks static libc. Build static Go race
executables against musl when the C toolchain and Linux target use the
project defaults. Keep an explicitly selected C toolchain or custom
target platform on its own libc.

nodes.title: Skip memory usage scans while restoring checkpoint pages
nodes.summary:
Both sides added tests at the end of save_restore_test.go. The rebase preserves the published restore test and the newly merged exit-after-saving tests. All 69 allocator cases passed together on Linux AMD64, with no skips.

Prior source-specific evidence:

The approved runtime page-size amendment is published in #15322 at 7b9b29bfb, replacing 8cb774707. No contributor decision remains pending. The earlier restore regression treated hostarch.PageSize as a constant. The runtime page-size change in #15802 makes it a variable and removes the save/restore test guards. This five-expression amendment uses a uint64 runtime value and adjusts the comparisons and casts; the production restore guard is unchanged.

The actual combined #15322/#15802 product source on ec4ced798 passed TestLoadFromWithUpdateUsage in a real ARM64 guest with 65,536-byte pages. The source had no test build tags. Exactly one regression executed, and its result was authenticated 4.80 seconds after native execution. This is focused runtime page-size compatibility evidence, not a new full allocator or race run.

Published 7b9b29bfb has the same tree as the qualified five-expression revision. Earlier full-suite and race results remain bound to 8cb774707; current public checks and maintainer review are tracked separately.

Earlier 8cb774707 regression and validation:

The published amendment pauses memory accounting scans while restore installs the saved commitment ranges. In the regression, a scan counted an omitted page halfway through restore: both control runs reported 8,192 committed bytes when only 4,096 had been restored. The full allocator suite, both Nogo architectures, and two race-enabled executions passed on the published commit. Ayush has the results and the revised patch.

followup.nextAction: Follow review and checks on #15322.

settledReviews.head: 5f651fdc090433d2f5f8d370793e57e90745c40f
settledReviews.title: Run Go and C++ tests on native architectures
settledReviews.body:
The test runner for a C++ test can still target AMD64 when its binary
has been cross-compiled for ARM64. Select the target platform on the
test rule itself and constrain its test execution group to a native
worker. Use the real C++ test rule exported by rules_cc for inheritance
so its test transition also applies to the runner.

Add optional architecture variants to Go and C++ test declarations.
Provide suites for atomicbitops and posix_error so one invocation can
exercise both architectures. Ordinary test targets remain available.
settledReviews.note: Tamir asked to use with_cfg 1.0.2 and to include the range-diff in the amendment question.

nodes.title: Current public-CI qualification
nodes.status: Remote ARM64 selection verified; full unit and QEMU SDK runs remain incomplete
nodes.summary:
The mixed unit and non-hybrid profile selectors submit eligible ARM64 Firecracker tests while keeping independent KVM and Nogo exclusions. The original workflow ran all 23 selector tests on a remote AMD64 worker. The new case exercised a retained graph of 29 configured ARM64 actions for 15 owners. These were selection checks; the 15 workloads were not executed by this run.

On a native ARM64 Ubuntu 22.04 worker, Bazel ran the docprocessor (9 cases), Go SDK (49), and Python SDK (43) tests at 38745c527. All three test targets ran uncached and passed. Nogo analyzed the standard library and produced 10,895,578 bytes of facts.

An AMD64 worker built the ARM64 kernel and ext4 guest image at 38745c527. The image assembly action now selects tar for the worker’s architecture. Its output digests matched the Bazel build report.

At its deadline the AMD64/ARM64 unit run at d943b4a177 had attempted 656 of 668 targets: 174,566 cases passed, 52 failed and 69 skipped. Five more targets passed all 34 cases on the same source. The root build test and both AMD64 NVIDIA tests ran in a second job. A native ARM64 run executed both NVIDIA tests: 60 cases passed, and nine skipped for unavailable driver sources. Only the AMD64 and ARM64 cgroup tests still have no attempt at d943b4a177. Both passed on the corrected source in #16496.

Of 357 analyzer-dependent targets, 356 built; the remaining cgroup target required local compilation. These builds do not count as test attempts. The ARM64 SDK and docprocessor guest run separately stopped before any of its 58 cases because QEMU exhausted temporary disk.

Release qualification is separate. On cb548161f5, the mixed release smoke ran 32 cases successfully and skipped one bwrap case. AMD64 ran in Firecracker and ARM64 under QEMU. The optimized releases have also passed CLI checks on both native architectures.

With the rules_go coverage change in #16507, the coordinator and Sentry built on AMD64 and ARM64. On AMD64 both the coverage and race-plus-coverage releases reported Sentry source lines and passed the KCOV syscall test. At d837256cb, the instrumented releases passed KCOV with systrap and ptrace in AMD64 Firecracker and ARM64 QEMU guests. Native ARM64 KCOV at 38745c527 remains unmeasured.

followup.disposition: The SDK suites passed on native ARM64. The earlier QEMU run exhausted temporary disk before testing.
followup.nextAction: Check the QEMU disk request if the SDK tests need to run in that guest. Keep the historical unit and cgroup limits with their original source.

nodes.status: Short pilot passed; full ping pair timed out
nodes.summary:
The complete ping pair timed out on both native host architectures at the original 300-second limits, in the first ICMPPortExhaustion case. Neither completed a case; 36 cases per owner were unstarted. Independent saved review bound both failures and the retained progress, without a speedup or cause claim. Earlier observations:

The paired mincore pilot passed both original 300-second actions, five cases on each native AMD64 and ARM64 OCI host. Independent review bound the 16 remotely inspected native tools, actual action inputs and byte-identical guest kernel, initramfs and payload. This short pair does not establish a speedup. The complete shared-filesystem ping pair is now accepted at eac536ce6 under its unchanged 300-second deadlines and full 37-case selection; its results are pending.

The resumed pilot passed graph routing and built both host archives, then its inspection step stopped on a BEP source-file path lookup before any TestRunner. The owner is preparing a narrow lookup correction; native-tool proof and guest execution remain unqualified. The source and guest choices are unchanged, and the partial evidence is being sealed.

Earlier observations:

The unchanged reviewed pilot resumed once at 588d3e6d3 after the pinned logical indexes became reachable again. Its original method, package checksum, exact-package fallback, two complete mincore targets and deadlines are unchanged. Results and native ARM64 host-tool proof remain pending; both prior zero-action failures are retained.

Earlier observations:

The reviewed source adds explicit ARM64-host tools for two existing complete mincore guests while preserving their payload, guest images and 300-second deadlines. Both pilot attempts stopped before execution. The first failed on the pinned AMD64 libexpat package. A single continuation used the standard Bazel exact-URL fallback; both official mirrors matched the existing package checksum. That continuation then failed when all four pinned jammy/main/amd64 package-index formats returned HTTP 503, before reaching the package fetch. There is no host-tool, ELF, placement, guest-runtime or timing result. Both saved failures are independently reviewed and retained. No further unchanged retry is planned while the immutable input prerequisite is unavailable. This fork pilot is not awaiting contributor review.

followup.disposition: Short pilot passed; full ping pair timed out

settledReviews.title: Give the NVIDIA ABI test its driver headers

contributorReview.head: 4b9a9bc5d270b5a54af336142496284af3f5cf05
contributorReview.title: Compare NVIDIA driver ABIs using declared source archives
contributorReview.body:
The NVIDIA ABI test clones a driver repository during each comparison.
Without Git or network access, the test fails before Clang can compare
the driver’s ioctl definitions with the corresponding nvproxy types.

Give the ABI test and driver differ the same pinned header archives
as Bazel runfiles. Record versions without a public source tag so
the test can distinguish them from missing build inputs. Developers
can also pin a candidate version for the differ before nvproxy adopts
it. Keep these archives development dependencies of the gVisor module.

Checking the installer checksums still requires network access. Move
that check into its own test. The existing parity suite runs both
tests, while the ABI target can run offline on every supported version
with published headers.
contributorReview.summary: Review the full offline ABI change after #17112, #17114 and #17151. The same commit now moves the network-dependent installer checksum test to its own target.

items.body:
[🤖] 1 issue found:

- **[minor · concurrency]** Re-enabled metric_test flakes under CPU load from profiling restart race (`Makefile:269`, inline)

[🤖] **[minor · concurrency] Re-enabled metric_test flakes under CPU load from profiling restart race**

This change makes all three `make unit-tests` CI jobs run `//pkg/metric:metric_test`, but `TestMetricProfiling` fails intermittently when the CPU is busy, as it is during `make unit-tests`. `writeProfilingMetrics` (`pkg/metric/profiling_metric.go:645-647`) signals `doneProfilingMetrics` before it clears `profilingMetricsStarted`, so `StopProfilingMetrics` can return while the flag is still set. The next subtest's `StartProfilingMetrics` then fails with "profiling metrics have already been started". The race predates this PR and does not depend on the architecture; the exclusion removed here kept it out of CI.

**Suggested fix:** Fix the race before removing the exclusion, or keep `-//pkg/metric:metric_test` until it is fixed. In `writeProfilingMetrics`, capture the channel when the goroutine starts and clear the flag before signaling:

```go
func writeProfilingMetrics[...](...) {
	done := doneProfilingMetrics
	...
	sink.Close()
	profilingMetricsStarted.Store(false)
	done <- stats
	close(done)
}
```

Capturing `done` is required: with a plain reorder, the next `StartProfilingMetrics` reassigns the global while the old writer still uses it. The race detector then reports a race between lines 287 and 647, and runs panic with "send on closed channel" (100/100 runs failed). Verified: with the fix, 0 failures in 1,100 loaded runs and 220 race-detector runs.

<details><summary>Details (evidence, reproduction and test code)</summary>

**Evidence:** `StopProfilingMetrics` returns right after it receives from `doneProfilingMetrics` (line 748). `StartProfilingMetrics` needs `profilingMetricsStarted.CompareAndSwap(false, true)` (line 264). If the writer goroutine is descheduled between the send and `Store(false)`, a Start that follows Stop fails.

Results of `bazel test //pkg/metric:metric_test --nocache_test_results --runs_per_test=N` on a 32-core amd64 host ("paired" means PR head and head+fix ran at the same time):
- 32 parallel runs (bazel default): head 4/200 failed.
- Paired, 32 parallel runs each: head 32/400 and 14/400; fix 0/400 and 0/400.
- `--config=race`: head 9/40 and 20/80; fix 0/40 and 0/80 (the 80-run pair ran concurrently). No DATA RACE reports.

Every failure is `metric_test.go:1228: StartProfilingMetrics error: got 'profiling metrics have already been started'`, spread over six subtests. Runs pass when executed one at a time on an idle machine.

`TestProfilingMetricsRestartAfterStop` (attached) restarts profiling 200 times right after `StopProfilingMetrics`. Paired under load, it failed 110/300 runs at head and 0/300 runs (60,000 restarts) with the fix.

The original #10045 failure is fixed: an ARM64 build of the test under qemu-aarch64 passes at head and fails with "did not panic" when the IsNaN check is removed.

**Reproduced with a test** (`pkg/metric/metric_test.go`): `bazel test //pkg/metric:metric_test --nocache_test_results --runs_per_test=300 --test_output=summary   (run concurrently with: <same command>; slot fix = worktree + scratch/max/fix.patch). Earlier runs used --runs_per_test=200/400 (existing TestMetricProfiling only) and --config=race --runs_per_test=40/80.` → Fails intermittently on the PR head under parallel load, always with 'profiling metrics have already been started'. Passes every run with the fix applied under the same concurrent load.

**Test code:**

```diff
diff --git a/pkg/metric/metric_test.go b/pkg/metric/metric_test.go
index cb33abdd9..9f0a3586a 100644
--- a/pkg/metric/metric_test.go
+++ b/pkg/metric/metric_test.go
@@ -1430,3 +1430,34 @@ func TestMetricProfiling(t *testing.T) {
 		})
 	}
 }
+
+// TestProfilingMetricsRestartAfterStop checks that StartProfilingMetrics
+// succeeds as soon as StopProfilingMetrics returns.
+func TestProfilingMetricsRestartAfterStop(t *testing.T) {
+	defer resetTest()
+	if _, err := NewUint64Metric("/foo", Uint64Metadata{
+		Cumulative:  true,
+		Sync:        true,
+		Description: fooDescription,
+	}); err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("NewUint64Metric: %v", err)
+	}
+	if err := Initialize(); err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("Initialize: %v", err)
+	}
+	dir := t.TempDir()
+	for i := 0; i < 200; i++ {
+		f, err := os.CreateTemp(dir, "profiling-metrics")
+		if err != nil {
+			t.Fatalf("CreateTemp: %v", err)
+		}
+		if err := StartProfilingMetrics(ProfilingMetricsOptions[*os.File]{
+			Sink:    f,
+			Metrics: "/foo",
+			Rate:    time.Millisecond,
+		}); err != nil {
+			t.Fatalf("iteration %d: StartProfilingMetrics: %v", i, err)
+		}
+		StopProfilingMetrics()
+	}
+}
```

</details>

Stop now clears the started flag after receiving the writer’s final statistics. The send is the writer’s last access to the channel, so an immediate restart can safely replace it. Fixed in a52b53673b4b5d9585685592d9c188197bb7f520.

settledReviews.head: 8bc1587d96559fa14081e54fb4f93e92ea3350d3
settledReviews.title: Pin Docker 29.9.3 for Compose host networking
settledReviews.body:
The cached test images for AMD64 and ARM64 contain Docker 29.7.2 and
Compose 5.4.0. That plugin does not grant Buildx Bake the network.host
entitlement when a Compose build requests the host network, so the
build fails.

The tag in tools/images.mk hashes the files in images/basic/docker.
Moving the floating docker:29-dind tag leaves that hash unchanged.
Pin the official Docker 29.9.3 multi-architecture image to give the
recipe a new cache key and pick up Compose 5.7.0, which grants the
requested entitlement [1].

[1] https://github.com/docker/compose/commit/43a5d5a25
settledReviews.summary:
Publish the one-line official Docker image pin on #16076 and reply to Etienne with the native results?

git -C ~/code/gvisor range-diff --creation-factor=999 ec776316b^! 8bc1587d9^!

contributorReview.head: e4c8bd1605791c5b9afd48ba81b7966a6bec5ca3
contributorReview.title: Validate restore kinds against destination types
contributorReview.summary: Approve the revised tests in this single submission commit, and open the PR after the reference-array change lands?
contributorReview.body:
Empty arrays and maps could succeed against an incompatible destination
because their element loops never attempted a store. Zero references
could likewise bypass destination validation.

Select the operation from the destination kind before validating its
wire representation. Keep Nil as a no-op, retain interface delegation
and manual array-to-slice loading, and use the existing reference
resolver and collection decoders for the actual stores.

Let Go type assertions validate each destination representation
directly. The existing state error boundary wraps failed assertions with
the object context, without a generic helper call for each restored
value.

The legacy decoder accepts arrays in slices and unwraps interfaces into
scalar destinations. Save these three inputs with the wire engine so
Load exercises those conversions when graph checkpoints are the default.

nodes.head: dffb3d3c3f7850994b8059fad487b379d1943862
nodes.title: Check for zero values while encoding legacy checkpoints
nodes.summary:
The legacy checkpoint encoder now checks the value it has already read to decide whether to omit a field. Unlike the previously approved 15f2d7624, this revision preserves the sign of floating-point zero and of each complex component. It applies directly to #16718.

On Linux/amd64, saving a 32-packet UDP receive queue took 632.1 µs before and 607.0 µs after (−3.98%, p=0.000, 16 matched pairs). Both arms used the legacy encoder and produced the same 12,690 checkpoint bytes. This measures legacy Save; graph is the default encoder.

Replacing the sign-aware checks with arithmetic comparisons lost negative zero in four wire cases; all six graph cases passed. The first run also exposed two missing test imports. With those imports fixed, ordinary and race builds each ran both test targets on the proposed tree: all 15 signed-zero records and 16 wire-representation and struct-hook records passed, with no skips. The review commit has the same tree as the tested 139053514; its message links the measured legacy benchmark.

followup.disposition: The revised encoder and its benchmark record are approved.

settledReviews.head: dffb3d3c3f7850994b8059fad487b379d1943862
settledReviews.title: Check for zero values while encoding legacy checkpoints
settledReviews.summary: Approve dffb3d3c3 for submission after #16718 lands? It preserves negative zero and reduced the time to save a 32-packet UDP queue with the legacy encoder by 3.98% on Linux/amd64.
settledReviews.body:
The wire encoder inspects the type of each field to decide whether to
omit it, then dispatches on its kind again to write it. Use the value
already read by each encoder case to decide whether the field can be
omitted. Whole arrays still need to account for struct save hooks and
the sign bit of floating-point elements.

Typed zeros in interfaces and other full-value contexts preserve their
wire types. An ordinary field containing negative zero keeps its sign,
including either component of a complex number.

The graph encoder is the default. The 32-packet UDP receive queue

settledReviews.head: 76747cfd5daf8bc061c2fb5f0af3019805d8e387
settledReviews.title: Package Clang headers with the NVIDIA parser
settledReviews.body:
The NVIDIA driver differ writes driver_ast_parser to a temporary
directory before parsing driver headers. That detached executable can
fail to find Clang's builtin stddef.h and stdint.h because those files
are not beside it. Package the headers from the parser's LLVM source
with the Go wrapper and pass their resource directory explicitly.
Disable host standard-header lookup so worker-installed headers cannot
silently supply the parser's inputs.

Keep the Clang license text and inline notices with the header archive.
Give the direct parser test the same declared resource archive and
exercise stddef.h and stdint.h in its existing fixture. Clean up the
wrapper's resource directory after each driver parity subtest.

Declare the ZIP output explicitly so Gazelle can resolve the Go embed
before Bazel builds the archive.
settledReviews.summary:
Gazelle scans the source tree before Bazel creates builtin_headers.zip. Declaring the filename on pkg_zip lets Gazelle resolve the existing Go embed. The upstream Gazelle command passed in a clean checkout; the original parser test ran uncached and the CLI still contains the complete archive.

nodes.title: Make pkg/state cheap and fast
nodes.summary: Parth was invited to lead the rewrite in the posted Oct 24 reply. The Nov 9 handoff reports a four-worker Nginx measurement of the shipping graph and wire codecs. All 78 warm restores served the expected bytes. Time from starting restore through a curl inside the guest was 4.12% shorter uncapped and 12.56% shorter with a quarter-CPU parent cap. With the ordinary OCI quarter-CPU limit, the restore command was 4.90% shorter and the first-response timing was inconclusive.

settledReviews.head: 451b92800b9cb82262dc8a735388f7cf4d17d895
settledReviews.title: Post the Nginx restore and first guest response measurements
settledReviews.summary: Post this measured handoff for the pkg/state rewrite?
settledReviews.body:
@parth-opensrc, I measured how soon Nginx could serve a request with the [default graph codec](https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/6e6276344) and the wire codec in the same runsc binary. The timer started before `runsc restore` and stopped after `runsc exec curl` read a 1 KiB response from the restored server. All 78 restores preserved the four workers and returned the expected bytes.

With the ordinary OCI ¼-CPU limit, the graph codec shortened the restore command. The first HTTP response was too variable to distinguish the codecs (p=0.219). The last row adds the same limit to the parent cgroup, so the parent stays capped when runsc raises the sandbox’s startup quota.

```text
                                                     │  wire.txt   │              graph.txt              │
                                                     │   sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base                │
Restore/unlimited/through_first_http_response          85.52m ±  5%   81.99m ±  4%   -4.12% (p=0.010 n=12)
Restore/oci-quarter/restore_command                    48.97m ± 10%   46.57m ±  7%   -4.90% (p=0.045 n=12)
Restore/ancestor-quarter/through_first_http_response   346.3m ±  7%   302.8m ± 16%  -12.56% (p=0.017 n=12)
```

These were warm, uncompressed checkpoints. I’d keep both the restore command and first guest response in comparisons of future decoder changes. [Benchmark source](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/blob/6bd21891a/.github/qualification/state_working_set/measure.py#L307-L367) · [Full benchstat and samples](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42472687037/artifacts/13614821367)

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

nodes.head: 03e02dbb31d4510556da404e54fd25f1450a6719
nodes.title: tcp: reject acknowledgments beyond sent data
nodes.summary:
Proposed 03e02dbb3 changes only the PacketImpact test relative to published 8dd08c771. The production receive path is byte-identical. The test permits native Linux to silently discard the two ACKs of unsent bytes. It still requires the unchanged challenge ACK from gVisor and checks that only the continuation reaches the application.

The qualifier applied the two-file 03e02dbb3 proposal to mixed integration 373937b75 and selected only the established-state test. Four uncached TestEstablishedUnaccSeqAck runs passed on AMD64 and ARM64 (24 subtests and four parents, zero skips). For the two probes acknowledging unsent bytes, native Linux 6.18.57 sent both challenge ACKs, native Linux 5.10.0 sent neither, and Netstack sent both on each architecture. All eight flows acknowledged and delivered the distinct 12-byte continuation at the rejected sequence number.

The approved future-ACK repair is delivered independently on public 7bffefa. Both complete product postimages and patch identity match approved 3d17. It rejects invalid payload before consumption or sender ACK processing; the separate unread-FIN investigation remains agent work. Published as #16378, open and ready for review, with exact provider head readback.

Historical source-specific validation:

Reject ESTABLISHED segments that acknowledge unsent data before delivering their payload or passing their acknowledgment to the sender, and send an unchanged acknowledgment through the existing limiter. The shared test checks that rejected payload is not delivered and valid traffic can continue. Public-base proposal 3d17e956611c17719835876ac9d1d63c4c85a38e was the independently qualified pre-delivery source with no prerequisite PR. The test-only baseline d517 retains native FAIL and proves both invalid payload deliveries; corrected 245c passes native Linux and netstack plus TCP Nogo and goimports (four remote uncached owners, 16 positive XML records). This focused result does not cover FIN-specific rejection, limiter saturation or performance.

settledReviews.head: 03e02dbb31d4510556da404e54fd25f1450a6719
settledReviews.title: tcp: reject acknowledgments beyond sent data
settledReviews.body:
Reject established segments that acknowledge unsent data before consuming their payload or updating sender state. Send the current acknowledgment through the existing limiter, as required by RFC 9293.

Check that gVisor sends the unchanged acknowledgment. Linux kernels without [1] discard the segment silently. On both stacks, send distinct continuation data at the rejected sequence number and check that the application receives those bytes.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/42726ec64
settledReviews.summary: Publish 03e02dbb3 on #16378 with the qualified test change and the same TCP implementation?
settledReviews.note: Approved for publication.

nodes.head: 056d21cee8bc662737520aca579c2bc5d5936e85
nodes.title: Wait for the systemd test daemon's journal entry
nodes.summary:
The systemd tests now wait for their daemon's greeting in the journal instead of assuming an active service and main PID mean the record is already available. Both system and user service tests continue to read their own journals and fail if the greeting never appears. Contributor-approved exact source 056d21cee8bc662737520aca579c2bc5d5936e85 is delivered as open, ready-for-review PR #16391. No prerequisite or contributor decision remains.

The public Buildkite 52341 cgroup-v2 attempt missed the greeting and its retry passed. That log does not establish whether the process had written the record or journald had processed it. Private validation held the system service's write until its first real journal query returned: the original assertion failed and the correction passed. The ungated packaged user-service case passed in both. Each run used one uncached remote AMD64 test action and the same source-built systemd image, with no skips or missing cases. The original native exit 3 and FAIL verdict are retained; the corrected native exit 0 and PASS verdict are separate. The corrected result contains three positive XML records: the two named cases and their Go parent. No whole-systemd-suite or other-CPU coverage is claimed.

Original execution finished at 20:29:23.885 UTC, with its FAIL verdict after 0.54 seconds and local verification after 4.60 seconds. Corrected execution finished at 20:29:03.961 UTC, with its PASS verdict after 0.42 seconds and local verification after 6.41 seconds. Neither run needed manual recovery. The artificial write gate exists only in private validation; the proposed public change is confined to test readiness.

followup.nextAction: Follow exact-head CI, matching imports and maintainer review through the existing intake. Preserve the controlled original failure and corrected success; no repeated contributor decision or broader systemd coverage claim.

nodes.head: e396b8c8af7d751c252fee657c20441972468cee
nodes.title: Keep TCP’s slow-start threshold across repeated timeouts
nodes.summary:
The approved e396b8c8a proposal is delivered as #16419 at d13561b12 with an identical diff. No contributor decision remains pending. Current public checks and maintainer review are tracked on the PR.

A ten-segment flight set the slow-start threshold to five segments with Reno and seven with CUBIC on the first timeout. When the same retransmission timed out again, the sender reduced the threshold to two. The published change preserves five or seven until a timeout reaches new data, as RFC 5681 requires. In separate tests with no ACK and a half-segment ACK, the old code failed four cases per run; both corrected runs passed all 13 cases. These tests cover repeated timeouts on the same bytes; #16393 reported advancing oldest data.

Broader validation passed 536 records across TCP, race, packet and analyzer checks, with one existing RACK skip. All seven packet cases passed. Each analyzer passed for AMD64 and ARM64; the runtime checks were on AMD64.

nodes.head: 8427512c2e8f6c0f1ece278d57df65202da6f0e8
nodes.title: Avoid redundant TCP ssthresh cuts on timeout
nodes.summary:
An eight-segment CUBIC flight entered fast recovery. The receiver SACKed the seven segments past the hole and held its cumulative ACK fixed. When the repair timed out, Linux kept ssthresh at 7. The previous head 4a4e33cfc reduced it from 14 to 9. Fork source 8a79ae452 held it at 14. All four no-ACK and half-segment-ACK packet cases across the two stacks and all eight Reno/CUBIC repeated-timeout sender cases passed on the paired run. The standalone amendment 8427512c2 simplifies the reduction condition. On that exact source, gVisor kept ssthresh at 14 as cwnd dropped from 17 to 1 on entry to Loss. Both of its no-ACK and half-segment-ACK packet cases and all eight Reno/CUBIC repeated-timeout sender cases passed on fresh local TestRunner executions.

The earlier message-only amendment 4a4e33cfc was published with its PR body synchronized. It names retransmitTimerExpired as the destination of the one-segment congestion-window reset. The parent and source tree are unchanged, so the existing packet evidence applies; that message-only decision is complete.

The published packetimpact test at 67260334d reads TCP_INFO after two retransmission timeouts. Both the no-ACK and half-segment-ACK cases passed on Linux and gVisor in fresh AMD64 runs. The reply on Lucas’s original review thread describes both cases. The earlier instrumented test measured the threshold directly: with no ACK, Linux held at 5 and gVisor at 4; after a half-segment ACK both reduced it to 2.

Earlier implementation at c25ba441f: It starts a new loss episode on any advancing cumulative ACK, including a partial-segment ACK, while a SACK alone does not reset the episode. A zero-window probe with no data in flight retains the congestion window and threshold. The focused remote qualification passes 425 records. If #15604 lands first, synchronize its two new HandleRTOExpired test calls with this signature; neither PR independently requires the other.

Earlier source-specific record:

The approved e396b8c8a proposal is delivered as #16419 at d13561b12 with an identical diff. That submission was completed. Current public checks and maintainer review are tracked on the PR.

In separate tests with no ACK and a half-segment ACK, the old code failed four cases per run; both corrected runs passed all 13 cases. These tests cover repeated timeouts on the same bytes; #16393 reported advancing oldest data.

Broader validation passed 536 records across TCP, race, packet and analyzer checks, with one existing RACK skip. All seven packet cases passed. Each analyzer passed for AMD64 and ARM64; the runtime checks were on AMD64.

The integration at 185276b5b, which includes this fix, also passed its selected public socket slice: 11 targets and 38 sharded attempts, with 1,686 positive records, 32 known skips and no failures or missing results. Coverage includes ordinary AMD64, emulated ARM64 variants including 64 KiB pages, and separate AMD64 UNIX-stream save/restore cases. The TCP suite itself excludes save/restore. The approved amendment is now published on #16419 at 8427512c2. The contributor approved the additional CUBIC comparison and the reply was posted on Lucas’s original thread.

settledReviews.head: 8427512c2e8f6c0f1ece278d57df65202da6f0e8
settledReviews.title: Avoid redundant TCP ssthresh cuts on timeout
settledReviews.summary: The contributor approved publication of the exact 8427512c2 amendment. The new comparison reply is a separate decision.
settledReviews.body:
The first timeout of a ten-segment flight sets ssthresh to five
segments with Reno or seven with CUBIC. Without an advancing ACK,
the next timeout recomputed ssthresh from the collapsed flight or
congestion window, bringing it down to two. RFC 5681 requires holding
the previous threshold on repeated timeouts [1].

Track whether the retransmit timer has fired since the last advancing
ACK. In timeout recovery, even an ACK that covers only part of the
retransmitted segment permits a new threshold reduction. A SACK alone
does not [2][3]. Move the one-segment cwnd reset from Reno and CUBIC's
HandleRTOExpired methods into retransmitTimerExpired so it applies on
every data timeout. CUBIC still restarts its epoch.

Fast recovery already reduced ssthresh for its outstanding flight.
Keep that threshold when the timer interrupts fast recovery [2]. The
ACK handler leaves recovery once its last byte has been cumulatively
acknowledged. With an eight-segment flight and no cumulative ACK
progress, gVisor reduced CUBIC's threshold from 14 to 9. Linux held
its threshold at 7.

A zero-window probe when no data is in flight indicates flow control,
not packet loss. Keep the congestion window and ssthresh while the
sender waits for the peer to reopen its window [4].

Exercise both loss paths on the wire. Read TCP_INFO after consecutive
timeouts with no ACK or an ACK covering half a segment. For fast
recovery, selectively acknowledge the seven segments after the hole
and compare ssthresh before and after the head retransmission times
out.

[1]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5681#section-3.1
[2]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/net/ipv4/tcp_input.c#L2137-L2165
[3]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/net/ipv4/tcp_input.c#L3801-L3805
[4]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/net/ipv4/tcp_timer.c#L350-L393

settledReviews.head: 8427512c2e8f6c0f1ece278d57df65202da6f0e8
settledReviews.title: Reply to Lucas with the CUBIC timeout comparison
settledReviews.summary: Post the additional Linux and gVisor comparison in response to Lucas’s review? The approved code amendment is already published.
settledReviews.body:
@manninglucas, the PR includes `TestRTOAfterPartialACK`, and the commit message explains why data timeouts reset `cwnd` to one in `retransmitTimerExpired`. I also reproduced the timeout during fast recovery. With no cumulative ACK progress, Linux kept `ssthresh` at 7 and gVisor cut it from 14 to 9. With this change, gVisor keeps it at 14. The no-ACK and half-segment ACK cases passed on both stacks, and all eight Reno/CUBIC repeated-timeout cases passed. [Original comparison](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42373671016/artifacts/13574977842) · [Corrected comparison](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42378653816/artifacts/13577603869) · [Final amendment tests](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42380102504/artifacts/13578306497)

nodes.head: dd63198c66946d7a38279478369bf269243a6ef4
nodes.title: Build the TLDK plugin against musl
nodes.summary:
The proposed musl port is on hold for a DPDK and toolchain investigation. The plugin patch applied to DPDK 18.11. It failed on 18.11.11, 19.11.14 and 25.11.4 even when applied alone. The TLDK fork calls rte_pktmbuf_dynamic_pool_create, which the current LTS lacks. An upgrade needs a TLDK port. The LLVM build selected only sys/queue.h from its declared GNU sysroot. Its 19,539 bytes matched the supplier’s header.

The tested musl port keeps the DPDK stack trace available across the Go-to-C boundary. #15153 moved the optional plugin build into its external repository. The revision defines the same TestDumpStack there, supplies the two Go sources to its build sandbox, and runs it from make plugin-network-tests. The source files and both vendor patches match the approved revision byte for byte. TestDumpStack passed through Bazel on native AMD64 with GNU and musl. The default build excludes the plugin.

In a separate musl link comparison at f28370914, the plugin runsc binary linked. The plugin Sentry stopped at the systrap stub link rule tracked by #17067. The successful TCP and UDP guest tests at b317c6e36 used static GNU libc.

On the reviewed stub changes, all 10 AMD64 and 11 ARM64 offsets matched their ELF symbols and the musl CLI linked. The Sentry then stopped in the old //vdso:vdso rule when /bin/ld could not emit AArch64. This optional plugin port remains under investigation. Alpine packages sys/queue.h in bsd-compat-headers, separately from musl-dev.

The declared LLVM compiler built and installed static AMD64 runsc and plugin Sentry binaries through make runsc-plugin-stack and make refresh. The installed plugin initialized and exchanged TCP and UDP payloads across the bridge. Both architectures’ vDSOs linked. The test ran once on AMD64 with no skips. The workflow’s final XML-copy step failed on an omitted size field after the test passed. The repaired exporter recovered the exact 85-byte XML and rejected all four size and digest mismatches.

Make ran TestDumpStack uncached on Linux AMD64. With the same musl target in both flag orders, Bazel 9.3.1 selected the caller’s scratch_build_amd64 worker for the test, Go link and archive. These mixed-worker checks ran analysis only. Bazel 8.8.1 rejects the inherited test execution group when it loads the optional plugin package.

The in-tree AMD64 plugin compile and network-test jobs both invoke Make. Its Bazel command runs the client installed by the default builder from the repository pin, 9.3.1. No in-tree plugin job selects Bazel 8.8.1. Explicitly loading the optional plugin package on proposed source 8aaa1cb43 with Bazel 8.8.1 did crash with a duplicate test execution group. Whether downstream callers require that client remains unknown.

The pinned alipay/tldk revision cec8ff773 is the head of main. The repository advertises no tags, and its two other branch heads, 84493034e and 78c896b3b, are respectively two and six commits behind main. Updating to a newer published TLDK release cannot supply the missing DPDK port. The plugin patch still applies only to the tested DPDK 18.11 base.

followup.disposition: Native execution and mixed-worker selection verified on Bazel 9.3.1. Bazel 8.8.1 cannot load the optional test rule.
followup.nextAction: Keep the optional port on hold. Establish downstream requirements for Bazel 8.8.1 before changing compatibility, and assess the TLDK source changes needed for newer DPDK. The in-tree plugin jobs select 9.3.1. The ordinary compiler migration is independent.

nodes.title: Reproduce slow Reno recovery after burst loss
nodes.summary:
Switching master 975fb1722 to CUBIC completed all five 512 KiB transfers in the reporter’s M003 replay in 312–339 ms. Each run dropped the same 24 first transmissions. None reached a retransmission timeout. Stock Reno stalled in three of five runs, while #16495 recovered all five after one timeout each.

On the M003 Reno replay after #15785, three of five burst-loss transfers on master 975fb1722 stopped at byte 134,684. Two of five stopped at the same byte on 451b92800, before the tail-loss probe timeout floor. Each stalled transfer reached the 35 s deadline with seven retransmission timeouts. With the public #16495 fix (ffac28a03) replayed on that master as 766bc97e9, all five delivered the complete 524,288-byte payload in 0.651–0.787 s with one timeout each. All three no-loss controls verified the payload.

Earlier replay: On 14e1d0324, three of five Reno M003 transfers stalled at byte 134,684 of 524,288 through the 35 s deadline. Two finished. With #16495, all five finished in 0.648–1.211 s and preserved the payload hash. Both no-loss controls passed. The stock result on 597f36270 was five stalls in five runs. The reporter confirmed that their separate FreeBSD connection used Tailscale 1.80.0 without TCP timestamps. Its internal recovery sequence remains unknown.

Earlier Reno/CUBIC comparison: With the public recovery fix, Reno finished all four burst-loss transfers in 0.653–0.782 s. On its parent Reno stalled three times at 134,684 of 524,288 bytes (35-second deadline); the fourth transfer finished in 2.092 s. CUBIC completed all four on each source (0.288–0.325 s) and all four no-loss controls passed. These are the same reporter-supplied program and worker, with the four combinations run in balanced order. A separate replay on the FreeBSD router’s Tailscale 1.80.0 gVisor pin also stalled with RACK on and completed with RACK off. The review guide records which configuration each fix was tested on.

LGTM. This is a small, test-only change that does what it says:

1. The `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE` drop is the right fix for `TestCreateController`. `generic_permission()` would otherwise let a privileged worker create the subdirectory under the 0555 parent. The only cleanups that run afterwards are owner-permitted `chmod` and `RemoveAll`, so they keep working.

3. I checked the remaining `runsc/cgroup` tests, and none of them need a host cgroup mount or D-Bus, so removing `local` looks safe.
4. Optional nit: mention in the package doc that importing `capabilitytest` locks main to the initial thread through `init()`.

The PR merges cleanly into current master.

The PR is based on a recent master and neither touched file has changed since, so I expect no conflicts.

settledReviews.head: c2a9426436643ee79e60d34a4e3b6bf4a88decce
settledReviews.title: Build runsc and Sentry coverage binaries with rules_go
settledReviews.body:
The coverage genrules fetch two Go distributions, rebuild the toolchain
to disable cmd/go's internal-import check, and fetch modules during the
build. None of those downloads are inputs to the action. A change to a
Go package also makes the coverage target rebuild the entire SDK.

KCOV reads Go's internal coverage data because the Sentry must decode
it in process [1]. Build the coverage variants with the same declared
SDK and dependencies as runsc and Sentry. rules_go invokes the compiler
directly and uses atomic counters, so KCOV needs no modified SDK.
All four binaries built from runsc/main.go share its direct imports.

Keep the existing package exclusions. Disable cgo in ordinary coverage
binaries so they run in a minimal mount namespace, and retain race
detection and lock checking in the race variants.

[1]: https://github.com/golang/go/issues/76098

settledReviews.head: c329a6e31a5968a410831950c8a457ee243384c8
settledReviews.title: Build the runsc sidecars with the C toolchain
settledReviews.body:
Proposed PR description:

The FD parker, proc unmounter, and sentry prewarmer each compile and link a C file through a shell genrule. Give Bazel the source and link options directly so it can run the compiler and linker as separate actions without an intervening shell.

Use one rule for the three executables. Each provides its own entry point and needs no runtime libraries. Keep the public target names and filenames: the release installs the sidecars beside runsc in gvisor-bin/, and the sidecar tests use those paths to find them in the build tree.

Do not inherit an allocator, sanitizer runtime, or hosted linker features when building these syscall-only executables. Expose freestanding_executable through the build adapter in //tools:defs.bzl. Its transition clears --custom_malloc and removes sanitizer features and sanitizer link options.

Mark the inner cc_binary manual so wildcard builds select the public wrapper and reach the binary through that transition.

settledReviews.head: 1dbbcd6767ab1362d3ec9a7739d3a34aceb8bb2d
d6786915fa60f2dc04fc6969fc8ebf3274b39328
settledReviews.title: Initialize the FIFO writer generation in the shared pipe constructor
settledReviews.summary:
Publish the conflict repair and request fresh review from Lucas? The seven original FIFO cases passed on Linux and both gVisor filesystem modes. Four pipe tests and the production and test analyzers also passed.

git -C ~/code/gvisor range-diff 1dbbcd676^! d6786915f^!
settledReviews.body:
A writer opens and closes a FIFO while one reader holds it open. A
second nonblocking reader then opens the same FIFO. Linux reports
POLLHUP to the first reader only; gVisor remembers that the pipe once
had a writer and reports POLLHUP to both.

Record the writer generation when a nonblocking reader opens a FIFO
without a writer. If the last writer has closed, report POLLHUP only
when that generation has changed, as Linux does [1][2]. Once another
writer opens and closes, both readers see the hangup.

A nonblocking writer that finds no readers returns ENXIO without
advancing the generation [3]. Otherwise a writer that never opened
could cause a concurrent reader to report a hangup.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/fs/pipe.c#L1156-L1164
[2]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/fs/pipe.c#L686-L691
[3]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/fs/pipe.c#L1172-L1181

LGTM. Retaining only `readOnly` on `awaitingMountContext` after `FSCONFIG_CMD_CREATE` drops the already-consumed (and unsavable) `vfs.GetFilesystemOptions`, and marking `reconfParamsContext` and `mountfd.Fd` as `+stateify savable` cleanly enables checkpoint/restore across `mount_fd_test`.

**Security:** Modifies checkpoint/restore state for `fsconfigfd` and `mountfd` descriptors without altering capability checks, mount flag enforcement, reference lifetimes, or host boundaries, and eliminates a checkpoint-time panic when those descriptors are open.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-By: Claude

Re-verified at 5c76963. The only change since 0aa163b is a rebase onto #15513 that moves the `{ReadOnly: readOnly}` substitution from `GetFilesystem` into the new `PeekFilesystem`, so `fsmount(2)` options, including the `MountTooRevealing` input, match master.

**Security:** `MountTooRevealing` gets the same `ReadOnly` value as on master, and the `lockReadOnly` it sets still reaches the new mount. No permission checks changed.

nodes.summary:
One Bazel target stages a Debian package and two tarballs for each architecture. The revision maps generated-source filenames in the stamped release profile so a direct build and the staging target embed the same names. Ordinary developer builds keep their configured source paths.

Twelve fresh package actions ran on native workers for their target architecture. The AMD64 CLI printed release-20261106.0. A separate check found that netgofer in those packages still reported (devel). The version prerequisite now sets the same label on both programs; both native architectures passed the matching and mismatching release checks.

The release line tables use bazel-out/cfg/bin for generated files. Reading those files required the matching configured output directory. Debugger source substitution has not been tested.

contributorReview.head: 1824f3ee0a9e500491535331312ac08fe8da5004
contributorReview.title: Stage both release architectures with Bazel
contributorReview.body:
The release job builds each architecture separately, copies files into
a staging directory, then extracts the compressed tarballs to identify
the architecture again when signing them.

Build the two Debian packages and four tarballs with one command:
bazel build //debian:release-artifacts. Keep each architecture's files
together so the publisher can select the destination from the path.
Require all six files before signing. A caller with a prebuilt set
can sign it without starting Bazel.

Map output paths in the release_version profile. Go records generated
source filenames in the executable, and the architecture transition
otherwise adds a configuration suffix that a direct build does not use.
Keep physical generated-source paths available to ordinary debug builds.

nodes.head: 00aaa82b9e9cda8dc25dbe1df6e07a56c68302c5
nodes.title: Review the TCP recovery flight estimate
nodes.summary: On the exact PR, four live repairs were missed and five more left cwnd five with nine outstanding. A common-send-path fork counted the four, emitted one and preserved repair progress. The combined sender removed those four copies when RACK marked them lost again.

settledReviews.head: 00aaa82b9e9cda8dc25dbe1df6e07a56c68302c5
settledReviews.body:
After RACK marks #2 lost, retransmitting it clears `s1.lost`. This
branch then counts #2 once, and the `HighRxt` branch below counts it a
second time. In this PR’s tail-loss test, the ACK of #1 opens a
five-packet window, but [only #2–#5 are sent](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/e771617b-851e-4019-a76e-f73015f02f74).
[Omitting the second count](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/e3b6733c-2ae1-4ac3-a4a8-93f4a7b9a126)
lets #6 go as well, with GSO both on and off.

Can the flight estimate distinguish a **lost original** from an
**unacknowledged tail probe** whose original might still arrive? The
[probe case](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/4a34011d-e824-431a-a00b-a35326e809ef)
has the opposite error: four transmissions are outstanding at a window
of 11, yet the next write sends eight new packets rather than seven.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

settledReviews.head: 00aaa82b9e9cda8dc25dbe1df6e07a56c68302c5
settledReviews.body:
The two RACK changes release a reproducible stall. The combined
#15634 and #16738 sender counted 44 RACK-lost tail packets against
a congestion window of five. With your changes it sent the short
repair and four more on the first ACK [1].

On your exact head, the next ACK covered only that short repair.
The four other repairs were still unacknowledged, and RACK had not
marked them lost. SetPipe counted none of them. The earlier SACKs
still classified their sequence ranges as lost, and HighRxt stopped
at the short repair. Sending five more left nine outstanding with a
window of five. Updating HighRxt only in the RACK loop gave the same
result because the ordinary send loop also repairs from writeNext
after a timeout [2].

A small fork change records the last byte actually retransmitted in
the common send path and excludes a retransmission once RACK marks it
lost again. On both your head and the combined sender the short ACK
then released one repair. When the peer acknowledged only that later
repair, the combined sender marked the four earlier repairs lost and
resent them. Your head retained the four that RACK still considered
in flight [3] [4]. RFC 6675 also advances the high-water mark on
ordinary recovery retransmissions. Linux separately tracks copies
retransmitted after loss [5] [6].

Could you rebase the RACK changes and cover both sides of that ACK?
Master already advances writeNext after an RTO retransmission. #15634
also preserves the clone's delivery and loss state. Please keep the
case where the original and its probe might both be in flight [7].
The full-transfer control did not reproduce the long stall, so it
doesn't establish a throughput effect [8].

[1]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41108811393/artifacts/13002067553
[2]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41111079975/artifacts/13004156935
[3]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/compare/00aaa82b9...a1da0f98e
[4]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41112566996/artifacts/13006150199
[5]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6675.html#section-5
[6]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/7d0a66e4b/net/ipv4/tcp_input.c#L1320-L1342
[7]: https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15432#discussion_r4416541513
[8]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41104025638/artifacts/13000928053

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

nodes.title: Review LoadValue callback snapshots
nodes.summary: Posted the LoadValue callback aliasing regression inline on the reviewed PR head.

settledReviews.head: 573f6bb9c2b6701af0270b33b55b7035a4abb55b
settledReviews.body:
@parth-opensrc, this boxes the caller’s destination by reference. After
`Load` returns, assigning to the field can change a scalar the callback
already received:

```go
src.LoadValue(0, &x.n, func(v any) { x.saved = v }) // uint64(11)
// After Load returns:
x.n = 22
```

The [matched test](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/blob/dcaa864e7/pkg/state/graph_loadvalue_snapshot_test.go#L42)
kept `x.saved` at 11 with the legacy reader but observed 22 with the
graph reader. A typed copy inside the callback stayed 11 with both.
[Original run](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/858adf22-8ee6-4cd3-967c-ba4b5a5d40f9).

Could ordinary `LoadValue` snapshot the value when it calls the
callback? [This prototype](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/5c28e8d33)
[keeps 11 with both readers](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/6fc0d435-5595-4817-a6c1-52f1f64c8dd4).
I found no direct in-tree caller; stateify uses the separate
`LoadValueTo` API.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

nodes.head: 1702e63c4673bf8c00df82a1613c2359895fbe20
nodes.summary:
The stock tar writer starts with #!/usr/bin/env bash. Its first release action failed on the shell-free AMD64 worker. With a native rules_python launcher and static CPython, the existing rules_pkg tar actions produced both architecture archives and all nine executable inputs matched on each. A native ARM64 runner booted its installed Sentry.

The supplier prototype also started py_binary and py_test with relocated runfiles and a manifest. Bazel 7 WORKSPACE users need the launcher repository registered through py_repositories. The prototype starts CPython twice to prepare interpreter options. On the conventional AMD64 host, a trivial program took 36.55 ms with the prototype and 33.25 ms with the stock launcher (20 paired samples).

contributorReview.head: 488b298b86176fbb4dd442b9b3c54d4ecfbcc935
contributorReview.title: Remove overlay waiters from their original file
contributorReview.body:
A mutable overlay file description can switch from its lower file to its upper file after copy-up. A waiter registered before the switch still belongs to the lower file. Removing it from the current upper file leaves it receiving notifications after cancellation.

Keep the lower reference until its last registration is removed. Track which entries belong to the upper file only while the two sets of registrations overlap. This preserves the backing file across nested overlays and same-version checkpoint and restore.

settledReviews.head: ed3f77eb2dc84b35f85083caac2acea26e682444
settledReviews.body:
A dual-stack wildcard bind reserves the port for IPv4 and IPv6. Connecting to a mapped peer sets `effectiveNetProtos` to IPv4 and releases the IPv4 reservation. Cleanup then misses the remaining IPv6 reservation. Could it release the family the endpoint still owns?

[This syscall test](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/blob/1d322cb0b/test/syscalls/linux/socket_inet_loopback.cc#L263-L323) closes the connection with a reset and rebinds the same port. [Linux accepts both wildcard binds](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/0df634cb-62b9-46b0-ba07-8c04ed3142f0). [On this head](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/992daf38-8b09-46ad-8003-cac6bbf8e5f2), the IPv4 bind succeeds, but the IPv6-only bind returns `EADDRINUSE`.

Review by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

followup.disposition: Merged through export #16989. A separate test suggestion remains on closed export #16775.
followup.nextAction: The export comment suggests additional restore cases and asks about cross-version support. The original author can consider that follow-up. The comment did not request a review from Tamir.

nodes.head: b9d613ad6ba7e5bd73b88ca498bf3ecf7f13c699
nodes.title: Add an opt-in native POSIX test wrapper
nodes.summary:
Dmitry Zbarsky’s open PR adds an opt-in native POSIX test wrapper. Its head b9d613ad6 conflicts with Bazel master a765dc177 in the coverage resolver and the wrapper test’s filesystem dependency. Tamir’s fork at aa90c0a75 preserves the upstream conditional coverage behavior and the filesystem header used by the new POSIX tests. The prepared revision applies to the inspected master source. A current-master build and the maintainers’ cross-compilation concern remain open. On gVisor’s ordinary Ubuntu worker, Bazel 9.3.1’s shell wrapper failed two otherwise successful TCP handshake tests when the qualification requested ZIP artifacts. The host lacked file and zip. The default unzipped mode retains individual files, but its wrapper still invokes file to collect MIME metadata.

Across 164 PacketImpact manifests, stock Bazel 9.3.1 put a file-type error in all 424 MIME fields. In an AMD64 Linux sandbox with file blocked, the archived static wrapper wrote application/octet-stream for two PCAPs and a Go log containing control bytes, and text/plain for an ASCII manifest. It preserved a filename containing a space and a literal %. The outer stock Bazel wrapper still reported its own file error.

followup.nextAction: Follow the author’s revision of #30837 and the maintainers’ decision about prebuilt wrappers for cross-platform executors.

nodes.title: GC: Suspend Go GC during boot, checkpoint, and restore.
nodes.summary:
Parent 706b124a2 and c31b2adc2 each restored the same parent checkpoint and verified all 100,000 tmpfs files. With a sibling holding 760 MiB under a shared 1 GiB limit, the OOM killer killed the sibling on both revisions. Both restore processes survived and completed verification. The two unpressured baselines had zero OOM kills. Each configuration ran once.

The 36 measured one-CPU restores on each build reached the first verified read in 670.0 ms on the parent, 554.0 ms with #16134 alone and 547.9 ms on this PR. Benchstat found no difference between the PR and #16134 on this workload (p=0.750).

On c31b2adc2, saving 100,000 empty tmpfs files took 3.98% longer than on its parent 706b124a2. Time through Sentry exit increased 3.64% and peak sampled Sentry RSS increased 1.33%. Each revision ran one warmup and 12 measured saves on native AMD64 with systrap, four CPUs, a 2 GiB limit, and uncompressed graph checkpoints. All 26 checkpoints restored the full tree with zero OOM kills. The earlier 30.12% RSS increase was measured on a48b7a12c against its own parent.

settledReviews.head: 5068ecb10e0ca383cc00791cc4a655b7a90a626f
settledReviews.body:
On the call to gccontrol.Suspend in SuspendGCForRestore:

@parth-opensrc, this uses the limit from sandbox creation. If the user lowers the limit before restore, the kernel enforces the new value but GC still budgets against the old one.

I saved the existing 50,000-file workload under 2 GiB in both cases and restored it with memory.max at 200 MiB. Creating the restore sandbox at 200 MiB gave Go a 99.93 MiB limit and restore succeeded. Creating it at 2 GiB and lowering it with Container.Update before Restore gave Go a 1,023 MiB limit. The restore RPC returned EOF and memory.events recorded one OOM kill, versus zero in the control. The [test output and cgroup counters](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41285846799/artifacts/13075252336) are from the same run.

On the earlier revision, [reading the limit when the host sends Restore](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/07696b6af) let [both restores finish](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41235711507/artifacts/13055496610) with a Go limit of about 99 MiB and no OOM kills. Could Sandbox.Restore and Sandbox.Checkpoint pass the current effective cgroup limit with the RPC? The guest /proc checkpoint starts SaveAsync inside the Sentry. When that path has no fresh host limit, it could keep ordinary GC enabled.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

On the read of memory.events in the restore test:

@parth-opensrc, on cgroup v2, MakePath takes a controller name and returns the cgroup directory regardless of that argument [1]. Both Stat calls here therefore succeed as long as the directory exists, even if memory.swap.max is missing. The failure diagnostic later tries to ReadFile the directory, too, so it drops the OOM counters when restore fails.

Could these use filepath.Join(probe.MakePath(""), "memory.max") (and similarly for memory.swap.max and memory.events)? That makes the optional swap check and the OOM report inspect the intended files. If skipping systems without the memory controller is required, Install can itself fail before these checks.

There is a second reason to read those counters on failure: with the 200 MiB cap applied during fixture setup, the [sentry was OOM-killed during Save](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41235498081/artifacts/13055292180) before this test reached Restore. The same happened with ordinary GC; on this worker the proposed policy declined to suspend anyway. Giving only the checkpoint writer 2 GiB let the restore assertion run against a real 200 MiB cap.

[1]: https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/5068ecb10/runsc/cgroup/cgroup_v2.go#L436

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

settledReviews.head: a48b7a12cb3bd615c48f9b36d353c02a6463a929
settledReviews.title: Share the graph checkpoint results with Parth
settledReviews.body:
@parth-opensrc, I tried a non-resuming checkpoint with the graph state engine, now the default on master. On 100,000 empty tmpfs files, the PR took longer to save and used more memory than its parent.

I used systrap on Linux/amd64, four CPUs, no sandbox CPU quota, a 2 GiB memory limit, and uncompressed checkpoints. Each column has 12 measured saves after one warmup, in balanced order. The columns are the parent (`0bbcbf9de`), the #16152 save-only reference (`79637cb45`), and this PR (`a48b7a12c`). Both deltas are relative to the parent.

```text
Save/checkpoint_ns                                               354.4m ± 2%                    360.2m ± 4%       ~ (p=0.143 n=12)                   366.8m ± 4%  +3.50% (p=0.020 n=12)
Save/checkpoint_exit_ns                                          426.7m ± 2%                    432.1m ± 3%       ~ (p=0.319 n=12)                   447.3m ± 4%  +4.81% (p=0.001 n=12)
Save/observed_save_exit_rss                                         427.1Mi ± 1%                   430.4Mi ± 0%       ~ (p=0.101 n=12)                 555.8Mi ± 0%  +30.12% (p=0.000 n=12)
```

The first two rows are time to checkpoint return and to Sentry exit (`m` = milliseconds). The last is peak sampled Sentry RSS over that interval. All 39 archives contained graph frames and restored all 100,000 files. [Full benchstat and results](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41802364888/artifacts/13309574814).

Which state engine and compression setting did your C4 `bigheap` runs use? That would let us compare the same save path across the two workloads.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

settledReviews.head: 8147e9ad3c95c67a0a9dd560f37aff9d7842f861
settledReviews.body:
Could you schedule the probe after accounting for the ACK? When two
segments are outstanding and the first is acknowledged, schedulePTO
still sees two. This guard preserves that timer for the lone remaining
segment. In the packet test the PR retransmits the last 10 bytes at
20 ms (twice the measured RTT) [1]. Moving the timer calculation below
ACK accounting sends those bytes at the 50 ms RTO and keeps the three
existing tests passing [2].

[1]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41140493959/artifacts/13018229764
[2]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/b0b469219

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Yes, arming a PTO on that ACK matches the Linux call order. The remaining difference is its deadline. On 32045814e the ACK ended SACK recovery with one newer segment outstanding and 20 ms left on the old retransmission timer. The probe retransmitted that segment 20 ms after the ACK.

Linux uses a full RTO from an advancing ACK [1]. Ignoring the old deadline on an advancing ACK [2] kept the wire quiet at 20 ms and sent the same 10-byte tail at 50 ms, exactly one RTO after the ACK. Both versions passed the four existing timer tests [3].

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/7d0a66e4b/net/ipv4/tcp_output.c#L3073-L3081
[2]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/114f689c8
[3]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41536170137/artifacts/13184662456

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

nodes.title: Forward new SYNs received in TCP TIME_WAIT
nodes.summary: The author applied the tested guard: an unexpected SYN-ACK and a repeated FIN are ACKed with the old sequence numbers in TIME_WAIT. Only a bare SYN may reopen through the forwarder. The revised tests also cover a forwarder that declines the connection.
