settledReviews.head: e503a89e87b363812834ccaa96eb503446490faa
settledReviews.body:
Could we keep the TIME_WAIT endpoint for this SYN-ACK? With these packet fields, Linux ACKs the SYN-ACK with the old connection’s sequence numbers. Repeating that connection’s last FIN gets the same ACK. On this head both packets get RSTs: the forwarder rejects the SYN-ACK, but by then the old endpoint is already gone.

Restricting TIME_WAIT reuse to a SYN without ACK or RST keeps both ACKs and still accepts a genuine reopening SYN. Here are the [packet traces](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41153077876/artifacts/13024367271), the [tested guard](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/compare/9a707824b...2bc369a8a), and [the corresponding Linux check](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/7d0a66e4b/net/ipv4/tcp_minisocks.c#L253).

I tried delivering the first SYN before draining the queue. The client still got `ECONNREFUSED`: the forwarder records the request before its goroutine registers an endpoint.

[This change](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/936ad90db) tries the registered endpoint first and, if there is none, offers the queued packet to the handler that accepted the opening SYN. Both the client and the forwarder completed the handshake. The single-SYN and declined-SYN cases still passed. I’d limit the fallback to this unlocked path because [outgoing port reuse](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/ed8a800c0/pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/endpoint.go#L2419-L2434) drains the same queue while holding two endpoint locks. [Packet traces](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41588109156/artifacts/13208872158).

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

nodes.title: Loopback TCP panic after restoring a GKE pod snapshot
nodes.summary: Posted the approved request for GKE to map the checkpoint writer and restore builds to the timer and RNG fixes. The reporter confirmed one recurring client port across successive checkpoints of the same sandbox; the other affected sandbox used a different port. The July test covered live connections on the same tuple, but neither checkpoint contained a server-side TIME_WAIT connection. The Unix socket workaround stopped the reported TCP panic. settledReviews.body:
@SecretSun, I wouldn’t change `--allow-connected-on-save` for the 127.0.0.1:8081 connection. In [the July source you identified](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/9f653e577/pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/endpoint_state.go#L48-L67), TCP only marks a connection for termination if the route lacks save/restore support. The [loopback device advertises that support](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/9f653e577/pkg/tcpip/link/loopback/loopback.go#L83-L85).

I [tested the public July 21 release](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41168603665/artifacts/13030331016) without that flag. I checkpointed and restored twice with a connection from port 43425 already accepted on port 8081 and another connection still in the accept queue. Both exchanged bytes after each restore, and a fresh connection from 43425 reached the listener. That didn’t reproduce the panic.

For the checkpoint crash, a TIME_WAIT timer can remove a connection from the demuxer. July didn’t wait for those callbacks before serializing the kernel; [2337c1f9f](https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/2337c1f9f) made it wait. The August 31 release you tested includes the fix. Can someone on the GKE side confirm whether the failing build includes it? We don’t know which map was being written.

For the nil endpoint, do the other crashes from the same checkpoint show the same client port, or a small set of recurring ports? [Lookup tries an exact connection before the listener](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/9f653e577/pkg/tcpip/stack/transport_demuxer.go#L77-L108). The source ports would help distinguish a stale connection entry from a problem with the listener itself.

settledReviews.head: 63d3761ddffe329a13d142d91dd61cceeec76fcd
settledReviews.body:
@EtiennePerot, @milantracy: I tried `POSIX_FADV_WILLNEED` on the local
state file with the existing reader. On a cold checkpoint it saved about
3% of kernel load time in paired rounds; buffering saved 41%. Here are
the cold rows from [benchstat][1] (milliseconds, 18 restores per column):

```
             │    direct    │               advice                │                buffer                │
             │ kernel-ms/op │ kernel-ms/op  vs base               │ kernel-ms/op  vs base                │
Restore/cold     777.3 ± 4%     751.0 ± 3%       ~ (p=0.091 n=18)     450.5 ± 3%  -42.04% (p=0.000 n=18)

             │   direct   │              advice               │               buffer               │
             │ cli-ms/op  │ cli-ms/op   vs base               │ cli-ms/op   vs base                │
Restore/cold   809.4 ± 4%   784.1 ± 2%       ~ (p=0.091 n=18)   489.2 ± 3%  -39.56% (p=0.000 n=18)
```

With all three input files **warm**, benchstat didn't distinguish the
readers. Comparing buffered with direct *within each round*, though,
the restore command was slower in 15 of 18 rounds: median +2.2%
(95% interval +0.3% to +5.0%). The kernel-load difference was less
clear: +1.3% (−0.6% to +4.9%). This is consistent with the hot CLI
regression in the PR; it doesn't establish a hot kernel-load regression.

The [108 restores][2] used the [same executable][3] on one 4-vCPU
Linux worker, in balanced order, with a 12.2 MiB state file and a
513 MiB pages file. CLI time ends when the background restore command
returns. Memory and pipe contents were checked afterward.

I also tried the six requested OCI quotas on a listening four-worker
Nginx. Each quota had its own checkpoint, and all three readers restored
the same bytes within each quota. Here are the medians of the six
paired percentage changes for buffering versus direct reads. HTTP
time runs from starting restore through the first verified 1 KiB
response to a guest `curl` launched with `runsc exec`.

| Application CPU quota | Cold kernel load | Cold first HTTP | Warm first HTTP |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.25 | +0.2% | +7.9% | +3.0% |
| 1 | −2.2% | +0.2% | −0.4% |
| 2 | −3.4% | +1.3% | +0.4% |
| 4 | −8.8% | −1.1% | +0.7% |
| 16 | −9.4% | −1.4% | −3.0% |
| Uncapped (19 CPUs) | −9.7% | −1.0% | −0.7% |

Buffering shortened cold kernel load in all six pairs at both 4 and
16 CPUs. It reached the first HTTP response sooner in three and four
of those pairs, respectively. Across the 72 pairs, buffering reached
HTTP sooner in 33 and WILLNEED in 36. At 0.25 CPU, five of six cold
buffered restores reached HTTP later. Individual differences ranged
from −19% to +20%. All 216 restores served the expected bytes on the
first request and on a subsequent 16-request burst. [Quota results][4]

The Nginx state files were only 301–343 kB. The buffered reader used
two 512 KiB chunks, so the whole state file fit in its first data read.
This sweep cannot choose a queue depth for larger files. It used the
default creation and lifecycle CPU policies. The background reader
uses the application CPU count, and the test verified each sandbox’s
application quota after restore. [Reader sizing][5] · [CPU policies][6]

Posted on behalf of @tamird.

[2]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41186223756/artifacts/13037505941
[3]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/d3066814d
[4]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41297735728/artifacts/13080207857

settledReviews.head: 3d868e9c6466e4fdca0c5ee3ef151b34baed485a
settledReviews.title: Retry promptly when a TCP ACK contradicts an earlier SACK
settledReviews.body:
A receiver under memory pressure can discard data it previously
reported receiving. If its cumulative ACK stops inside a packet that
it selectively acknowledged in full, waiting for the retransmission
timeout can delay recovery. A SACK for only the tail of that packet
does not establish the same contradiction.

Give the receiver half a round trip (at least 10 ms) to advance its
ACK before retransmitting, as Linux does [1]. Keep enough of the
reported range to distinguish a whole transmission from a suffix as
ACKs advance. Check the original packet and any shorter retransmission
during the existing walk that updates SACK credit.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/net/ipv4/tcp_input.c#L2247-L2256
settledReviews.note: Tamir approved submission after #15634.

followup.disposition: Tamir approved submission after #15634. The live restore under that prerequisite checked repeated SACKs and genuine reordering. The whole-packet and suffix-only timer measurements used live connections without a restore.

contributorReview.head: 49d0bc55abb2e09059cb18d87eebf60f72caa12a
contributorReview.title: Let Bazel cache and remotely execute the Gazelle check
contributorReview.summary: Review the motivation for running Gazelle as a Bazel build action and the direct Bazel command for applying reported diffs.
contributorReview.body:
Presubmit checks whether the Go sources and their BUILD files agree.
With bazel run, Bazel builds the launcher, but the launcher scans the
checkout on the CI runner every time. A change outside the packages
managed by Gazelle still pays for the scan, and a remote worker cannot
run it on the runner's behalf.

Run Gazelle in diff mode as a build action. Its inputs include files
matched by go:embed and BUILD files containing inherited directives, so
a change to either invalidates the result. Share the package list, flags
and repository map with the fixer so that bazel run //:gazelle_fix
applies the reported diff.

three. With timestamps, the server can send 128 bytes before its next

contributorReview.head: c53942792678277f0195068aa41ad17620dd9dd1
contributorReview.title: hostinet: skip the TCP linger wait on task exit
contributorReview.summary: Open the host-network fix after #16787 lands with the shared process-exit syscall fixture?
contributorReview.body:
A guest exiting with the last reference to a TCP socket can wait out
its entire SO_LINGER timeout. Linux skips that wait when the closing
task is exiting [1]. With host networking the sentry thread closes the
socket on the guest's behalf and the host sees a running task.

Disable positive linger before the last host close on task exit. Keep
zero linger enabled so a peer still receives the requested reset [2].
The process-exit syscall test checks both cases with host networking.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/net/ipv4/af_inet.c#L426-L437
[2]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/net/ipv4/tcp.c#L3095-L3101

settledReviews.head: 858aa5b72f7172309231b6352886973414c28f44
settledReviews.title: Test SACK on a connection accepted with a SYN cookie
settledReviews.body:
Queue three bytes in the order a, c, b on an accepted cookie connection. Linux and gVisor acknowledge 1, 1, then 3 bytes. When the peer negotiated SACK and timestamps, the middle ACK also reports the received interval [2,3). Omitting either option suppresses the block. Clearing SACK only on the accepted socket breaks that assertion even though the SYN-ACK still advertised it.

The ordinary handshakes and the stack-wide SACK-disabled cases stay in the Go suite. This test and the separate peer-window test apply in either order.

nodes.summary: Checklocks can verify the mutex at a semaphore lookup. settledReviews.head: b68f40e4e358798ba034116cdb4c8194bb1c7c07
settledReviews.title: Check the mutex protecting semaphore waiters
settledReviews.body: All three callers already hold the set mutex. Both architecture analyzers passed. Releasing the mutex around the SETVAL call made checklocks diagnose the missing lock on each architecture.
settledReviews.note: Tamir asked to annotate sem.waiters and suggested giving sem a pointer to its owner’s mutex to keep the change small.

settledReviews.head: 9385a07c9a80422e092a786b68303b1686102095
settledReviews.title: Check the set lock when accessing SysV semaphores
settledReviews.body:
Waking a waiter reads the semaphore value and removes the waiter from
its queue. Direct access to those elements previously went unchecked
because checklocks could not associate each sem with its owning set.

Guard the existing slice with the set mutex and require the lock to
look up a member or wake its waiters. Size can read the length without
the lock because a semaphore set cannot be resized.
settledReviews.note: Retain sem.wakeWaiters() without a second lookup; give the semaphore a link to its protecting lock.

settledReviews.head: 8d8a461be1c6d2cfa6a7594a39f0f1d1715c0557
settledReviews.title: Check the set lock when accessing SysV semaphores
settledReviews.body:
Waking a waiter reads the semaphore value and removes the waiter from
its queue. Guard the slice with the set mutex and require that mutex
when waking waiters. Callers pass the set whose lock they hold and
reuse the semaphore they just updated.

Size only reads the length of the slice. That length is fixed when the
set is created, so callers can read it without the mutex.
settledReviews.summary: May I open this change once #16806 merges? Each caller passes its locked Set to the member’s wake method. SetVal reuses the member it already looked up, and each semaphore keeps its existing fields. Checklocks on AMD64 and ARM64 caught unlocked indexed access to waiters and value, and a wake after unlock. Both writes through previously saved pointers escaped the analyzer. The caller must supply the Set that owns the member. All four native Linux package tests passed, including TestUnregister.
settledReviews.note: Tamir asked whether checklocks should express that a returned reference remains valid only while the lock is held.

followup.disposition: The semaphore proposal remains on hold. The experimental checker flags both a correctly owned wake and a wake using the wrong set.
followup.nextAction: Determine how checklocks can follow the owning mutex through derived pointers and account for whether a called method releases the mutex or retains the pointer.

settledReviews.head: 6e1f1e7005d85fa0e2f04d75c530abf1ba384490
settledReviews.title: tcp: report hangups when a stream closes
settledReviews.body:
An application can wait for EPOLLRDHUP without requesting EPOLLIN. If
the peer sent FIN, that wait timed out on gVisor. A socket shut down
locally for reading likewise appeared open until a poll for readable
data updated the cached receive state. Closing both directions then
hid the read hangup and did not report POLLHUP.

Read the receive queue's closed flag directly. Once the local endpoint
has queued FIN, a closed receive queue also means both directions have
shut down. Linux reports POLLRDHUP for the first condition and POLLHUP
for the second [1].

Processing a peer FIN takes a socket out of ESTABLISHED before closing
the receive queue. Skip the queue lock for EPOLLRDHUP on an established
socket without a local read shutdown request. Check the queue if there
was a request since it may have failed before connect.

Wake read-hangup waiters on a peer FIN or local read shutdown, and wake
hangup waiters when the second direction closes. Exercise both paths on
IPv4 and IPv6, including the EPOLLRDHUP-only watch from #6015 and a
watch that requests no events when SHUT_RDWR leaves data unread.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/net/ipv4/tcp.c#L558-L562
settledReviews.note: Contributor approved 6e1f1e700 for submission after both #16808 and #17123 merge.

settledReviews.head: 6f070847add9ac9bf0d19c96dee873e84f9594d9
settledReviews.title: Ask Stephan to cherry-pick the resolver and C unwinder fixes
settledReviews.body:
@geligeli, could you cherry-pick these two fixes onto `glibc-static` in order?

1. Go’s cgo DNS resolver links with `-lresolv`. The static sysroot needs `libresolv.a` for that link. Its 19 archive members and 61 defined symbols match glibc 2.44 on AMD64 and ARM64. [Resolver commit](https://github.com/tamird/hermetic-llvm/commit/d779c2896) · [Reference builds](https://github.com/tamird/hermetic-llvm/actions/runs/42125450746)
2. A static C program that calls `pthread_cancel` still fails to link without the C++ runtime archives. glibc needs eight `_Unwind_*` symbols. With the LLVM unwinder on the C link, the native AMD64 test joins the canceled thread and observes `PTHREAD_CANCELED`. The ARM64 archive also defines all eight symbols. [Unwinder commit](https://github.com/tamird/hermetic-llvm/commit/1273f916b) · [Failing link](https://github.com/tamird/hermetic-llvm/actions/runs/42157263660) · [Native test](https://github.com/tamird/hermetic-llvm/actions/runs/42158767867)

settledReviews.head: c16f3c5e55d1740154b7ddfa0300ef0dff0202ce
settledReviews.body:
Can a second TCP read that still gets EAGAIN go through the normal wait/deadline path? `recvClosed` stays set across `connect(AF_UNSPEC)`. I called `shutdown(SHUT_RD)` on a fresh TCP socket (ENOTCONN), disconnected with AF_UNSPEC, then connected to a listener. With the peer open and no data queued, Linux waited for the 150 ms receive timeout and returned EAGAIN; this change returned EOF immediately. Both subsequently received the peer’s byte. Without the disconnect, Linux and this change both correctly returned EOF.

On TCP, the second host read already returns zero for a real read shutdown. That leaves the synthetic EOF for datagram sockets, without clearing the flag on every connect. [Shared syscall test](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/blob/5f7d378a3/test/syscalls/linux/tcp_socket.cc#L230-L277) · [native IPv4/IPv6 and hostinet IPv4](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41327870699/artifacts/13092287012) · [hostinet IPv6](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41328486242/artifacts/13091944899).

Thanks, the stream path now handles the reconnect. Could we also exclude AF_PACKET from synthetic EOF? On a packet socket, shutdown(SHUT_RD) returns EOPNOTSUPP. With protocol 0 and a 150 ms receive timeout, Linux still waited and returned EAGAIN on both SOCK_DGRAM and SOCK_RAW. Hostinet returned EOF in 92 and 87 µs respectively. Both timed out normally before shutdown.

[Shared syscall test](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/blob/c72e091cd/test/syscalls/linux/packet_socket.cc#L97-L129) · [Linux and hostinet results](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41575061199/artifacts/13202768324).

settledReviews.head: 1165b33ea7500227832c74e5c82e0b7230d52a0f
settledReviews.body:
Could we check that the callback returns with the same locks it had on entry? With one element, a ContainsFunc predicate that unlocks e.mu and returns true leaves the following delete(e.entries, key) unguarded. checkFunction returns the callback’s exit state here, but the caller still treats e.mu as held.

Comparing lock identity and mode catches both the unlock and an exchange for another mutex. Unlocking and reacquiring e.mu inside the predicate still passes, as do the bound-method examples. [Tested change](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/a79d4bf1b) · [AMD64 and ARM64 analyzer results](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41340536537/artifacts/13098361016).

settledReviews.head: 0bf36f79214fa3be21b86435714026a0ed1b1c42
settledReviews.body:
`SortedFunc` runs the supplied iterator before it calls the comparator. In [this example](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/blob/0038cb10c/tools/checklocks/test/callbacks.go#L97-L109), the iterator unlocks `globalMu` and the comparator reads a field guarded by it. Checklocks accepts that read on this head. [AMD64 and ARM64 results](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41504589303/artifacts/13171655273)

I tried [inferring this from the helper body](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/75000d12b). A helper can call its predicate directly, or forward it to another helper with the same guarantee. If it can run unknown code first, the predicate doesn't inherit the caller's locks. That covers the original `slices.ContainsFunc` example and a helper in another package, and diagnoses the unprotected read here. [Analyzer results](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41507063340/artifacts/13171775780)

settledReviews.head: 1af4ae880239496a8470baaa16f34b131d4fe045
settledReviews.body:
The existing detector can miss a delayed original here. With RACK off, the first advancing ACK echoed the original packet’s timestamp (4294967290), which preceded the first repair (994). Because the timestamp wrapped, this branch didn’t run and `ssthresh` stayed at 2 packets instead of returning to 10.

The same thing happened without wrap after a second timeout cleared `retransmitTS`. Changing only the comparison then restored 10 for a genuine second repair. [Keeping the first repair’s timestamp for the whole recovery episode and comparing in serial order](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/compare/47d4d443c...1c3a16f77) distinguished the original from both repairs in [all eight packet traces](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41348536380/artifacts/13100039686). A separate detector fix would cover both cases for this response.

Review by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

nodes.head: 3c8aa1d51dcfb99a39d967c45046483cd42c561d
nodes.title: Retransmit the SYN-ACK when a peer repeats its SYN
nodes.summary:
When the client repeats its SYN, stock gVisor sends a bare ACK. Linux and the fix resend the SYN-ACK immediately. sendSyn now takes no arguments. It sets the passive SYN-ACK timestamp on a packet-local copy. Only retransmitSyn charges retries.

Linux and the approved 3c8aa1d51 revision passed the same four packet cases. The peer requested a retransmission 550 ms after its SYN. Linux replied after 2.3 ms and gVisor after 3.3 ms. Both waited one more second for the timed retry. All three handshake tests and both architecture analyzers also passed. The approved change is now open as #17206 at 1f50f4698 on the landed counter in master.

On the published 1f50f4698, the original TestRepeatedSynInSynRcvd passed uncached on a local AMD64 Linux Netstack TestRunner. It requires matching sequence and acknowledgment numbers on both SYN-ACKs before the same 500 ms deadline. After an immediate third SYN and completion of the handshake, the accepted socket reported exactly one retransmission. The original Go log and clean single-case XML agree.

settledReviews.head: 22d8cfc02a0c99c00fc9e9a97160d3dae8208b48
settledReviews.title: Retransmit the SYN-ACK when a peer repeats its SYN
settledReviews.body: When the client repeats its SYN before the retransmission timer fires, stock gVisor answers with a bare ACK. Linux and the fix reply immediately with the missing SYN-ACK, suppress a third immediate request, and report 1 ms RTT on the accepted socket. A prototype that reused the first local timestamp reported 1,553 ms. The final revision also matches Linux at the signed timestamp boundary.
settledReviews.note: Separate SYN retransmission accounting from sending the SYN.

settledReviews.head: 3c8aa1d51dcfb99a39d967c45046483cd42c561d
settledReviews.title: Retransmit the SYN-ACK when a peer repeats its SYN
settledReviews.body:
A passive TCP handshake answered a repeated SYN with a bare ACK. A
peer that missed the SYN-ACK then had to wait for the handshake timer
to retransmit it.

Resend the SYN-ACK for the original sequence number, subject to the
existing out-of-window response limit. A successful send restarts the
pending timer at its current interval and is charged to the accepted
socket. Give each passive retry its current transmit timestamp so the
final ACK can supply the initial RTT. This follows the Linux
request-socket path [1].

The packet test repeats the SYN before the initial timeout and checks
the sequence and acknowledgment numbers on the second SYN-ACK. A third
SYN immediately afterward leaves the accepted socket with one retry.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/net/ipv4/tcp_minisocks.c#L679-L719
settledReviews.summary: Open the revised passive SYN retry fix after #16809 lands? The four packet cases passed on native Linux and corrected gVisor.

settledReviews.head: 10f9a0f0d126d5fae773c18275bdaa8bc0ec3ae3
settledReviews.title: Unsandboxed GoStdlib actions include packages excluded from GoSDK.srcs
settledReviews.body:
An ordinary gVisor `//:release` build on Linux ARM64 used cached standard library archives containing `crypto/internal/sysrand/internal/seccomp`. The Go analyzer rejected that package because it was absent from the declared SDK sources. Four of the six cached `GoStdlib` outputs contained the same eight extra packages. Forcing fresh sandboxed stdlib actions let the release and its guest smoke test pass. The cache records do not identify how the original producers ran. [1]

On Linux AMD64, three fresh builds declared the same 5,931 SDK source paths. They used rules_go v0.63.0, Bazel 8.8.1 and Go 1.27.3, with race and cgo enabled. [2]

```
                               Archive packages   Listed packages
Sandboxed                                   370               370
Unsandboxed                                 378               384
Unsandboxed, declared sources only          370               370
```

Both builders recursively copy the physical SDK's `src` directory into a temporary GOROOT. That makes files excluded by the SDK rule, including `net/internal/socktest`, visible to `go install` and `go list` outside a filesystem sandbox. The archive tree and JSON list cover different sets of packages. Comparing each against its own sandboxed inventory gave an exact match after the change. [3]

Would you accept passing `GoSDK.srcs` to both builders and copying those files into the same relative paths under GOROOT? The proposal applies the tested production change to current master at f9689452c. Its package-list test leaves `net/internal/socktest` physically present in the SDK while omitting it from the source arguments. With rules_go as the root module, the original directory copy reported that package and the proposed builder omitted it. Both export modes passed on the proposal. [4] [5] [6]

[4]: https://github.com/tamird/rules_go/commit/10f9a0f0d
[5]: https://github.com/tamird/rules_go/actions/runs/41389254683/artifacts/13116369389

settledReviews.summary: Review the proposed Gazelle report. Opening a public tamird/bazel-gazelle fork would also allow the tested change to be prepared as a single upstream commit.
settledReviews.body:
Loading `def.bzl` reads `GO_ENV` at the top level. In a WORKSPACE build, `bazel query //:gazelle` fails if the Go repository configuration is unavailable, before Bazel can return the target label. With Bzlmod, building the ARM64 vDSO from gVisor’s LLVM integration as a downstream dependency evaluates a root-only go_deps override before compiling any C. [Query regression](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42348869753/artifacts/13564836743)

I propose reading the generated environment through a private label attribute on the Gazelle runner. In a prototype against Gazelle master, the query succeeded and the downstream vDSO linked. The runner scripts stayed byte-identical to their originals in both Bzlmod and WORKSPACE, including the precedence of per-target environment overrides. [Build and runner comparison](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42347782649/artifacts/13564785819)

Filed by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

settledReviews.head: 0c8fe8397654defd60ac60ff9eb59e3ba1a6deea
settledReviews.title: Report retransmitted segments in TCP_INFO
settledReviews.body:
A program reading tcpi_total_retrans always saw zero, even after its
peer withheld an acknowledgment and the socket retransmitted the same
data five times. Return the endpoint's cumulative retransmission count.

Charge a retransmitted GSO batch by its number of TCP segments. Count
an active SYN retry when TCP attempts it [1]. An accepted socket
inherits successful SYN-ACK retries [2][3]. The listener keeps its own
count.

Exercise the three lifetimes through getsockopt. Observe the active
socket in SYN-SENT, the passive socket after accept, and the data
socket after the retransmissions are acknowledged.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/net/ipv4/tcp_output.c#L3393-L3399
[2]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/net/ipv4/inet_connection_sock.c#L905-L912
[3]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/net/ipv4/tcp_minisocks.c#L549-L556

Upstream issue

settledReviews.body:
Yes. With Go 1.26.7 on linux/amd64, building `cmd/objdump` with an empty cache compiled 113 packages. After building `pack`, `covdata`, and the rules_go builder, it compiled 18. Both runs produced byte-identical executables. [Package lists](https://github.com/tamird/rules_go/actions/runs/41620131612/artifacts/13222458262)

I'd keep the executable rule either way. A reusable analyzer can depend on `objdump` without asking each consumer to configure its SDK, and a cross-compiled test can request `buildid` for its own platform. An SDK option could supply the host tool ahead of time. That would save those 95 compilations when the analyzer runs, but an ordinary Go build using that SDK would build `objdump` even if it never runs the analyzer. Would you prefer to include that option here?

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

settledReviews.head: 3f09760978f08d3dfba28a63885c0533f2b03a02
settledReviews.title: go_repository requires a host env executable on Bazel 8
settledReviews.body:
Gazelle prepends `env -i` to repository commands on Unix. On a Linux
client without `env` on PATH, even a command given by absolute path
fails. I reproduced this with Gazelle 0.51.3 and Bazel 8.8.1.

    env_execute(ctx, ["/fixture/printenv"], environment = overrides)

    "execvp(env, ...)": No such file or directory

Could Gazelle clear the environment with `repository_ctx.execute` on
Bazel 8 and newer? Setting an inherited variable to `None` removes it.
With this change, the child received an explicitly empty value and
inherited `TMPDIR`. The unrelated parent variable was absent. Bazel 7 could keep using `env -i`.

[Repository rule](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/blob/999b71a83/.github/qualification/gazelle-native-minimum.py) · [Bazel 8 API](https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/blob/c8217fdd2/src/main/java/com/google/devtools/build/lib/bazel/repository/starlark/StarlarkBaseExternalContext.java#L1833-L1840)

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

nodes.head: 1b56b8506d2eb230d46bf8f95ab1242c9a81298a
nodes.title: Honor TCP_USER_TIMEOUT after reaching the keepalive probe count
nodes.summary: With TCP_KEEPCNT set to one, stock gVisor closed the socket before a second probe even when TCP_USER_TIMEOUT granted it more time. Linux and the fix respected that timeout, and all three passed the ordinary probe-count control.

evidence.label: Original packet traces and named controls
Linux
Stock gVisor
Fixed gVisor
Published gVisor PR

settledReviews.head: 1b56b8506d2eb230d46bf8f95ab1242c9a81298a
settledReviews.body:
A socket with TCP_KEEPCNT set to one can close after its first
unanswered keepalive probe even when the application has asked TCP to
wait longer. Linux uses the user timeout to decide when to close such
a socket [1].

Use the probe count only when TCP_USER_TIMEOUT is zero. Exercise both
configurations on the wire with an idle peer that never answers probes.

[1] https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/7d0a66e4b/net/ipv4/tcp_timer.c#L825-L839

nodes.head: d51e6c370f6e1e6da11a7ad463a8f86236f877ac
nodes.title: Run governance and license checks on the Buildkite agent
nodes.summary: Buildkite build 53913 ran the two governance comparisons in the dedicated job and all three unit jobs. The proposed revision keeps them in the unit jobs and runs license verification on the agent. Native Make verified all 220 entries and rejected a catalog missing abseil-cpp.

settledReviews.head: d51e6c370f6e1e6da11a7ad463a8f86236f877ac
settledReviews.title: Run license CI natively and deduplicate governance
settledReviews.summary: Replace the published commit on #16904 with this revision?
settledReviews.body:
Buildkite runs the same two comparisons for CODEOWNERS and MAINTAINERS.md in the governance and unit jobs. In build 53913, the dedicated job and all three unit jobs reported both tests [1]. The first-pass unit job uses the same Make target, which includes //:all.

Remove the dedicated governance job from both pipelines. Keep make governance-check available for running just those comparisons.

The license check builds the checker, then runs it to query the dependency graph through Make. Run that job on the agent in both pipelines. Let the nested queries use the selected Bazel installation and the agent's remote-cache options.

Buildkite overlays hook exports on the agent's original environment. Unsetting USE_BAZEL_VERSION allowed an inherited 8.5.0 to reach Bazelisk on a checkout pinned to 8.8.1 [2]. Export the checkout's version and shut down the native server when the job finishes.

The shared failure hook calls Make to clean and shut down Bazel even when the job never used the builder. Those calls can start a builder on a cold agent [3]. Keep reporting failed test logs and let the existing container sweep stop running builders.

[1]: https://buildkite.com/gvisor/pipeline/builds/53913
[2]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42462374395/artifacts/13609898731
[3]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/7e2f75125
settledReviews.note: Approved for publication.

evidence.label: 220 license records, 52 remote build actions and a missing-entry control
Clean and stale comparison results and Buildkite log handoff
Original job, including its diagnostic guard failure
Agent provides the remote cache before repository hooks
Shared remote CI pilot

nodes.title: Identify the failed client call for GKE bridge TCP resets
nodes.summary:
Lorenzo captured both ends of 14 failed exchanges. In every pair the client reset a copy of the SYN-ACK from the bridge MAC with a changed source port. The server received the reset on port 9000 before accepting the connection. The first public runsc release containing bridge fix d4be3ed28 is 20261012.0. We asked Lucas whether GKE Sandbox v1.36.4-gke.2377000 includes the fix.

A matched comparison of source-built July runsc 9f3e9a3fb and July plus only the landed bridge change d4be3ed28 (9ffcd1079) recorded two ECONNRESETs in 4,000 stock exchanges and none in 4,000 patched exchanges. Each arm ran 2,000 exchanges per close order in a separate offline Linux VM. Both stock errors were server-first: one on sendall and one on recv_echo.

evidence.label: Reply to Lorenzo and question to Lucas about the GKE release
Lorenzo’s captures from both endpoints
First public runsc release containing the bridge fix
Public July release: client-first and server-first close orders
Forwarding controls on July and current public gVisor
Docker-in-gVisor results for both close orders
Posted results and question for the reporter
Same Docker 27.5.1 fixture on Linux runc 1.5.2: 2,000 exchanges per close order, zero errors; Linux retained zero SNAT hits
July Docker fixture: paired endpoint headers and application observations
Matched offline Linux VMs: July stock 2/4,000 resets, bridge-only change 0/4,000
Fixed source: July plus only the landed bridged-transit delivery change
Landed production bridge change

settledReviews.body:
I reproduced `ConnectionResetError` outside GKE with Docker 27.5.1 inside public runsc 20260727.0, using your Python close sequence over the `t1` bridge with `srv` as the hostname. The client saw `ECONNRESET` on 3/2,000 client-first exchanges and 2/2,000 server-first exchanges. The first failure in each run was `recv(1)` after `sendall`; other calls also reported resets. [Per-operation results and setup](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41704494513/artifacts/13265691217).

On your GKE build, could you record which call first raises the exception (`create_connection`, `sendall`, or `recv`) and its errno? That would let us compare the failure you see with this public release. If you already have a trace, the client port for that failed exchange would help match it.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Thank you for capturing both ends. In all 14 failed exchanges, the client saw a copy of the server’s SYN-ACK from the bridge MAC with its source port changed. The client reset that port, and the server saw the same reset translated back to 9000 before it accepted the connection. That puts the failure in the handshake, before either side chooses who closes first.

[d4be3ed28](https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/d4be3ed28) stops delivering transit unicast to the bridge’s local IP stack, which removes the routed copy in this path. With just that change our July Docker fixture went from 2 resets in 4,000 exchanges to 0 in 4,000. [Matched runs](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41910309875/artifacts/13364018365)

The first public runsc release containing the fix is [20261012.0](https://github.com/google/gvisor/releases/tag/release-20261012.0). @manninglucas, can you confirm whether GKE Sandbox v1.36.4-gke.2377000 includes that fix, or point us to the person who can?

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

nodes.summary: Posted the approved measured suggestion on the SACK candidate loop. The candidate loop can skip allocations and scoreboard lookups for segments ending before the new SACK block. A single late SACK on a 128-segment queue took 3.60 µs at the PR head and 0.94 µs with the overlap check.

settledReviews.head: df000e6d7a2ca32aea30416c12cf257c79806c50
settledReviews.title: Suggest skipping SACK candidates that cannot change
settledReviews.body:
Could we skip segments that end at or before `sb.Start` here? Inserting this SACK block cannot change whether those segments are covered. The sender still walks past them to find the block, but it can skip both the append and the second scoreboard lookup. A partially overlapping segment still needs both checks because adjacent SACK blocks can merge.

I timed one new SACK near the end of a 128-segment send queue in `handleRcvdSegment`, with RACK disabled. `stock` is this PR and `fixed` adds the overlap check.

```text
                                                │    stock     │               fixed                │
                                                │    sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base               │
SACKAccountingQualification/queue=128/sack=far    3604.5n ± 1%   937.2n ± 5%  -74.00% (p=0.000 n=8)
```

Allocations fell from seven to two per ACK. Both versions gave the same Outstanding count for duplicate and partially overlapping blocks, including across sequence-number wrap. [One-line change](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/ffd2dc90a) · [Benchmark and controls](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41757174160/artifacts/13289470471).

settledReviews.head: b79cad51119968aff3e0027237e3d646d00b6a4c
settledReviews.title: Start the Bazel builder only for images that need it
settledReviews.body:
Buildkite checks CPU and GPU images in shards. A shard containing only Dockerfiles can check manifests and rebuild missing images with Docker alone. Loading the Bazel wrappers first starts a builder that the shard never uses.

Load the public Bazel wrappers only when an inventory or image check also requests a goal that needs them. Images with Bazel-built contexts already invoke a separate make copy, which keeps the caller’s choice of native Bazel or the Docker builder.

All 12 shard selections kept their image names, order and context targets. The routing checks ran on AMD64; ARM64 selection was checked without building ARM64 images. In a real AMD64 run, native Bazel staged the Alpine image and Docker built the symlink-resolv Dockerfile. Once both manifests were in the loopback registry, Make found them without another Docker build or load.

settledReviews.head: 8cdb6eb0da66ecf93b0a5e32a2ee970016833a5a
settledReviews.title: Keep the target's descriptor table stable during lookup
settledReviews.body:
A task can replace its file descriptor table during unshare or exec. A
lookup from another task must hold the target's mutex until it has
acquired a file reference. The descriptor table's own lock does not
protect the task's table pointer.

Use the existing UnshareFdTable operation during exec and share procfs's
locked lookup with pidfd_getfd. For exec tracing, take the sibling's
stdin and stdout references from one table under its mutex. Collect
process metadata and release those references after unlocking.

Four fresh analyzer wrappers for kernel and proc production and test
code passed with both AMD64 and ARM64 analysis sections. The five
selected PIDFD cases passed on native AMD64 and under systrap: ten
passes, no failures or skips. This does not establish concurrent exec
or procfs runtime coverage [1].

The separate protected TestPIDFDGetFDConcurrentUnshare race fixture
remains unqualified. With the same native fixture and flags, the build
exited 1 at //vdso:vdso: gettimeofday in vdso/vdso.cc conflicts with the
host sys/time.h declaration. No TestRunner, Go race case, XML or test
ELF was produced [2]. The earlier build failures remain recorded
separately [3, 4, 5].

settledReviews.head: d164666c63241ac965864c976a0e9cf447f96c02
settledReviews.title: Ask for a resolution witness and a real clock round trip
settledReviews.body:
Review summary (COMMENT):

Two questions about the new clock tests.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

Inline comment at pkg/tcpip/stdclock_test.go:43 RIGHT:

If the clock stays at one value, `span` and `want` are both zero, so this resolution check passes. The reverse can happen on a busy runner: the elapsed span includes time when this goroutine couldn't sample the counter. Could the test require observing a positive step below 50 µs before an independent deadline? That distinguishes the coarse clock without requiring a minimum number of reads per second.

Inline comment at pkg/tcpip/stdclock_test.go:67 RIGHT:

Could this exercise `state.Save` and `state.Load` into a fresh clock? Calling the two hooks on the same object also passes if the generated restore path never calls `afterLoad`. #16711 already has a round trip that checks both the restored and the still-running clock; we can share it when the changes meet.

settledReviews.head: fb98ff4ca16818deea71b420bef46b956c4b258f
settledReviews.title: Reply about the Windows clock tests and Go 1.28
settledReviews.body:
Thanks, @adios-404. Your Server 2022 result explains why one fine step isn’t enough. Counting positive steps against a separate deadline addresses my resolution concern, and loading the saved state into a fresh clock addresses my restore concern.

I’d use `windows && !go1.28` for the QPC file and keep the resolution test enabled on Go 1.28 and later. [Go’s change](https://github.com/golang/go/commit/16d46baf6) gives `time.Since` a 100 ns monotonic clock on Windows. The test will still catch a regression before Go 1.28 ships.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

followup.disposition: The author added the requested Windows version gate and retained both revised tests.
followup.nextAction: No response or code change is outstanding from this review.

nodes.title: Keep the x86 vDSO gettimeofday alias independent of libc headers
nodes.summary: Give the weak gettimeofday alias a separate C++ identifier while preserving its ELF name and kernel signature. The AMD64 vDSO checks passed with old and current glibc headers and byte-identical outputs. This is independent of #16586, which changes the BUILD file and leaves the declaration unchanged. The receipt’s separate protected-FD link failed before any test; that result does not qualify FD behavior.

evidence.label: One-file source proposal on upstream 6dcadf4a8
Fresh local Bazel vDSO/export and clock-fallback checks; separate FD link remains red

Production AMD64 ELF from identical parent vDSO sources

settledReviews.head: cf2264788a7cfe5302a96311d314bf715d50de9a
settledReviews.title: Keep the x86 vDSO gettimeofday alias independent of libc headers
settledReviews.body:
The x86 vDSO exports a weak gettimeofday at __vdso_gettimeofday. Newer glibc headers declare the timezone parameter as void*, while the kernel entry point takes struct timezone*. Redeclaring gettimeofday with the kernel signature prevents the vDSO from compiling with those headers.

Give the alias its own C++ identifier and the existing ELF name. Its type comes from the kernel entry point, leaving the weak binding and calling convention intact.

The parent built with the glibc 2.27 header, the change with that header, and the change with Ubuntu 24.04’s native header produced byte-identical AMD64 ELFs. All nine versioned functions kept their offsets and bindings relative to the production export. Both gettimeofday entry points returned time between the two host clock samples and zeroed the supplied timezone with the parameter page uninitialized.

nodes.head: f05cd8923fb8aa27186834df01d7433085db41f1
nodes.title: Review the ACK for a segment that fills a gap
nodes.summary:
The author applied the restore fix. The new head has the same Git tree as the tested fix, including the regression. The original packet test showed that a filled gap was acknowledged immediately in both modes; the restore test confirmed that the outstanding 500 bytes were acknowledged without waiting for the next 1,000 bytes.

On a loopback request/reply workload, stock sent four segments for a single write. Enabling #16953 and using #17082’s default each reduced that to two. When the client split a request across two writes with Nagle enabled, median time per request was 40.18 µs on stock, 40.414 ms on #16953 and 40.393 ms on #17082. With Nagle disabled, the corresponding medians were 39.33, 26.45 and 25.91 µs. All 36 sample runs completed without retransmissions.

On native Linux, the sender observed an ACK 6–14 µs after the receiver started setting TCP_QUICKACK following a read (four trials). Without that request, the ACK arrived 40–41 ms after the data. On controlled packet clocks, #16953 with delayed ACKs enabled waited 40 ms in both cases. #17082 sent the ACK immediately on request. With the receive-side MSS fixed at 536 bytes, both PRs acknowledged the second 536-byte segment immediately when the peer advertised MSS 536. When only the peer’s advertised MSS changed to 1,460, #16953 waited 40 ms and #17082 still acknowledged immediately.

nodes.summary: At veth MTUs of 1500 and 3000, Linux advertised TCP MSS values of 1460 and 2960 in the SYN. Stock gVisor advertised 1446 and 2946; the fix matched Linux. Setting loopback to 1234 also read back as 1220 on stock and 1234 on Linux and the fix. This corrects a 14-byte header deduction; #16957 separately keeps the peers’ MTUs independent.

settledReviews.head: 679d20c1ba36918979ce60e0f7619c3c72738d03
settledReviews.title: Use the configured MTU for veth and loopback
settledReviews.body:
The Sentry configures veth and loopback with the maximum IP packet size. Since 66defd3cc, the Ethernet wrapper treats that value as a complete frame budget and subtracts the header. A veth MTU of 1500 consequently becomes 1486 for both netlink and the TCP route. Setting the loopback MTU has the same discrepancy that 35d3c6eb7 originally fixed.

Register both virtual devices with an Ethernet wrapper that uses the network MTU from the underlying endpoint. Both devices pass complete frames to the receiving stack and have no separate frame-size limit.

settledReviews.title: Post the partial-first-ACK finding on #17023
settledReviews.body:
If the first ACK covers half of the retransmitted segment, this leaves `spuriousTimeoutResumed` false. In [your six-segment test with that one change](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/7a60344d2), the next ACK still covers segments 1 and 2, and three duplicate ACKs then newly SACK segments 4 through 6. The full-ACK control retransmitted segment 3; the half-ACK case sent nothing with the retransmission clock held fixed. Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

settledReviews.head: 465bf4e9edc2095d5673177f3be3cac1544fd26e

The next RTO or entry into fast recovery sets its own recovery point and clears the exception. The partial-first-ACK test covers the trace I reported. Thanks for adding it.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

settledReviews.head: 963e83a9586fe9ea5331bd4e3e30d53d45386d66
settledReviews.title: Post the two-packet timeout finding on #17022
settledReviews.body:
Could timeout recovery use the number of packets in flight here? In the [packet test](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/9696b5abe), an earlier timeout set the slow-start threshold to 2. ACKs then grew the congestion window to 10. Only two packets were in flight when the next timeout fired. Once the sender detected that timeout was spurious, this assignment restored the threshold to 10. [RFC 4015 §3.1, step 0](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4015.html#section-3.1) gives max(2, 2) = 2.

[Changing the timeout capture to use the outstanding count](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/a10d0b8eb) kept the threshold at 2. The control that echoed the retransmission’s timestamp also stayed at 2 on both versions. Could you add this application-limited case to the timeout tests? [Packet results](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41994453265/artifacts/13399329303)

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

settledReviews.head: d0439e8b83fafeff675910fc544a393fb5d9f85c
settledReviews.title: Reply about restoring the initial slow-start threshold
settledReviews.body:
Yes, I’d restore `InitialSsthresh` in the timeout case. [RFC 4015 §3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4015.html#section-3.1) step (0) saves max(FlightSize, ssthresh), so a false alarm with five packets in flight should preserve the initial threshold. Step (9) bounds the immediate send separately through cwnd. Could you update the existing five-packet RTO assertion? The finite-threshold two-packet case now matches the trace.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

settledReviews.head: c02d0940fd57e7c31432c81164f3e58f41795286
settledReviews.title: Confirm the revised timeout result on #17022
settledReviews.body:
Thanks, Aditya. This addresses my concern. I ran the same five-packet test on both revisions. The earlier sender restored a threshold of 5. On c02d0940f the initial threshold survived and cwnd was 4. The two-packet case still restored 2. [Packet tests](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42194565719/artifacts/13491802727)

nodes.head: 5d6ca5025d9dfe7e1dff121d55ee5a6027338237
nodes.title: tcp: retry a contended endpoint after serving its queued peers
nodes.summary:
PR #17045 now publishes the qualified dispatcher amendment at 5d6ca5025, with the two existing blank lines restored in dispatcher.go as requested. The approved description is live and the reply was posted in the reviewer’s thread.

The dispatcher gives queued peers a turn, retries a contended endpoint immediately if its lock has become available, and queues new arrivals behind the retry. On the previous head 2ec7b59ad with the regression test, it yielded after the listener unlocked and processed no packets. Candidate ba2c7a721 processed the packet without yielding. All 47 TCP case records (33 top-level tests) and both AMD64 and ARM64 Nogo sections passed on an AMD64 Linux runner. The only changes between that tested candidate and the public head are the two blank lines.

On one virtual AMD64 CPU running TamaGo Go 1.27.3, the reporter’s revision 1cea747ef serviced the ready listener in all three trials. The goroutine holding the other listener’s lock then went five seconds without running. With this PR, the lock holder resumed and both queues drained in all three trials. All six unlocked controls completed.

settledReviews.head: c74632e3cb3438ebf9322754e23c35bf56c9be58
settledReviews.title: Remove stale file descriptor lock requirements
settledReviews.body:
GetFDs locks the file descriptor table itself. Task.mu protects a
caller borrowing the table from a task. A caller that owns a table
reference can enumerate it independently of any task.

VFSPipe.newFD initializes a new descriptor and takes the address of
the underlying pipe. VFSPipe has no mutex named vp.mu, and neither
pipe creation nor open holds a pipe mutex when calling newFD.

nodes.head: 005743727b3d80d373085133b5da9cd906cc9d7c
nodes.title: Build the systrap signal stub with the C toolchain
nodes.summary:
Published as #17067 at 005743727, the approved dfd4d4774 patch rebased without changes onto da95e9bce. On an AMD64 worker, GNU compiled and linked both target stubs. The two raw blobs matched their ELF sections, and the existing nm-based generator produced all 10 AMD64 and 11 ARM64 offsets with their exact ELF values. The job built both consumers; it ran no tests or guest. #16516 is not a prerequisite for this PR.

The review on the published head reports an implicit allocator and internal toolchain features that do not suit a freestanding stub. Fork amendment 7f6ecfff6 reuses #16522’s freestanding adapter at 244010f9c and disables the x86 medium code model. It has not been applied to the public PR and must wait for #16522 to land. #16516 remains independent.

In the GNU control, a forced allocator made the published stub fail to link; enabling the named x86 medium-model feature produced a 60-byte .lbss outside .crblob. The amendment built all three sidecars and both stub architectures with those settings. Both raw blobs and all 10 AMD64 / 11 ARM64 offsets matched the published baseline. The configured-option reporter failed after those builds; the initial raw option values were not retained, so its exact comparison failure is unknown. A separate readback ran three successful cqueries and no builds: both the direct wrapper edge and prior filter selected the private producer with allocator None, while an ordinary target retained the forced allocator. The private toolchain has not been tested.

#17089 would remove the pagesize_64k setting used by the current #17067 source. Fork integration c157b4d8f applied the native C rule to #17089’s runtime page-size layout and removed the obsolete local_defines selection. On one x86_64 GNU builder with 4 KiB pages, the generator reproduced all 10 AMD64 and 13 ARM64 export offsets from the linked stubs. Each embedded blob matched its own ELF section. All offsets moved relative to the shell build, and the full blobs differed. This cross-build included no guest boot.

A subsequent runtime test on c157b4d8f booted the same ARM64 Sentry and release manifest in two QEMU TCG guests on an AMD64 host. Each fresh test ran a systrap workload as PID 1. On the 4 KiB guest, the kernel page size, AT_PAGESZ and sysconf all reported 4,096 bytes. On the 64 KiB guest, all three reported 65,536 bytes. Both exited successfully. The Sentry contained the same signal stub verified in the GNU cross-build.

settledReviews.head: d4e65b135f3f4e6dbb811a59c38917bdb382d6c3
settledReviews.title: fdbased: start packet processors when a receiver attaches
settledReviews.summary: Open this receive-worker fix? Native AMD64 passed 18 receive cases, three live-save cases, four muxed cases and Nogo.
settledReviews.body:
Closing an FD endpoint before attaching it to a NIC leaves its receive
workers asleep. The constructor starts the workers, but only the read
loop signals them to stop. An unattached endpoint never runs that loop.

Create the queues and their workers when a dispatcher attaches. Each
receive loop delivers to that dispatcher and stops its own workers on
exit. A single processor still delivers inline.

On detach, close each queue before waking its reader. A reader already
returning from a receive syscall can then neither deliver the pending
batch nor enqueue the rest of it. Workers can finish delivering packets
already removed from their queues without blocking NIC removal on a
network stack callback.

For injectable endpoints, report attachment from the dispatcher used by
InjectInbound.
settledReviews.note: Use e.wg.Go and reconsider the extra processor-manager slice allocated for each attachment.

nodes.title: Align packet ring blocks to the host page size
nodes.summary: On a 64 KiB ARM64 Linux kernel, fdbased.PacketMMap rejects its own block size before asking Linux to allocate the ring. Rounding the block from 2,101,248 to 2,162,688 bytes let the receiver deliver 40 UDP datagrams through its 32-frame ring. On native AMD64 with 4 KiB pages, both versions used the same 2,101,248-byte block and delivered all 40. This affects callers selecting PacketMMap on an AF_PACKET socket. settledReviews.head: dec1b82660c2974f5b98b2c5ab88d0857b34adb8
settledReviews.title: Open the PacketMMap host-page fix
settledReviews.body:
The fd-based PacketMMap receiver needs 32 frames of 65,664 bytes.
Their combined size is a multiple of 4 KiB, but not 64 KiB. On a
64 KiB host the endpoint rejects its own ring size before asking Linux
to allocate the ring.

Round the single block up to a host page and map the entire block.
The padding is smaller than a frame, so Linux still counts 32 frames
and the receiver can use the same offsets on both hosts.

nodes.head: b5062f2222f563af2f39c4cc2e57cd1194634146
nodes.title: Review delayed ACKs after gap recovery and rejected replies
nodes.summary:
At b5062f222, draining the receive queue after a full-size 1,460-byte PSH segment triggered the delayed ACK. On four fresh connections, the ACK followed the start of the draining read by 0.99–3.45 ms on Netstack and 0.45–1.23 ms on native Linux 6.8. Leaving one byte queued or omitting PSH kept the ACK at 40.5–41.9 ms from packet arrival on both stacks. All eight uncached tests passed on AMD64, four with native Linux and four with Netstack.

Earlier measurements at 981034f8b:

The delayed-ACK estimate can now shrink after repeated smaller segments. Two cases failed on the previous head, 10555b8fe. All 11 tests passed on native AMD64 at 981034f8b, including the 511-byte stream with and without PSH and the earlier gap and rejected-send cases. Ayush’s November 6 reply explains the changes.

On a loopback request/reply workload, stock sent four segments for a single write. Enabling #16953 and using #17082’s default each reduced that to two. When the client split a request across two writes with Nagle enabled, median time per request was 40.18 µs on stock, 40.414 ms on #16953 and 40.393 ms on #17082. With Nagle disabled, the corresponding medians were 39.33, 26.45 and 25.91 µs. All 36 sample runs completed without retransmissions.

After 24 individually acknowledged segments, Linux ACKed a pushed 1,460-byte segment within 0.33–0.75 ms of starting the read that drained the socket. The PR waited 29.84–30.85 ms. Leaving one byte queued or omitting PSH kept both stacks near 40 ms from packet arrival. Each case ran on four fresh connections per stack. All four Linux test runs and all four netstack runs passed on AMD64. The workflow reported failure because its capture reader required all 1,514 Ethernet bytes. The capture retained 1,500 bytes, including every TCP header. The corrected reader verified the original packet lengths, sequence numbers and timestamps.

settledReviews.head: f2447eb8a6a1ef5f8bf7447b11605e56ec02a83c
settledReviews.title: Post one review with two packet traces
settledReviews.body:
pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/rcv.go:84

Could we send the cumulative ACK immediately when a segment fills the last receive gap? By the time this condition runs, the queue is empty. After the 16 quick ACKs, the [packet test](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/79dc3a63d) sent byte 807 before byte 806. On this head, ACK 808 waited 40 ms after byte 806 arrived. The [four-line change](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/aa0c1c8cc) sent ACK 808 immediately and still delayed the ordinary in-order ACK for 40 ms. [Packet traces](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42165403428/artifacts/13478877935) · [RFC 5681 §4.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5681#section-4.2).

pkg/tcpip/transport/tcp/snd.go:1909

Could we keep the ACK pending if the link accepts no packet carrying it? Here `MaxSentAck` advances and the timer stops before `sendRaw` reports whether anything went out. In this [packet test](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/ef3c057c1), the link rejects the one-byte response with `ErrNoBufferSpace` but accepts pure ACKs. The socket stayed established and sent no ACK by 40 ms. With the write accepted, the response carried the ACK and no extra packet was needed. [Packet traces](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42166057647/artifacts/13478329386).

@botirkhaltaev, I reproduced this. After the client wrote first and read a one-byte reply, the PR sent its ACK at 40 ms on the test clock. settledReviews.head: dcad6d56792cbd5c65195ad64f3a57628e605f70
settledReviews.title: Open the TCP listener handshake lock PR
settledReviews.body:
A TCP listener copies its socket options into a new child while both
endpoint mutexes are held. A forwarder starts the same handshake
without a listening endpoint. Sharing an optional listener pointer hid
the listener lock from checklocks and required suppressing the check at
the option copy.

Copy the options and reserve the tuple on the locked listener. Let the
forwarder create its child directly, and share registration and the
SYN-ACK on the locked child. Only the forwarder waits for the handshake
to finish.
settledReviews.note: The listener refactor is approved subject to explaining the moved checklocks suppressions.

settledReviews.body:
A TCP listener copies its socket options into a new child while both
endpoint mutexes are held. A forwarder starts the same handshake
without a listening endpoint. Sharing an optional listener pointer hid

Copy the options and reserve the tuple on the locked listener. Let the
forwarder create its child directly, and share registration and the
SYN-ACK on the locked child. Only the forwarder waits for the handshake
to finish.

is no child to lock. The constructor can now transfer the child lock to

settledReviews.head: 93305f85d83ce534321bb231e0d09af6dd4bf8b5
settledReviews.title: Open the decoder benchmark fixture PR
settledReviews.body:
Since 364ac92ba, BenchmarkDecoding has passed the object it just
encoded back to the decoder. That lets gob reuse objects from the
source. A new Sentry cannot reuse the objects in the old one.

Clear the root before each decode. With the populated slice fixture,
gob reused the backing array and all 1,024 pointers to a single
object. From an empty root it decoded 1,024 distinct objects. The
graph decoder allocated a new backing array and one shared pointee
in both cases.

Ten interleaved pairs on linux/amd64 measured the cost of decoding
into the two destinations [1].

```text

                       │    sec/op    │    sec/op      vs base                 │
```

nodes.title: Let a packaged child select its own runfiles
nodes.summary:
Upstream hermetic-launcher #96 at 0b5abb565 contains the finalizer and launcher stub. They let a packaged child select runfiles containing its bootstrap. Review identified that the default toolchain still pins a finalizer that rejects the new option and a template without its marker. The prepared Starlark API at 44a48ed35 can land with the pin update after the maintainers publish a tag containing both binaries.

The combined implementation at cb36641e5 passed all 22 launcher integration cases on native AMD64. An independently packaged Python child failed with the stock launcher and with the option unset. Naming its stage-two bootstrap selected the child’s own runfiles and started it. Direct launches and launches from a parent that declared the child also passed. The Starlark companion was prepared on 2d0fdd797. Its tree differed from the tested implementation by one README line. The final upstream revision changes only a Windows test fixture’s manifest filename and its comment. The finalizer, stub and companion implementation are identical to the versions tested on AMD64.

evidence.label: Upstream finalizer and stub change, 0b5abb565
Prepared Starlark API for the joint binary pin update
Original review finding on the prebuilt finalizer and template
Windows test fixture filename correction relative to the companion’s parent
Native AMD64 supplier suite and packaged-child comparisons
Supplier workflow for releasing and pinning prebuilt binaries
Approved issue filed with hermetic-launcher
Two unmodified Linux packages, direct invocation and parent dependency controls
rules_python handles a caller whose runfiles tree omits the child
Additional partial-tree and executable-alias controls

settledReviews.title: Let a packaged child select its own runfiles
settledReviews.summary: Let a rule name a required runfile so a separately installed child uses its own runfiles when the parent’s tree lacks that file.
settledReviews.body:
Running an independently installed Python plugin from a Bazel-built parent fails before Python starts: the launcher inherits the parent’s `RUNFILES_DIR`, which lacks the plugin’s bootstrap script. The same plugin runs directly. [Reproducer](https://github.com/tamird/rules_python/actions/runs/42210914546/artifacts/13498603725).

I propose letting a rule name one required runfile. `rules_python` would name the child’s stage-two bootstrap. Use the inherited source if it contains that file. Otherwise use the child’s adjacent runfiles for both path resolution and the environment passed to the child.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

settledReviews.head: 902bee9176a0a78a435db3df2ebffe1d2a9794e5
settledReviews.title: Check the mutex protecting TCP keepalive options and probe counts
settledReviews.body:
TCP_KEEPIDLE, TCP_KEEPINTVL and TCP_KEEPCNT can be read without
locking the endpoint. Their getters take the keepalive mutex, which
also protects updates to the probe count when an ACK arrives or the
keepalive timer expires. Annotate these fields so checklocks can
detect accesses that hold only the endpoint mutex.

nodes.title: Release the stack mutex before draining a removed NIC
nodes.head: 39d28d4ef5d4a11aa5f8756d62bf99e1cd02816d
nodes.summary: Stack.Wait held the stack mutex while waiting for a receive worker. That worker needed the mutex to find the input interface. Six lifecycle cases passed under the race detector and 16 real socket transfers completed teardown. After those runtime checks, the only source change removed an obsolete comment. Nogo passed the final revision on AMD64 and ARM64. On both, it rejected moving the unlock below the call to closeRemovedNICs.

settledReviews.head: dcad6d56792cbd5c65195ad64f3a57628e605f70
settledReviews.title: Open the TCP listener handshake lock PR
settledReviews.body:
A TCP listener copies its socket options into a new child while both
endpoint mutexes are held. A forwarder starts the same handshake
without a listening endpoint. Sharing an optional listener pointer hid
the listener lock from checklocks and required suppressing the check at
the option copy.

Copy the options and reserve the tuple on the locked listener. Let the
forwarder create its child directly, and share registration and the
SYN-ACK on the locked child. Only the forwarder waits for the handshake
to finish.
settledReviews.note: The listener refactor is approved subject to explaining the moved checklocks suppressions.

settledReviews.head: abc461928f2488ac0aaf1a3ec046a3ee0b200c79
settledReviews.title: Check both locks when a listener accepts a SYN
settledReviews.body:
A TCP listener copies its socket options into a new child while both
endpoint mutexes are held. A forwarder starts the same handshake
without a listening endpoint. Sharing an optional listener pointer hid
the listener lock from checklocks and required suppressing the check at
the option copy.

Copy the options and reserve the tuple on the locked listener. Let the
forwarder create its child directly, and share registration and the
SYN-ACK on the locked child. Only the forwarder waits for the handshake
to finish.

Look up the route before creating the child. If the lookup fails there
is no child to lock. The constructor can now transfer the child lock to
each caller without suppressing checks on the error paths.
