nodes.head: 4eb27c4081e535d69c1257998a6c94256d9812e2
nodes.title: Run the source presubmit on native AMD64 and ARM64 workers
nodes.summary:
The source coordinator built all 3,246 ARM64 roots on efaf79761 across six configurations. No root was missing, failed, or unexpected. The four runsc and Sentry coverage executables and the metric archive’s object member were AArch64. BuildBuddy executed 321 actions remotely and served 48,239 remote cache hits. This was a build of default outputs and ran zero tests.

Tamir approved 4eb27c408, which runs the statefile permission tests as UID 65534. Its BUILD rule selects //test/rbe:source_presubmit, introduced by its parent d78fe07a0. The test change ships with that configuration.

One mixed Bazel invocation built the 2,887 top-level build-only labels in their selected configurations and all 728 test targets. It executed 374 uncached test shards on native AMD64 workers and 374 on native ARM64 workers. Of the 748 shards, 747 passed. The ARM64 runsc/cmd shard failed its five Sentry posture comparisons. The five corresponding gofer comparisons passed. All five Sentry diffs report a thread with a different Seccomp_filters count from the process. The gofer cases check its environment. A separate hosted ARM64 6.8 run observed an extra pidfd on the fourth default Sentry repeat. A retained-helper control reproduced that observation on stock. Waiting through the proc umounter’s Go handle fixed it, and all ten original comparisons passed on the uninstrumented corrected runtime. The Linux 5.10 per-thread reporting failure remains open. In a two-thread control, the ARM64 Linux 5.10.0 worker enforced the filter on both threads but increased the procfs count only on the thread that installed it. The AMD64 Linux 6.18.57 worker increased both counts. Linux fixed that reporting bug and backported the fix to 5.10.60. In isolated QEMU guests, the public 5.10.0 image and BuildBuddy #11090’s proposed 6.1.0 image both enforced the filter on both threads. Only the 6.1.0 image reported the increase on both threads.

The separate native ARM64 wildcard selects //runsc:runsc_race_coverage, //runsc/cmd/sentry:gvisor_sentry_race_coverage and //pkg/metric:metric_cc_proto. Across all 11 mixed cquery partitions, encompassing 16,709 distinct pkg/runsc rows, those three targets and their generated output paths appeared only in AMD64 configurations. Both inventories used the same source tree, 4305e961c. The mixed selection on 4305e961c omitted those ARM64 defaults. The local Go standard-library analyzer could not run with processwrapper-sandbox, so the comparison produced no new binaries. The separate native wildcard projection also omitted some selected rows.

A targeted build on x86_64 produced the three ARM64 defaults for //pkg/metric:metric_cc_proto: the generated C++ source, header and libmetric_proto.a. The archive contained an AArch64 ELF object. A separate analysis of coordinator change efaf79761 selected all 3,246 original ARM64 root labels (2,882 build-only labels and 364 existing test labels), with zero missing or extra. It checked 321 roots outside pkg and runsc, including four aliases. Eight shell controls checked propagation of build and test failures. The 747 passing shards out of 748 belong to the earlier mixed test execution.

The frozen local qualifier (7b920f2cd) checks which labels belong to each of the six Bazel configuration groups across all 3,246 roots. It compares CPU, platform, mnemonic and tool-configuration flag, then inspects the metric archive and four runsc and Sentry ELF binaries. In the earlier mixed analysis and physical run, all 728 test labels kept their original group membership while every raw configuration checksum changed. The separate PacketImpact family analysis on 61a9e54af selected all 164 mixed tests. Dependency build failures prevented any of them from running. The pristine baseline and the requested ARM64 3,246-root build remain separate qualification steps.

Once the common RBE source presubmit runs the native AMD64 netfilter syscall test upstream, it can replace the “Nftables native syscall tests” Buildkite step and its nftables-syscall-runc-tests Make target. On fork 1b8d903a7, AMD64 Linux 6.18.57 matched all 267 named Buildkite results (262 passed, five skipped). ARM64 Linux 5.10.0 passed six and skipped 261. The test’s kernel-version guard accounted for all 256 additional skips. The separate “Nftables docker tests” step still uses the image.

On fork 1bda86e0c, the two ARM64 guest syscall suites expanded to the same 915 test labels as Buildkite #53930: 907 syscall and eight rtnetlink owners, comprising 257 ptrace and 658 systrap variants. Their shard counts yield 1,671 runs. The query found 87 ordinary performance variants and zero ARM64 companions for them. Buildkite also selected 2,837 build-only roots. This query measured test membership and attributes; whole-lane execution and build-only coverage remain open. Buildkite’s Make target supplied --cxxopt=-Werror, which the mixed profile at 1bda86e0c did not set.

Of those 2,837 additional labels in the earlier configured-root census, 2,525 are generated test launchers and 312 are other build roots. Following the ARM/Linux srcs, data and deps from the 257 selected fixtures in the source reaches 305 of the 312. Five remaining binaries cover the other seven labels: memfd_test, sigaltstack_test and the three socket_bind_to_device test binaries, including their sigaltstack_check and socket_bind_to_device_util dependencies. Earlier builds linked all five ARM64 binaries and sigaltstack_check, then verified the same outputs by digest. The mixed selector at 1bda86e0c omitted those five build roots.

Five owners on 1bda86e0c ran uncached on native ARM64 Ubuntu Firecracker workers. Ptrace uname and systrap uname with directfs each passed all four named cases, with zero skips. Three rtnetlink owners failed before their guest scripts started: systrap bridge, ptrace bridge and systrap setlink. All three logged a connection reset in containerManager.SetNetworkArgs during default-loopback setup, produced empty XML, and reached zero fixture assertions. On the original systrap bridge run, its filesystem gofer exited after the read-only bind remount of the root filesystem returned EBUSY. Runsc then reported the SetNetworkArgs reset. The log does not identify what kept the mount busy. The ptrace bridge and systrap setlink TestRunners used the same verified AArch64 runsc (SHA-256 552148f89…) and Sentry (132e77dfd…). The initial uname test binary was linked on an AMD64 distroless worker.

All five original TestRunners received 1,000 millicpu. The effective memory estimates were 300 MB for each uname owner and 220 MB for each rtnetlink owner. Repeating systrap setlink with its original timeout, Linux 5.10.0 and CPUs 0–3 raised the VM’s measured MemTotal from 186,960 KiB to 508,760 KiB with a 512 MB request. Both runs failed in SetNetworkArgs before the guest script started, and the VM’s oom_kill counter stayed at zero in both.

Using test scratch for overlay backing in 0a851bf99 let all three rtnetlink tests start on Ubuntu. Each guest then failed because ip was missing. With the same source and the existing pinned Istio networking image, both bridge variants each delivered two distinct TCP messages, and systrap setlink verified the MTU, rename, MAC address and three cleanup checks. Across the six uncached ARM64 Firecracker tests, / and /tmp had mount ID 25 and TEST_TMPDIR had mount ID 38. Both images used the same runsc and Sentry binaries, and each action received 1 CPU and 220 MB. The standalone gVisor proposal changes only the overlay backing path. The networking image remains a separate fork integration.

On research/mixed-arm64-syscalls at 6ed4ed427, Bazel ran //test/rtnetlink:arm64_syscalls through its checked-in worker settings. All eight bridge, route, setlink and veth owners passed across ptrace and systrap on uncached native ARM64 Firecracker TestRunners using the pinned Istio networking image. Each bridge delivered two TCP messages. Both route tests observed two, one and then zero routes to 10.0.0.0/24 after successive deletions and recovered the original routing table. Both veth tests checked the restricted move and exited successfully. Bazel exited zero. All 3,777 recorded compile and link actions were AMD64 scratch-worker cache hits. Together with the two earlier uname owners, 10 distinct owners have passed out of the 915 selected for the ARM64 syscall lane. The full 1,671-shard guest run remains open.

The mixed ARM64 selector at fbeacd531 adds the five standalone syscall binaries. Both single-architecture profiles select zero of those five through the new group. Aquery showed -Werror last on the native, guest and standalone C++ fixtures and their checked dependencies. The unrelated AMD64 control kept -Wno-error. In the first build on 9ae8c6df6, Clang rejected two delete signatures missing noexcept. No test ran. The fork then integrated #15368 at 403195966.

On the corrected source, AMD64 scratch workers cross-linked all five AArch64 standalone binaries and the native RSEQ test binary. All six links were fresh. The three socket links consumed the same socket_bind_to_device_util object. The separate sigaltstack_check and freestanding RSEQ helper outputs matched their cached ARM64 links. One uncached native ARM64 Firecracker TestRunner passed all 13 RSEQ cases with no skips. The five standalone binaries were build-only. The allocator contract test did not run. Guest coverage remains 10 of 915 owners across the earlier runs.

A historical ARM64 archive contains 1,671 XML reports matching all 915 selected owner names. For 46 owners, every recorded case was skipped or suppressed (392 skipped, 22 suppressed). Seven UDP external-networking owners accounted for 176 setup skips because the fixture found loopback but no addressed non-loopback interface.

The mixed fork at 6daca2aa7 selects 1,171 existing AMD64 syscall owners, comprising the same 257 ptrace and 658 systrap names as ARM64, plus 256 native Linux owners. Adding the 257 KVM owners and the separate tcp_serv_nogo analyzer reproduces all 1,429 Buildkite #53930 names. The three AMD64 smoke tests ran uncached on Firecracker. Native and ptrace uname each passed all four cases with no skips. The systrap bridge on the networking image delivered both TCP payloads and removed its bridge and namespaces. Its shell transcript records the results. The XML is empty. The October Actions/Docker qualification ran 1,172 owners on an earlier source and host route. Of those, 1,164 passed and eight native owners failed.

Buildkite selected 3,753 AMD64 labels, comprising 1,429 tests and 2,324 build-only labels. Bazel loading identified 2,012 allsave wrappers and 312 other producers. The ordinary AMD64 suite reaches all 224 distinct fixture labels used by those wrappers. Five standalone fixture roots, their signal-stack helper and their shared socket utility were missing from the AMD64 closure. Two older RSEQ rules have since been replaced by the native rseq binary.

On mixed fork a023961f0, building //test/syscalls:standalone_fixtures produced six AMD64 ELF executables in fresh LLVM link actions on scratch workers. The outputs were memfd_test, sigaltstack_test, sigaltstack_check and three socket_bind_to_device binaries. All three socket links consumed the same verified utility object. The ARM64 configured query returned the same five default output paths as the previous ARM64 build. This invocation built the AMD64 fixture group only and ran no tests. This comparison did not build the 2,012 wrapper outputs or the full wildcard.

On ARM64, all 176 UDP cases in the seven original guest owners also skipped on fbeacd531 for lack of an addressed non-loopback interface. Adding a dummy interface failed with EOPNOTSUPP before GTest in all nine guest and native owners. On the separate fork at ff35512db, a bridge with no ports let all 176 guest cases pass. IPv4 native and IPv4 host-network systrap had passing TestResults. The other six guest wrappers failed because runsc warned that Linux had rejected the raw socket receive and send buffer requests on eth0 (4,194,304 bytes requested, 425,984 available). Native IPv6 passed six of eight cases. Both multicast join/leave cases sent 200 bytes but timed out receiving them. Their sender bound ::1 without selecting loopback as the multicast output interface. The receiver had joined on loopback.

The corrected fork at cf2339899 passed all eight uncached Firecracker TestRunners. Seven ARM64 owners passed 146 cases, and the original AMD64 native IPv6 owner passed all eight cases. None skipped. Both native IPv6 multicast joins selected loopback on the sender and received the payload. Each of the six Netstack logs retained the two eth0 socket-buffer warnings and the usable 425,984-byte buffer size. The earlier IPv4 ARM64 native and host-network controls each passed 38 cases on ff35512db. On the separate standalone patch e1a7eb4e5, one AMD64 systrap case passed and completed 11 restores. Bazel exited 0. The reporting script failed to recognize the BEP finish identifier.

nodes.head: 2ab3d20352bb6bd468cbd6d4d1d9d7b7b955bdc9
nodes.title: Unmap the host packet ring when its endpoint closes
nodes.summary:
PR #17111 releases the packet-ring mapping when its endpoint closes. Closing the PacketMMap endpoint left 2,101,248 bytes mapped on a native AMD64 host with 4 KiB pages, even after the caller closed the socket. On the tested fix the mapping remained accessible after detach and was gone after the first and second Close. An 88-byte UDP packet delivered before close still held its original payload. Restore copied zero ring bytes and closing the restored dispatcher left the live owner’s mapping intact.

The original Linux results cover 1a8b1b84c. The final change keeps the slice if Munmap fails so a later Close can retry. The page-size alignment and worker-lifetime changes are independent.

evidence.label: Native AF_PACKET mapping, retained UDP packet and checkpoint control
Only change after the native tests: keep the mapping on unmap failure

settledReviews.head: 2ab3d20352bb6bd468cbd6d4d1d9d7b7b955bdc9
settledReviews.title: Unmap the host packet ring when its endpoint closes
settledReviews.body:
Closing a PacketMMap endpoint leaves its roughly 2 MiB receive ring
mapped in the process, even after the caller closes the packet socket.
The endpoint creates the mapping and the stack stops its receive loop
before calling Close. Packets already delivered to the stack have their
own copy of the frame data.

Unmap the ring at that point. Leave the host mapping out of checkpoints
so a restored dispatcher cannot mistake a Go byte slice for a mapping.
settledReviews.summary: May I open the packet-ring teardown fix? Stock retained its 2,101,248-byte mapping after both the endpoint and socket closed. The tested fix released it while preserving an already delivered packet. The final error-path change retains the mapping for a later Close if unmap fails.
settledReviews.note: Published as #17111 at the reviewed commit.

nodes.head: 4867d503b71f6c13f0346778ca61373df04ed0ae
nodes.title: Allow TCP timeout repair after fast retransmissions
nodes.summary:
Under the loss burst reported on #16081, master closed a TCP connection on its second retransmission timeout. Sixteen sends of the first missing segment exhausted the configured limit of 15, including fast retransmits. This change measures how long data remains unacknowledged across timer expirations. All six heavy-loss transfers finished with the fix. The comparison covers the timeout decision independently of #16081’s recovery-performance changes.

A second packet test sets TCP_USER_TIMEOUT. Before the fix, the socket closed with ETIMEDOUT when newly outstanding data was only 497 ms old on an 800 ms timeout. Linux and the fix both transmitted the fourth segment. The submitted source drops six telemetry-only lines from the tested fixture.

Competing upstream fix counts timeouts after an advancing ACK
Master closed on the second timeout with 16 sends of the first missing segment
Six heavy-loss transfers, Linux timeout repair at 417 ms, and retry bounds
Two-flight packet test on native Linux, #16419, and the correction

settledReviews.head: 4867d503b71f6c13f0346778ca61373df04ed0ae
settledReviews.title: Allow TCP timeout repair after fast retransmissions
settledReviews.body:
Under the loss burst in #16081, the sender closed a connection after
two retransmission timeouts. It had sent the first missing segment 16
times. RACK repairs and tail probes consumed the same per-segment limit
as the retransmission timer.

Apply the configured retry budget to unacknowledged data on a repeated
timeout. Model the elapsed time with exponential backoff as Linux does
in tcp_model_timeout. A cumulative ACK permits the next timeout repair.
Persist probes keep their separate unanswered-probe limit.

TCP_USER_TIMEOUT selects an explicit deadline. When an ACK covers the
old recovery window, start a fresh deadline for later data still in
flight. The socket test checks that the sender can transmit again
after the old deadline has passed.
settledReviews.summary: Open the TCP timeout repair after #16419 lands? The packet tests cover the exhausted segment counter and a new flight’s user timeout.

settledReviews.head: 1de5b54a98a37c10fc0e71f7340df386ffaea4c3
settledReviews.title: Recognize instantiated method receivers in stateify
settledReviews.body:
Stateify scans every method in a package to find save and restore hooks.
A method on *Int[T] therefore makes generation panic even when Int has

where the Go parser supplies an index expression.

unused qualified spelling.

nodes.head: de11f9e09290b75ab5aa7291fb0d308244b72067
nodes.title: Keep TCP_USER_TIMEOUT tied to the oldest outstanding data
nodes.summary: The sender can time out new data at the old flight’s deadline and give its next retransmission the shortened timer. The sender now tracks the last byte of the old flight and keeps the backed-off retransmission interval for the next send. Linux and gVisor agreed on all four socket outcomes, with backed-off RTOs of 1.64 s and 1.60 s. Their exact retransmitted byte ranges differed in the partial-ACK case.

evidence.label: The previously tested two commits have an identical tree
Standalone Linux and corrected gVisor packet outcomes
Tested compatibility with the withdrawn #17113

settledReviews.head: de11f9e09290b75ab5aa7291fb0d308244b72067
settledReviews.title: Keep TCP_USER_TIMEOUT tied to the oldest outstanding data
settledReviews.body:
During loss recovery, a partial ACK can let the sender transmit new
data before the peer acknowledges all the old bytes. gVisor kept the
old deadline even after those bytes were acknowledged, so it could
close the connection while the new data still had time left. It also
shortened the stored retransmission timeout to fit the old deadline.

Track the last byte covered by the deadline. Once the peer acknowledges
it, use the transmit time of the oldest remaining segment to measure
the next timeout. Cap the pending timer at the deadline and preserve
the backed-off retransmission interval for the next send.

Exercise an ACK that covers the old data both before and after another
retransmission timeout.
settledReviews.note: Published as #17128 at the exact approved head.

followup.disposition: The approved source is public on #17128.
followup.nextAction: Follow upstream review and checks on #17128.

old deadline even after those bytes were acknowledged, so it could
close the connection while the new data still had time left. It also
shortened the stored retransmission timeout to fit the old deadline.

Track the last byte covered by the deadline. Once the peer acknowledges
it, use the transmit time of the oldest remaining segment to measure
the next timeout. Cap the pending timer at the deadline and preserve
the backed-off retransmission interval for the next send.

Exercise an ACK that covers the old data both before and after another
retransmission timeout.

settledReviews.head: 6c97901f75134c9f00493736db035f840f513331
settledReviews.title: Tie TCP_USER_TIMEOUT to the outstanding flight
settledReviews.body:
During loss recovery, a partial ACK can let the sender transmit new
data before the peer acknowledges all the old bytes. gVisor kept the
old deadline even after those bytes were acknowledged, so it could
close the connection while the new data still had time left. It also
shortened the stored retransmission timeout to fit the old deadline.

Track the end of the flight covered by the deadline. Once the peer
acknowledges it, start from the transmit time of the oldest remaining
segment. Limit the next timer wakeup without changing the backed-off
RTO. This also enforces the deadline when the peer has acknowledged
all data in flight but keeps its receive window closed.

Exercise an ACK covering the old flight before and after another
retransmission. On a closed window, require the socket to report
ETIMEDOUT before the next uncapped probe.
settledReviews.summary: The amended sender caps the timer wakeup on the closed-window path even after all data in flight has been acknowledged. In the controlled gVisor run the socket timed out at 809 ms with TCP_USER_TIMEOUT set to 806 ms. With that cap omitted, it was still open at 1,106 ms with an 803 ms setting. Both retained an 800 ms backed-off RTO. Native Linux timed out 1,040 ms after the test started, about 830 ms after its first probe. All six uncached Linux and gVisor packet tests passed, including both outstanding-flight cases. The final commit adds the symbolic errno to one test failure message.

processors asleep. New starts the goroutines, but only the receive

Closing an endpoint before attaching it to a NIC leaves its receive
processors asleep. New starts the goroutines, but only the receive
loop wakes them on exit. An unattached endpoint never runs that loop.

Closing an endpoint before attaching it to a NIC leaves its receive
processors asleep. New starts the goroutines, but only the receive
loop wakes them on exit. An unattached endpoint never runs that loop.

settledReviews.title: fdbased: give each receive loop its own packet processors
settledReviews.body:
Closing an endpoint before attaching it to a NIC leaves its receive
processors asleep. New starts the goroutines, but only the receive
loop wakes them on exit. An unattached endpoint never runs that loop.

Create the queues in the receive loop and signal its workers to stop
when it returns. Each loop delivers through the dispatcher passed to

attachment ended. A subsequent attach cannot make an old batch

settledReviews.head: d4e65b135f3f4e6dbb811a59c38917bdb382d6c3
settledReviews.title: fdbased: start packet processors when a receiver attaches
settledReviews.summary: Open this receive-worker fix? Native AMD64 passed 18 receive cases, three live-save cases, four muxed cases and Nogo.
settledReviews.body:
Closing an FD endpoint before attaching it to a NIC leaves its receive
workers asleep. The constructor starts the workers, but only the read
loop signals them to stop. An unattached endpoint never runs that loop.

Create the queues and their workers when a dispatcher attaches. Each
receive loop delivers to that dispatcher and stops its own workers on
exit. A single processor still delivers inline.

On detach, close each queue before waking its reader. A reader already
returning from a receive syscall can then neither deliver the pending
batch nor enqueue the rest of it. Workers can finish delivering packets
already removed from their queues without blocking NIC removal on a
network stack callback.

For injectable endpoints, report attachment from the dispatcher used by
InjectInbound.
settledReviews.note: Use e.wg.Go and reconsider the extra processor-manager slice allocated for each attachment.

settledReviews.head: 0a70689c3640ab660307b0548f76087316803748
settledReviews.title: Implement IPv6 multicast hop and loopback options
settledReviews.body:
OpenJDK’s DatagramSocketMulticasting test failed when #16059 exposed a
multicast-capable interface. Its default DatagramSocket reads
IPV6_MULTICAST_HOPS even when sending to an IPv4 group. Netstack
returned ENOPROTOOPT. In IPv4-only mode, the JDK reads IP_MULTICAST_TTL
and IP_MULTICAST_LOOP into a one-byte buffer, which netstack also
rejected [1] [2].

Keep IPv4 and IPv6 multicast settings independent. On a dual-stack
socket sending to an IPv4-mapped group, Linux uses the IPv4 TTL and the
IPv6 socket’s loopback setting [3]. Change the connected route’s
loopback policy when the application sets the option. A send that
already acquired the route keeps its original policy. With host
networking, forward IPV6_MULTICAST_LOOP to the host socket.

Five shared syscall cases cover option lengths, independent values, and
delivery over a real multicast interface. Stock delivered a packet after
the sender disabled loopback. Linux, corrected netstack and corrected
hostinet delivered the following packet with IPv4 TTL 11 [4] [5]. The
original Java test also completed on eth0 in both its default and
IPv4-only modes [6]. A focused writer test sends two packets after
changing the option. Mutating the old route incorrectly disables
loopback for the first packet; retaining its acquired route passes, as
do the full network suite and its analyzer [7].

[1]: https://buildkite.com/organizations/gvisor/pipelines/pipeline/builds/52852/jobs/01a18479-3be3-4571-8423-f723c54a33b6/log
[2]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41131750771/artifacts/13013753296
[3]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/7d0a66e4b/net/core/sock.c#L774-L790
[4]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41139775803/artifacts/13017933283
[5]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41143755175/artifacts/13020224398
[6]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41143755175/artifacts/13020616149
[7]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/41145500718/artifacts/13021260853

settledReviews.head: 30143217adf5ade390febe1a48447b334c874c2e
settledReviews.title: Review the Buildkite command and its failure attribution
settledReviews.body:
AGENTS.md, line 209
The documented command exits 126 on a fresh checkout because buildkite.py is mode 100644. The BUILD file currently exposes only the test. Once the entry point is settled, could the smoke test run that exact command with --help?

tools/buildkite/buildkite.py, line 469
If attempt 1 failed and its retry is still running, retried is already true. With --logs this skips the only completed failure, and the documented rule would call the retry a pass. Could we show the retry as pending and keep that failed log available until we actually observe a passing attempt?

tools/buildkite/buildkite.py, line 416
make testlogs includes FLAKY as well as FAILED and TIMEOUT (tools/bazel.mk:408). If one target passes on a Bazel retry and a different target fails the job, the hook annotates both and this lists both as failed_targets. Could we separate final failures from failed attempts, or call these annotated targets when their final status is unknown?

tools/buildkite/buildkite.py, line 318
A passing Go test can log a line like client_test.go:17: expected connection reset before a different test panics. This puts the passing test’s message in failure_lines without its PASS context. Could ordinary test messages stay in the excerpt unless they can be associated with a failing test?

nodes.title: Keep packet header views across short reads
nodes.summary: Each partial read on #16886 clones the header prefix to remove consumed payload. Removing the range in place preserves preceding views and their contents. Two connected sockets transferring 4 MiB in 64-byte reads improved from 56.72 to 69.02 MiB/s on AMD64 (16 pairs, p=0.010).

settledReviews.head: 664d9fdb50b6bf530aa98ae738cce3c3cf68b8b1
settledReviews.title: Keep packet header views across short reads
settledReviews.body:
A partial packet read rebuilds the header prefix each time it removes
bytes from the payload. On connected TCP sockets with 64-byte reads,
trimming takes 2.50 ms of CPU per MiB at e9abe5401. Walking and cloning
the header prefix accounts for 1.30 ms of that time.

Remove the consumed range directly from the buffer. Keep preceding views
in place and split a view only when it contains bytes on both sides of
the removed range. Clones retain their original contents.

Two connected netstack sockets transferred 4 MiB on two pinned AMD EPYC
7763 CPUs with MTU 1500 and GRO and GSO disabled. Each transfer checked
the received bytes and EOF. Benchstat compared 16 alternating pairs.

                                  │   e9abe5401   │               279ee9ded               │
                                  │      B/s      │      B/s       vs base                │
    ConnectedTCPRead/read=64-2      56.72Mi ± 14%   69.02Mi ± 14%  +21.68% (p=0.010 n=16)

BenchmarkPacketDataReadTo drained a 1536-byte packet with a four-byte
header in 64-byte reads.

                                              │ drain-e9abe5401 │           drain-279ee9ded           │
                                              │     sec/op      │   sec/op     vs base                │
    PacketDataReadTo/headers=4/fragments=1-2        3.449µ ± 1%   1.737µ ± 0%  -49.63% (p=0.000 n=16)
    PacketDataReadTo/headers=4/fragments=16-2       9.322µ ± 1%   7.383µ ± 1%  -20.81% (p=0.000 n=16)
settledReviews.summary: Open after #16886 lands? Across 16 alternating pairs, 64-byte connected TCP reads improved 21.68% with unchanged data and EOF. The 64 KiB control showed no significant change. The ordinary owners and focused race runs passed.

path added in c451fa7d6 borrows those blocks and the TCP probe copies

settledReviews.head: 2effeef1023e837ec9ccb143b856ce9c3648d498
settledReviews.title: Clear only used entries in the graph decoder
settledReviews.body:
The graph decoder clears five pointer-bearing tables before returning them to its pool. Clearing each table to capacity also writes through unused slots. Restoring 50,000 tmpfs files on AMD64 cleared 23,347,000 bytes for the kernel frame, including 2,015,680 unused bytes. ARM64 cleared 2,016,424 unused bytes for the same workload [1].

Clear each table to its length. A load sizes the type, object and target tables before filling them and only appends to the callback table. Any slots beyond those lengths were zeroed on allocation or cleared by the last load that used them.

The cost also carries over to small loads that reuse a large decoder. The Large case of BenchmarkSmallGraphAfterRestore decodes one uint64 after a graph of 50,000 objects on one AMD64 CPU, with GC disabled [2].

       │    sec/op     │    sec/op    vs base                │
Large    121891.0n ± 1%   686.8n ± 6%  -99.44% (p=0.000 n=12)

nodes.head: a8e54633f47fda892caa896ab37f3200b662cccf
nodes.title: Claim TCP processor queue membership atomically
nodes.summary:
Two peer queues can contend for the same TCP listener. Replacing the membership mutex with one atomic claim removed 63 net lines. On two AMD64 CPUs, rejected duplicate queue operations fell from 20.24 to 12.01 ns and a successful dequeue/requeue from 25.20 to 17.24 ns. The 16-pair benchmark measures queue operations. The ordinary and race TCP suites, both architecture analyzers and both single-processor scheduling controls passed.

A fresh-connection HTTP/1.1 benchmark on two CPUs found no statistically distinguishable change with one or 16 concurrent clients (16 alternating pairs, 2,048 requests per sample). Every response matched. In a separate 16-client run on the parent, both TCP processors queued the listener. Of 2,235 duplicate enqueue attempts, 1,133 found the listener already queued on the other processor.

evidence.label: Original benchstat, sixteen paired samples, race and Nogo results
Queue handoff, race checks and paired benchmarks
Correct reference-definition punctuation; same parent and source tree
Fresh HTTP connections on one listener: benchstat, original samples and dispatcher counts

followup.nextAction: Open the reviewed PR after #17045 lands.

settledReviews.head: a8e54633f47fda892caa896ab37f3200b662cccf
settledReviews.title: Claim TCP processor queue membership atomically
settledReviews.body:
Peers of a listening socket can hash to different TCP processors. An
endpoint has only one pair of queue links. Each processor takes a
second mutex on the endpoint to test or clear its queue membership
while holding its own queue mutex.

Claim membership before inserting the endpoint and release it after
unlinking it. Each processor still protects its own list. Removing the
membership mutex also removes its lock-order annotations.

Benchstat for ProcessorQueueMembership on two AMD64 CPUs [1].

                   │ 77f1abcbe.txt │            01da93c33.txt          │
                   │    sec/op     │   sec/op     vs base              │
DuplicateEnqueue-2     20.24n ± 0%   12.01n ± 0%  -40.66% (p=0.000 n=16)
DequeueRequeue-2       25.20n ± 0%   17.24n ± 0%  -31.60% (p=0.000 n=16)

DuplicateEnqueue times two queues concurrently trying to enqueue the
same already queued endpoint. DequeueRequeue moves the endpoint from
one queue to the other.

[1]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42366670610
settledReviews.summary: Open the single-commit TCP PR after #17045 lands. The existing fairness behavior and the two-queue handoff passed on both implementations.

nodes.head: ebcea451de61a61957c82527fa94241827267cde
nodes.title: Inspect inline MemoryFiles in Sentry checkpoint dumps
nodes.summary:
Use runsc statefile -checkpoint FILE (or -checkpoint -html FILE) to inspect existing Sentry memory checkpoints. The option is listed by runsc help statefile. Historical images have no unambiguous format marker, so the default generic command can still print incomplete output. On native ARM64, two original images had 64 and 62 regions. The generic text and HTML commands each reported 3 regions in the wire image and 4 in the graph image. Their output stayed byte-identical before and after the change. The explicit mode matched every region in both renderers. The same images restored PID 1 and two files of 8,192 bytes. Removing or duplicating the private MemoryFile failed on both encodings.

The revised tests remove 70 net lines relative to approved 2d112a931. Across ten files the full change adds 535 lines and removes 76. Tests account for 187 added and two removed lines. The 348 other additions include 29 BUILD lines. The two printers share graph traversal and use pgalloc’s format definitions to find the owner graph and consume one private MemoryFile per owner. The earlier draft added 407 non-test lines, compared with 348 here. EOF just after the first two graphs is valid for a split checkpoint and cannot identify an entirely missing inline tail without external context.

evidence.label: Revised native ARM64 test suites and four mutations rejected for their expected failures
Fresh native ARM64 inspection, private file controls and same-image restores
Generic and split controls, filesystem-only guest and permanent reader tests
Independent historical corpus with 59 and 56 regions
Published single-commit PR #17208

the earlier object-framed layout and the separate split-page layout.

nodes.title: Hash TCP SYN cookies without shared state
nodes.summary: The listener and child now calculate each SYN cookie hash locally. The qualified source has the same Git tree as the proposal. On both source versions the TCP package, two-architecture Nogo checks, handshake and close cases, and race and digest controls passed. In 16 alternating AMD64 pairs, creating and validating one cookie reduced serial time by 18.56% for IPv4 and 17.31% for IPv6. All four cases fell from 12 allocations to zero. The shared cases measure two goroutines using the same listener. The experiment measures cookie operations.

evidence.label: TCP owners, race and digest checks, 16 pairs and four benchstat rows
Published single-commit pull request

settledReviews.head: e12c6d5914f88ae1cb28f7ec107f5a28b38f5db3
settledReviews.title: Hash TCP SYN cookies without shared state
settledReviews.summary: Open this one-commit SYN-cookie change? The two serial create-and-validate cases fell by 18.56% and 17.31%, and all four cases went from 12 allocations to zero. The shared case is a microbenchmark. Live connection throughput was outside its scope.
settledReviews.body:
A listener creating a SYN cookie and a child validating a late cookie
both use the listener's hash object. Each hash locks that object, resets
it, and discards its state after computing the digest.

Use a local hash for each calculation and supply storage for its result.
Remove the listener's hasher, its mutex, and the lock exclusions that
callers had to propagate.

Each benchmark operation creates and validates a cookie. The shared
cases use one listener from two goroutines on AMD64. All four cases
went from 12 allocations (384 B) per operation to zero. Benchstat for
SYNCookieRoundTrip, with the common benchmark prefix omitted [1]:

               │   before   │             after
               │   sec/op   │   sec/op     vs base
IPv4/Serial-2    624.2n ± 1%   508.3n ± 3%  -18.56% (p=0.000 n=16)
IPv4/Shared-2    731.2n ± 2%   296.6n ± 1%  -59.44% (p=0.000 n=16)
IPv6/Serial-2    627.5n ± 2%   518.9n ± 1%  -17.31% (p=0.000 n=16)
IPv6/Shared-2    740.4n ± 2%   304.9n ± 2%  -58.82% (p=0.000 n=16)

settledReviews.head: 9c541c3ae1cd68df1741882480d5bf184396e695
settledReviews.title: Wait for the TCP benchmark proxy and verify the sender rate
settledReviews.body:
The client proxy connects to the server before it listens for iperf.
The benchmark can start iperf during that interval, ignore a failed
client, and report success with an empty throughput field.

Wait for the listener without consuming its first connection, checking
each child for an early exit. Propagate the iperf client status and
require a numeric rate from its final sender row. With parallel
streams, that row carries the aggregate throughput.

Exercise the receiver with a retransmission inside acknowledged data
and a second retransmission that extends into new data. Check the

The installed shell driver exited before iperf3 started when its directory contained a space. Six error and interruption controls passed. An interrupted proxy flushed a 1,475-byte CPU profile. The original workflow failed because its observer counted nested iperf3 interval objects. The corrected readback verifies the original logs. Parent shell-driver correction

settledReviews.head: e20198216672dfba7dd01052df660dcad47be013
settledReviews.title: Run the TCP benchmark from Go
settledReviews.summary: Open this one-commit Go replacement after #17184 lands? It preserves the Bazel target and passes six real transfer modes and six failure or interruption controls.
settledReviews.body:
When the installed TCP benchmark's directory contains a space, its
generated Bash script splits the unquoted PATH assignment. Bash
rejects the remainder as an invalid identifier before iperf starts.

Run the benchmark directly from Go. Create private mount, network and
PID namespaces, pass each helper argument separately, and reap the
iperf server and both proxies. Read iperf3's aggregate sender rate and
sample the selected proxy's CPU before shutdown so writing a profile
does not inflate the result. Keep the Bazel entry point and resolve
sibling helpers when the installed binary is invoked through PATH.

Let the kernel reclaim the veth pairs and bridges with the namespace.
Linux 3.2 contains the bridge teardown fix [1]. gVisor requires Linux
5.6 or newer.

[1] https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/1ce5cce89

nodes.head: 2306ebce48ca1fa926651eaa58ff07a6da0cef76
nodes.title: Stage release downloads and checksums with Bazel
nodes.summary:
Bazel already knows each archive’s target architecture. This revision stages the Debian package and both download archives for AMD64 and ARM64, with one SHA512 checkfile per archive. Tagged builds add the wheel and source distribution. Debian signing and APT index generation stay on the trusted release host. The earlier shell publisher a7e84cf82 was withdrawn after review.

The tested commit 3432ab916 has the same source tree as the proposal. Bazel configured four native archive checksums in both modes, one Flit action for a tagged release and none for an untagged one. The local staging fixture reproduced a failure when a declared wheel appeared as a symlink. The corrected stager checked the opened file, copied both distributions, and replaced them with an empty directory on the next untagged build. Default and prebuilt Make paths rejected an incomplete release before signing. The default archive build was suppressed for that control.

On the separate integration d6f54c947, twelve fresh remote actions produced eight payloads and six SHA512 checkfiles. The offline stock and candidate publishers agreed for head, nightly, tagged, older-tag, ignored-tag and prebuilt-input releases. Tagged host checksum calls fell from 16 to zero. A disposable key signed the APT outputs. The test intercepted Twine and performed no cloud publication.

The immediate parent bb565d846 combines the #16490 architecture split and the Flit prerequisites. Buildkite activation also needs the host Bazel bootstrap from #16904 and a working toolchain for both target architectures. The deployed release queue remains unverified. Both release jobs forward the worker’s Bazel cache and execution options. With the options unset, both invocations matched their previous arguments.

nodes.head: e12c6d5914f88ae1cb28f7ec107f5a28b38f5db3
nodes.title: Hash TCP SYN cookies without shared state
nodes.summary: The listener and child now calculate each SYN cookie hash locally. The qualified source has the same Git tree as the proposal. On both source versions the TCP package, two-architecture Nogo checks, handshake and close cases, and race and digest controls passed. In 16 alternating AMD64 pairs, creating and validating one cookie reduced serial time by 18.56% for IPv4 and 17.31% for IPv6. All four cases fell from 12 allocations to zero. The shared cases measure two goroutines using the same listener. The experiment measures cookie operations.

evidence.label: TCP owners, race and digest checks, 16 pairs and four benchstat rows
Published single-commit pull request

settledReviews.head: e12c6d5914f88ae1cb28f7ec107f5a28b38f5db3
settledReviews.title: Hash TCP SYN cookies without shared state
settledReviews.summary: Open this one-commit SYN-cookie change? The two serial create-and-validate cases fell by 18.56% and 17.31%, and all four cases went from 12 allocations to zero. The shared case is a microbenchmark. Live connection throughput was outside its scope.
settledReviews.body:
A listener creating a SYN cookie and a child validating a late cookie
both use the listener's hash object. Each hash locks that object, resets
it, and discards its state after computing the digest.

Use a local hash for each calculation and supply storage for its result.
Remove the listener's hasher, its mutex, and the lock exclusions that
callers had to propagate.

Each benchmark operation creates and validates a cookie. The shared
cases use one listener from two goroutines on AMD64. All four cases
went from 12 allocations (384 B) per operation to zero. Benchstat for
SYNCookieRoundTrip, with the common benchmark prefix omitted [1]:

               │   before   │             after
               │   sec/op   │   sec/op     vs base
IPv4/Serial-2    624.2n ± 1%   508.3n ± 3%  -18.56% (p=0.000 n=16)
IPv4/Shared-2    731.2n ± 2%   296.6n ± 1%  -59.44% (p=0.000 n=16)
IPv6/Serial-2    627.5n ± 2%   518.9n ± 1%  -17.31% (p=0.000 n=16)
IPv6/Shared-2    740.4n ± 2%   304.9n ± 2%  -58.82% (p=0.000 n=16)

[1] https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42370230508

nodes.head: a6536561c6f56d5e76a64cb0a62bef2d6f3aa5ba
nodes.title: Check the endpoint lock on the advertised TCP window
nodes.summary:
TCP uses the endpoint mutex to update the receive window, its sequence number and the buffered-byte count sampled at the last advertisement. The RTT estimator also holds the receive queue mutex when it reads the advertised window. This change lets Nogo check the existing endpoint lock at both RTT reads and in the segment acceptance and window helpers. It adds no runtime locks.

On the final commit, a fresh TCP Nogo run on native AMD64 reported zero findings for both Linux AMD64 and ARM64. On the preceding two-field version, TestZeroScaledWindowReceive passed on AMD64. Removing only the RTT helper’s endpoint-lock precondition produced three findings across its two accesses on each analyzer architecture. Each finding named the missing endpoint mutex and the held receive queue mutex. The final revision also covers the buffered-byte sample and leaves the tested Go statements unchanged.

evidence.label: Standalone proposal and permanent description
Final source and both TCP analyzer results
Scaled-window regression, stock and guarded analyzers, and the missing endpoint-lock control
Merged advertised-window update and scaled zero-window regression
Published single-commit pull request

settledReviews.head: a6536561c6f56d5e76a64cb0a62bef2d6f3aa5ba
settledReviews.title: Check the endpoint lock on the advertised TCP window
settledReviews.summary: Open this single-commit PR to check the existing endpoint mutex at the TCP receive-window fields and their readers?
settledReviews.body:
When sending an ACK, TCP records the receive window, its sequence
number and the amount of buffered data. Later window updates use
that snapshot. Segment acceptance and RTT estimation also read the
advertised window. The RTT estimator takes the receive queue lock
to update its sample, but the window writer does not hold that lock.

Have checklocks require the endpoint lock on the snapshot fields and
on the helpers that read them. Their callers already hold it.

followup.disposition: The approved change is on #17202 at a6536561c.
followup.nextAction: Follow #17202 for maintainer review and import.

settledReviews.title: Avoid shell actions in build_test
settledReviews.summary: Open this single-commit PR to build the test binaries as default outputs and run a private native helper?
settledReviews.body:
The root build_test uses sixteen shell actions to mark its Go test
binaries as built, then starts an empty Bash script. Workers without
bash or env cannot run those actions or the test.

Bazel finishes building a test target’s default outputs before it
executes the test. Expose the requested binaries as default outputs
and use a small test-only Go executable. This keeps the binaries out
of the test runfiles.

followup.disposition: Investigating the upstream Skylib build_test rule

nodes.summary:
gVisor’s PacketImpact POSIX server uses gRPC 1.84.0. This MODULE.bazel change raises its selected c-ares version from 1.34.5.bcr.2 to the already-released 1.34.9.bcr.1. The previous package staged two headers with CopyFile actions. On Linux AMD64 and ARM64, the updated package uses one symlink for ares_config.h and reads ares_build.h directly from source.

The corrected query and materialized headers are in the second receipt. The tests cover the IP-literal RPC and header staging. DNS lookup and a full server build on an empty worker remain unverified. The reviewed commit and the tested ca5436ed33 have the same tree.

The approved source a5f2d3278 was published in #17210 as d7750b39e with the same parent and file tree. The revised description explains why the BCR overlay selects a platform header while preserving header bytes. The builder’s GNU tools, Bash and coreutils have other consumers, and it has no c-ares-specific package to remove.

nodes.summary:
The four safecopy files in this standalone change are byte-identical to those already on #15181. On AMD64 CPUs with ERMS, large clears use REP STOSQ inside the existing fault handler. The standalone diff contains only safecopy code and tests. If it lands first, those files drop out on the next #15181 rebase. If #15181 lands first, it delivers the same files.

On one AMD EPYC 9V45 core, clearing a resident 64 MiB shared ext4 mapping took 1,826.2 µs ±4% on stock and 907.1 µs ±5% with ERMS (−50.33%, p=0.000, 12 samples per arm). Both arms passed 71 named fault-handling and unaligned-clear controls. The measured candidate used the same three runtime files and the same test file as this revision. After measurement, the job failed while building benchstat because a package-metadata dependency was missing. The official benchstat tool subsequently processed the 24 original sample rows without rebuilding the workload. No end-to-end overlay allocation timing was collected.

settledReviews.head: d20802a06d38ffc13ffcc17bc175d047eee232d9
settledReviews.title: Use REP STOSQ for protected amd64 clears
settledReviews.summary: Open the standalone safecopy PR, or keep these four files in #15181?
settledReviews.body:
The memory allocator clears recycled disk-backed pages through safecopy
so it can recover if a mapped write faults. The amd64 clearing loop
issues sixteen vector stores for every 256 bytes.

Use the Go runtime's 2 KiB threshold to amortize REP STOSQ startup on
CPUs with ERMS. Keeping the stores inside memclr lets ZeroOut recover
from a fault and report how many bytes it cleared.

BenchmarkZeroDiskBacked64MiB times the protected clear of a resident
64 MiB shared ext4 mapping. Each sample refills the mapping outside the
timer. Twelve alternating samples per build ran on one AMD EPYC 9V45
core [1].

     │    stock     │                erms                 │
     │    sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base                │
       1826.2µ ± 4%   907.1µ ± 5%  -50.33% (p=0.000 n=12)

nodes.head: 1f50f469810b7a38f9de87e8d84cbed627ed5730
nodes.title: Retransmit the SYN-ACK when a peer repeats its SYN
nodes.summary:
When the client repeats its SYN, stock gVisor sends a bare ACK. Linux and the fix resend the SYN-ACK immediately. sendSyn now takes no arguments. It sets the passive SYN-ACK timestamp on a packet-local copy. Only retransmitSyn charges retries.

Linux and the approved 3c8aa1d51 revision passed the same four packet cases. The peer requested a retransmission 550 ms after its SYN. Linux replied after 2.3 ms and gVisor after 3.3 ms. Both waited one more second for the timed retry. All three handshake tests and both architecture analyzers also passed. The approved change is now open as #17206 at 1f50f4698 on the landed counter in master.

On the published 1f50f4698, the original TestRepeatedSynInSynRcvd passed uncached on a local AMD64 Linux Netstack TestRunner. It requires matching sequence and acknowledgment numbers on both SYN-ACKs before the same 500 ms deadline. After an immediate third SYN and completion of the handshake, the accepted socket reported exactly one retransmission. The original Go log and clean single-case XML agree.

settledReviews.head: 22d8cfc02a0c99c00fc9e9a97160d3dae8208b48
settledReviews.title: Retransmit the SYN-ACK when a peer repeats its SYN
settledReviews.body: When the client repeats its SYN before the retransmission timer fires, stock gVisor answers with a bare ACK. Linux and the fix reply immediately with the missing SYN-ACK, suppress a third immediate request, and report 1 ms RTT on the accepted socket. A prototype that reused the first local timestamp reported 1,553 ms. The final revision also matches Linux at the signed timestamp boundary.
settledReviews.note: Separate SYN retransmission accounting from sending the SYN.

settledReviews.head: 3c8aa1d51dcfb99a39d967c45046483cd42c561d
settledReviews.title: Retransmit the SYN-ACK when a peer repeats its SYN
settledReviews.body:
A passive TCP handshake answered a repeated SYN with a bare ACK. A
peer that missed the SYN-ACK then had to wait for the handshake timer
to retransmit it.

Resend the SYN-ACK for the original sequence number, subject to the
existing out-of-window response limit. A successful send restarts the
pending timer at its current interval and is charged to the accepted
socket. Give each passive retry its current transmit timestamp so the
final ACK can supply the initial RTT. This follows the Linux
request-socket path [1].

The packet test repeats the SYN before the initial timeout and checks
the sequence and acknowledgment numbers on the second SYN-ACK. A third
SYN immediately afterward leaves the accepted socket with one retry.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/net/ipv4/tcp_minisocks.c#L679-L719
settledReviews.summary: Open the revised passive SYN retry fix after #16809 lands? The four packet cases passed on native Linux and corrected gVisor.

followup.disposition: Published the approved 3c8aa1d51 patch as a single commit on #17206 at 1f50f4698. The changed paths and all 123 ordered added or removed lines matched after the rebase.

prefix leaves the list unchanged.

that prefix only for inexact values. The decoder may need to skip their

nodes.title: Require timestamps to reuse a TCP TIME_WAIT port
nodes.summary: With one ephemeral port and no negotiated timestamps, Linux kept the old connection’s port in TIME_WAIT. Stock gVisor let the next connection reuse it. The fix checks whether the old handshake negotiated timestamps. All 25 timestamp-enabled takeover rounds also passed, normally and under the race detector.

settledReviews.head: b6b0132b75b6d770a8977a7ef388d844550eb5a6
settledReviews.title: Require timestamps to reuse a TCP TIME_WAIT port
settledReviews.body:
With only one ephemeral port, a new connection could displace the
previous connection in TIME_WAIT even if the peer had not negotiated
timestamps. Its last timestamp update was never initialized, so the
one-second age check passed. Linux keeps the port reserved in this
case [1].

Check that the old handshake negotiated timestamps before reusing
its port. Exercise both outcomes after the reuse delay. In the takeover
test, late ACKs race Connect within each round. Finish each round
before another stack's cleanup can abort its closing socket.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/net/ipv4/tcp_ipv4.c#L164-L167

nodes.title: Store zero-sized target pointers separately
nodes.summary: On a live rootless systrap sandbox with 50,000 tmpfs files, the complete checkpoint was 4.55% faster across 16 alternating pairs (p=.014). All 34 restores verified the files, including the two warmups. A separate counting-writer Encode fell from 118.9 to 115.7 MiB per save with one more allocation at the median.

settledReviews.head: 22134a44640f341afc4e3357fae072515dccbbf8
settledReviews.title: Store zero-sized target pointers separately
settledReviews.summary: Open this single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
A pointer to a zero-sized field can share its address with an enclosing object that the graph encoder has yet to visit. The encoder keeps a list of these targets to resolve after traversal, but reserves space for a pointer and its numeric address in every target.

Store the live pointer beside its target ID in the deferred list and derive the address from it during resolution. Clear those pointers before returning the encoder to the pool. On AMD64 the common entry shrinks from 48 to 24 bytes and the deferred entry grows from 4 to 16.

The complete Container.Checkpoint timing covers a running rootless systrap sandbox with 50,000 tmpfs files. Each build used one warmup followed by 16 measured checkpoints. [1]

```
                   │    stock     │               sparse               │
                   │    sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base               │
RootlessCheckpoint   275.4m ±  4%   262.8m ± 3%  -4.55% (p=0.014 n=16)
```

A separate comparison times state.Save to a counting writer after loading the kernel. The median allocation count rose from 100,936 to 100,937. [2]

```
                               │    stock     │               sparse                │
                               │    sec/op    │    sec/op     vs base               │
CheckpointFile/Encode            125.5m ±  3%   121.1m ±  2%  -3.49% (p=0.001 n=12)

                               │     stock     │               sparse                │
                               │     B/op      │     B/op      vs base               │
CheckpointFile/Encode             118.9Mi ± 0%   115.7Mi ± 0%  -2.63% (p=0.000 n=12)
```

[1]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42451269851/artifacts/13605948652
[2]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42450100175/artifacts/13606190410

The graph encoder can discover a pointer to a field before the enclosing struct. When the struct absorbs that field, it allocates auxiliary metadata and a slice to hold one child index.

Store a single child index directly in its parent. When a container absorbs multiple children, copy their indices once in discovery order so the encoder can splice their saved bytes into the parent.

nodes.head: cd9d815dcc6558cc8d5a9b0afcd118d0718c3ef1
nodes.title: Abort FUSE requests under the connection mutex
nodes.summary: Both FUSE transports already update background request limits under connection.mu. Holding that mutex through Abort closes the interval in which a host reply can claim a pending request after disconnect. All 33 runtime cases and both architecture lock analyses passed. Removing the nosave mutex changes the graph checkpoint layout fingerprint.

evidence.label: Abort, pending requests, restore and both analyzers
Saved field layout and unlocked-access controls
Published single-commit PR #17241

settledReviews.head: cd9d815dcc6558cc8d5a9b0afcd118d0718c3ef1
settledReviews.title: Abort FUSE requests under the connection mutex
settledReviews.summary: Open this single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
Both FUSE transports hold connection.mu when INIT updates the background request limits. Abort takes asyncMu under the same lock without accessing those limits. It then releases connection.mu between marking the connection disconnected and canceling outstanding requests. A host reply can claim a pending request in that interval.

Guard the background fields with connection.mu and keep it held through Abort. Wake callers waiting for INIT, cancel each pending request in place, then close the full-queue channel after its last notification.

The saved fields and their order stay the same. Removing the nosave mutex changes the graph checkpoint layout fingerprint.

followup.disposition: The approved change was published as #17241.
followup.nextAction: Follow upstream review on #17241.

nodes.head: 18e64362979d3736afd49753eb1504e029a3f2f4
nodes.title: Wait for the TCP burst before draining the socket
nodes.summary: In Buildkite #53913, TestReduceRecvBuf read all 8,193 offered bytes. It can free buffer space while the DUT is still processing the burst. The test now keeps the reverse TCP window closed until it has sent the burst and waits for the second byte of the DUT’s queued reply before draining the socket. In four fresh runs per stack, the reply acknowledged 5,600 bytes on Linux and 7,000 on gVisor. The application read that amount and then got EAGAIN in all eight runs.

evidence.label: Eight Linux and gVisor test results with independent packet captures
Earlier held-reader and drained-reader controls on both stacks
Original Buildkite full-read failure at line 210330
Approved change published as #17230

settledReviews.head: 18e64362979d3736afd49753eb1504e029a3f2f4
settledReviews.title: Wait for the TCP burst before draining the socket
settledReviews.summary: Open this single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
TestReduceRecvBuf failed after reading all 8,193 bytes it offered [1]. The test can call recv while the TCP receiver is still processing the burst. That read frees buffer space for later segments.

Queue a two-byte reply with the reverse TCP window closed. Open the window after sending the burst and wait for the second reply byte before draining the socket. Its ACK gives the accepted byte count. A one-byte zero-window probe cannot satisfy the wait.

[1]: https://buildkite.com/gvisor/pipeline/builds/53913#01a1b9e5-b60c-4642-adc2-60db34945a04

nodes.head: bb990fc8fd34475910cc2ae58a2809c70743e793
nodes.title: Use the exec platform for the module map generator
nodes.summary: The proposed revert removes #899’s forced musl build from the public module map generator. The AMD64 GNU execution configuration dropped from 1,352 musl compile actions and four musl archive actions to zero for this generator. With the same GNU target, the GNU and explicitly musl workers produced byte-identical 923,587-byte maps covering 3,397 header sizes. A Linux worker without the glibc loader must declare @llvm//constraints/libc:musl. LLVM 0.8.26 predates #899.

evidence.label: Opened upstream PR at the approved commit
Restore the generator’s original executable label and implementation
GNU and musl execution on AMD64, configured action counts and module map bytes
Merged change that forced musl for Linux generators
Conclusion of the separate six-helper proposal
Upstream merge at 8c66cda18

settledReviews.head: bb990fc8fd34475910cc2ae58a2809c70743e793
settledReviews.title: Use the exec platform for the module map generator
settledReviews.summary: Open this single-commit hermetic-llvm PR to revert #899?
settledReviews.body:
eb198127b forces the module map generator to use musl on Linux, even when the execution platform selects glibc. On an x86-64 GNU worker this puts 1,352 musl compile actions in the generator's build graph. [1]

Build the public module-map-generator target directly. The module map rule already requests its executable in the execution configuration, so the worker's libc determines how the generator is linked. A GNU worker can use its glibc loader and libraries. Linux workers without them must declare @llvm//constraints/libc:musl to get a static generator.

With the same GNU target, the GNU worker's generator had no musl compile actions. The musl worker's generator ran in a chroot without a C runtime. Both produced the same module map, including the sizes of its textual headers. [1]

[1]: https://github.com/tamird/hermetic-llvm/actions/runs/42430088604/artifacts/13597530149

followup.disposition: Upstream merged the approved proposal as 8c66cda18.
followup.nextAction: No further review action on #927.

settledReviews.head: e7991239d16479fee782b6c3e1bc1e8e954c2d10
settledReviews.title: Check locking for TCP zero-window probes
settledReviews.summary: Open this single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
e590314fe introduced TCP zero-window probes. The retransmission timer counts unanswered probes and enforces the user timeout. An ACK that reopens the peer's window resets the probe count and the start of that timeout. Both paths hold the endpoint mutex, but checklocks cannot diagnose an unlocked reset.

Annotate the probe state and require the endpoint mutex in the helper that clears it.

nodes.head: b6b0132b75b6d770a8977a7ef388d844550eb5a6
nodes.title: Require timestamps to reuse a TCP TIME_WAIT port
nodes.summary: With one ephemeral port and no negotiated timestamps, Linux kept the old connection’s port in TIME_WAIT. Stock gVisor let the next connection reuse it. The fix checks whether the old handshake negotiated timestamps. All 25 timestamp-enabled takeover rounds also passed, normally and under the race detector.

evidence.label: Single commit for review
Native Linux socket comparison
Stock and corrected tests, including all race rounds
Approved change published as #17229

settledReviews.head: b6b0132b75b6d770a8977a7ef388d844550eb5a6
settledReviews.title: Require timestamps to reuse a TCP TIME_WAIT port
settledReviews.body:
With only one ephemeral port, a new connection could displace the
previous connection in TIME_WAIT even if the peer had not negotiated
timestamps. Its last timestamp update was never initialized, so the
one-second age check passed. Linux keeps the port reserved in this
case [1].

Check that the old handshake negotiated timestamps before reusing
its port. Exercise both outcomes after the reuse delay. In the takeover
test, late ACKs race Connect within each round. Finish each round
before another stack's cleanup can abort its closing socket.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676/net/ipv4/tcp_ipv4.c#L164-L167
settledReviews.summary: Open the standalone PR to require negotiated timestamps for TIME_WAIT port reuse?

followup.nextAction: Follow #17229 for maintainer review and import.

nodes.head: 18e64362979d3736afd49753eb1504e029a3f2f4
nodes.title: Wait for the TCP burst before draining the socket
nodes.summary: In Buildkite #53913, TestReduceRecvBuf read all 8,193 offered bytes. It can free buffer space while the DUT is still processing the burst. The test now keeps the reverse TCP window closed until it has sent the burst and waits for the second byte of the DUT’s queued reply before draining the socket. In four fresh runs per stack, the reply acknowledged 5,600 bytes on Linux and 7,000 on gVisor. The application read that amount and then got EAGAIN in all eight runs.

evidence.label: Eight Linux and gVisor test results with independent packet captures
Earlier held-reader and drained-reader controls on both stacks
Original Buildkite full-read failure at line 210330
Approved change published as #17230

settledReviews.head: 18e64362979d3736afd49753eb1504e029a3f2f4
settledReviews.title: Wait for the TCP burst before draining the socket
settledReviews.summary: Open this single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
TestReduceRecvBuf failed after reading all 8,193 bytes it offered [1]. The test can call recv while the TCP receiver is still processing the burst. That read frees buffer space for later segments.

Queue a two-byte reply with the reverse TCP window closed. Open the window after sending the burst and wait for the second reply byte before draining the socket. Its ACK gives the accepted byte count. A one-byte zero-window probe cannot satisfy the wait.

[1]: https://buildkite.com/gvisor/pipeline/builds/53913#01a1b9e5-b60c-4642-adc2-60db34945a04

followup.nextAction: Follow #17230 for maintainer review and import.

nodes.title: Store a single absorbed graph child inline

settledReviews.head: 4774ec693b5ba804bff5918352ff1ff3722f2f65
settledReviews.title: Store a single absorbed graph child inline
settledReviews.summary: Open this single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
The graph encoder can discover a pointer to a field before the enclosing struct. When the struct absorbs that field, it allocates auxiliary metadata and a slice to hold one child index.

Store a single child index directly in its parent. When a container absorbs multiple children, copy their indices once in discovery order so the encoder can splice their saved bytes into the parent.

With a kernel restored from a checkpoint of 50,000 tmpfs files, BenchmarkCheckpointFile/Encode times state.Save to a counting writer. [1]

```
                            │    stock    │               inline               │
                            │   sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base               │
CheckpointFile/Encode         147.8m ± 1%   140.0m ± 1%  -5.33% (p=0.000 n=12)

                            │    stock     │                inline                 │
                            │     B/op     │     B/op      vs base                 │
CheckpointFile/Encode         118.8Mi ± 0%   114.6Mi ± 0%  -3.54% (p=0.000 n=12)

                            │     stock     │                inline                │
                            │   allocs/op   │ allocs/op   vs base                  │
CheckpointFile/Encode         100938.0 ± 0%   769.0 ± 0%  -99.24% (p=0.000 n=12)
```

Two independent trials timed the complete checkpoint of a running rootless systrap sandbox. The first found no detectable change. The second measured a reduction. Each used one warmup and 16 measured checkpoints per build. [2] [3]

```
                   │    stock    │               inline                │
                   │   sec/op    │    sec/op     vs base               │
RootlessCheckpoint   270.6m ± 3%   262.2m ±  7%  -3.12% (p=0.011 n=16)
```

[1]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42437428710/artifacts/13600866530
[2]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42441418004/artifacts/13602540039
[3]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42443424031/artifacts/13603111920

settledReviews.summary: Post the measured full-checkpoint result for #17231, #17232, #17233 and #17240 together.
settledReviews.body:
I measured the full `Container.Checkpoint` call for a rootless systrap sandbox with 50,000 empty files in tmpfs and compression disabled. I compared master at 975fb1722 with [#17231](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/17231), [#17232](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/17232), [#17233](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/17233) and [#17240](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/17240) together. Each build ran 16 measured trials on the same AMD64 worker, alternating which build ran first.

```text
                       │    stock    │                four                 │
                       │   sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base                │
RootlessCheckpoint       271.5m ± 1%   242.9m ± 5%  -10.51% (p=0.000 n=16)
```

All 34 checkpoints, including one warmup per build, restored successfully. After each restore the guest ran `/bin/true` and the test verified every file. [Benchstat and original samples](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42570572235/artifacts/13653214709).

nodes.head: 22134a44640f341afc4e3357fae072515dccbbf8
nodes.title: Store zero-sized target pointers separately
nodes.summary: On a live rootless systrap sandbox with 50,000 tmpfs files, the complete checkpoint was 4.55% faster across 16 alternating pairs (p=.014). All 34 restores verified the files, including the two warmups. A separate counting-writer Encode fell from 118.9 to 115.7 MiB per save with one more allocation at the median.

evidence.label: Combined checkpoint comparison of #17231, #17232 and #17233 on 50,000 files
Live 50,000-file checkpoint and 34 verified restores
Counting-writer Encode, allocation counts and cross-loads
Approved change published as #17232

settledReviews.head: 22134a44640f341afc4e3357fae072515dccbbf8
settledReviews.title: Store zero-sized target pointers separately
settledReviews.summary: Open this single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
A pointer to a zero-sized field can share its address with an enclosing object that the graph encoder has yet to visit. The encoder keeps a list of these targets to resolve after traversal, but reserves space for a pointer and its numeric address in every target.

Store the live pointer beside its target ID in the deferred list and derive the address from it during resolution. Clear those pointers before returning the encoder to the pool. On AMD64 the common entry shrinks from 48 to 24 bytes and the deferred entry grows from 4 to 16.

The complete Container.Checkpoint timing covers a running rootless systrap sandbox with 50,000 tmpfs files. Each build used one warmup followed by 16 measured checkpoints. [1]

```
                   │    stock     │               sparse               │
                   │    sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base               │
RootlessCheckpoint   275.4m ±  4%   262.8m ± 3%  -4.55% (p=0.014 n=16)
```

A separate comparison times state.Save to a counting writer after loading the kernel. The median allocation count rose from 100,936 to 100,937. [2]

```
                               │    stock     │               sparse                │
                               │    sec/op    │    sec/op     vs base               │
CheckpointFile/Encode            125.5m ±  3%   121.1m ±  2%  -3.49% (p=0.001 n=12)

                               │     stock     │               sparse                │
                               │     B/op      │     B/op      vs base               │
CheckpointFile/Encode             118.9Mi ± 0%   115.7Mi ± 0%  -2.63% (p=0.000 n=12)
```

[1]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42451269851/artifacts/13605948652
[2]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42450100175/artifacts/13606190410

nodes.head: 576430c42e0bb216b2611274a20d08463741c8a9
nodes.title: Reserve graph prefixes for inexact values
nodes.summary: The graph encoder writes a length prefix for inexact values. On a real tmpfs checkpoint with 50,000 files, reserving prefixes only for those values reduced the final output buffer by 1,007,616 bytes. Across 12 paired encodes, allocated bytes fell from 118.9 MiB to 117.9 MiB (−0.81%). Allocation count stayed at 100,937 per encode, and the timing difference was inconclusive (p=.551).

evidence.label: Combined checkpoint comparison of #17231, #17232 and #17233 on 50,000 files
50,000-file checkpoint, buffer capacities and original benchstat
Approved change published as #17233

settledReviews.head: 576430c42e0bb216b2611274a20d08463741c8a9
settledReviews.title: Reserve graph prefixes for inexact values
settledReviews.summary: Open this single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
Since 6fb2e9fe2, the graph encoder has reserved ten bytes for a length
prefix on every value object when sizing its output buffer. It writes
that prefix only for inexact values. The decoder may need to skip their
data until a reference supplies the exact type.

Use the object table's objInexact flag to reserve the prefix.

Encoding a kernel restored from a checkpoint with 50,000 empty tmpfs
files reserved space for 100,727 exact values' unused prefixes. The
output buffer shrank from 8,306,688 to 7,299,072 bytes. Both versions
made 100,937 allocations per encode. [1]

                      │    stock     │                fixed                │
                      │     B/op     │     B/op      vs base               │
CheckpointFile/Encode   118.9Mi ± 0%   117.9Mi ± 0%  -0.81% (p=0.000 n=12)

[1]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42431995900/artifacts/13598227954
