nodes.head: fe04aebd118f84df78dc0173e515f854d1809347
nodes.title: Start TCP checksum offload after the serialized IP header
nodes.summary:
With the experiment option enabled, checksum offload started four bytes early for IPv4 and eight early for IPv6. Using the serialized header length delivered the 21-byte write in all four option-toggle cases over a private veth.

Full-sized writes still need room for the IP option. The conservative prototype delivered all 72 transfers in the veth comparison but reserved bytes for sockets that never enabled the option. The first-use proposal kept their full payload. It reduced the next payload from 1,200 to 1,196 bytes on IPv4 or 1,192 on IPv6 when a socket actually enabled the option on a capable route. Both sizes survived two restores. The ordinary ACK-accounting fix credited a previously transmitted 1,200-byte packet once on each family. These cases use explicit Netstack settings outside #16393’s default.

evidence.label: Original peer and checksum-offset observations
All 12 corrected host-offload cases
Permanent IPv4, IPv6 and fdbased tests
Published as #17234 with both requested references
Native TCP packet sizing and delivery across 144 transfers
IPv4 checkpoint restore across NIC capability changes and independent Reno accounting observation
IPv6 option sizing and Reno window after one or two restores
Combined IPv4 and IPv6 restore packet and ACK observations
First-use sizing proposal
First-use and restore packets

settledReviews.head: 5b1967499a0d9bde3eb45444398089b48fa9149e
settledReviews.title: Use the serialized IP header for checksum offload
settledReviews.summary: Approved for submission after adding references [1] and [2] to the change record.
settledReviews.body:
078be6271 and cd70b0a4c added the experiment option to IPv4 and IPv6. With the option enabled, fdbased asks the host to start the TCP checksum at byte 34 or 54 of the Ethernet frame. The serialized IP headers put TCP at byte 38 or 62 instead.

Set GSO.L3HdrLen when each IP implementation writes the network header. Cover the experiment option with host offload enabled and disabled. Correcting the checksum lets a short write reach the peer. Full-size IPv6 writes at the route MSS still exceed the MTU.

followup.disposition: Published the exact approved code with the two requested citations.
followup.nextAction: Follow #17234 for maintainer review and import.

nodes.head: 5b9d447ba1bbfd67e6db860d585239167d1bc9f9
nodes.title: Guard POSIX timer teardown and checkpoint walks
nodes.summary: The timer syscalls, exec and final exit use timerMu for the interval timer table. Checkpoint takes the same lock when pausing and resuming the timers. The analyzer passed on AMD64 and ARM64. Removing the checkpoint pause lock reported the same unguarded read twice per architecture. The fork job recorded a failure because its result reader expected one diagnostic. Its original Linux and lockdep systrap tests passed, including save/restore with two pending timer IDs, their invalidation after exec, and exit with a newly armed timer. The syscall fixture is fork-only.

evidence.label: Signed timer-lock proposal
Original lock analysis, Linux syscall and lockdep systrap save/restore results
Published single-commit PR #17239

followup.disposition: The approved change was published as #17239.
followup.nextAction: Follow upstream review on #17239.

settledReviews.head: 5b9d447ba1bbfd67e6db860d585239167d1bc9f9
settledReviews.title: Guard POSIX timer teardown and checkpoint walks
settledReviews.body:
Timer syscalls use the thread group's timerMu to look up timers and allocate IDs. Exec and final exit instead copied the table into a slice under the signal mutex, then released that mutex to destroy the timers.

Hold timerMu while destroying the timers, as timer_delete already does. Drop the TaskSet and signal locks before destruction so a timer can finish delivering its signal. Clear the existing map for reuse after exec, without allocating a temporary slice.

Guard the table and next timer ID with checklocks. Take the same mutex when checkpoint pauses and resumes the group's timers.
settledReviews.summary: Open the single signed timer-lock change against gVisor master.

nodes.head: b2d9986a40604f82df42c322122ad61313104cfa
nodes.title: Allow build_test to run without a shell
nodes.summary:
Skylib’s build_test can use a declared marker tool on the execution platform and a declared runner on the target platform. Callers can supply either independently. Omitted tools retain their existing defaults. The private Linux consumer exposed 16 empty markers and one runner in its runfiles while building all 17 checked files.

On the earlier supplier revision, each real gVisor build_test built 16 manual binaries and passed: AMD64 natively and ARM64 through QEMU on the same AMD64 host. The receipt retains both test results and 32 link-output/marker-input pairs. The collector failed while reading the action graph, so those two runs do not establish the physical consumer runfiles or payload digests. Both ran through Bazel’s standard POSIX test harness. Replacing Bazel’s own shell wrapper is tracked separately in #30837.

The final revision keeps the same marker, runner and permanent test. All ten queried labels had the expected effective sizes on the final source. The checked-in reference matches the canonical Stardoc output.

evidence.label: Single-commit supplier proposal
Tested source with the same tree
Bazel’s separate POSIX test-wrapper work
Earlier supplier revision
Generated API reference on the final source
Canonical docs update, uncached docs test and Buildifier
Ten effective test sizes on the final source
Direct argument, test runfiles and deliberately broken consumer controls
Private fixture on Bazel 7.7.0, 8.5.0 and 9.3.1
Two real gVisor owners: native AMD64 and emulated ARM64

followup.nextAction: Follow review on #648.

settledReviews.head: b2d9986a40604f82df42c322122ad61313104cfa
settledReviews.title: Allow build_test to run without a shell
settledReviews.body:
build_test uses a genrule to create a marker for each batch of checked targets. Its test executable is also a shell script on POSIX. Both steps require a shell on the machine that runs them.

Let callers provide a tool that creates an empty file on the execution platform and an executable that runs on the test’s target platform. Pass the marker path as a single argument, including when the target name contains shell metacharacters. The markers keep the checked targets in the build graph when another test inherits only the runfiles, without adding their binaries to that test’s runfiles.

In gVisor, both the AMD64 and ARM64 tests built all 16 selected binaries. The AMD64 test ran natively and the ARM64 test ran under QEMU on the same worker. [1]

[1]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42494568795/artifacts/13622938785

nodes.head: b64ce83201bc89cc9d52186a15ba982b02b4266e
nodes.title: Use transmitted packet boundaries when processing TCP ACKs
nodes.summary: With an ordinary IPv4 route, one ACK for a pre-restore 1,200-byte packet grew Reno’s congestion window from 10 to 12 on #15634 after the new route limited payloads to 1,196 bytes. The follow-up counts recorded packet ends for data sent once outside recovery and credited the packet once, growing the window to 11. Three other native cases passed on both sources. A message-only revision preserves the measured source tree. The same one-packet overcount reproduced when an IPv6 restore added an eight-byte experiment option. With both fixes, the same old packet earned one credit at restored MSS 1,196 on IPv4 and 1,192 on IPv6.

evidence.label: One commit on the current #15634 head
Qualified prior wording, identical tree and direct parent
Native stock and candidate logs/XML for all four cases
TCP performance and recovery guide
IPv6 option sizing and Reno window after one or two restores
Combined IPv4 and IPv6 restore packet and ACK observations

followup.disposition: Tamir approved the proposal and the guide row. The migration result is now published in #16670.
followup.nextAction: Open the approved single commit after #15634 lands.

settledReviews.head: b64ce83201bc89cc9d52186a15ba982b02b4266e
settledReviews.title: Use transmitted packet boundaries when processing TCP ACKs
settledReviews.body:
The sender transmitted a 1,200-byte TCP packet before checkpoint. After restore, the route allowed 1,196-byte payloads. The sender divided the old packet's length by the new MSS and rounded up, so its cumulative ACK grew Reno's congestion window from 10 to 12.

For data sent once outside loss recovery, count the packet ends recorded at transmission. A queue split preserves those ends, so a partial ACK earns credit only when it crosses one. After a retransmission the recorded boundaries describe the latest copy, and during loss recovery the sender estimates how many copies remain in flight. Keep the existing estimate in those cases.

With this change, acknowledging the original packet grew Reno's window from 10 to 11 in the migration test [1].

[1]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42502020892/artifacts/13626101046
settledReviews.summary:
Approve opening the standalone PR after #15634 lands and adding this single migration row to the existing #16670 guide.

| One ACK grows Reno’s window by two after migration | #15634 → [ordinary ACK follow-up](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/b64ce8320) · [migration test output](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42502020892/artifacts/13626101046) | Restoring onto an IPv4 route with MTU 1,236 lowered the payload limit from 1,200 to 1,196 bytes. Acknowledging one 1,200-byte packet sent before restore grew the window from 10 to 12 on #15634 and from 10 to 11 with the follow-up. |

settledReviews.head: 5b9d447ba1bbfd67e6db860d585239167d1bc9f9
settledReviews.title: Guard POSIX timer teardown and checkpoint walks
settledReviews.body:
Timer syscalls use the thread group's timerMu to look up timers and allocate IDs. Exec and final exit instead copied the table into a slice under the signal mutex, then released that mutex to destroy the timers.

Hold timerMu while destroying the timers, as timer_delete already does. Drop the TaskSet and signal locks before destruction so a timer can finish delivering its signal. Clear the existing map for reuse after exec, without allocating a temporary slice.

Guard the table and next timer ID with checklocks. Take the same mutex when checkpoint pauses and resumes the group's timers.

nodes.title: Abort FUSE requests under the connection mutex
nodes.summary: Both FUSE transports already update background request limits under connection.mu. Holding that mutex through Abort closes the interval in which a host reply can claim a pending request after disconnect. All 33 runtime cases and both architecture lock analyses passed. settledReviews.head: cd9d815dcc6558cc8d5a9b0afcd118d0718c3ef1
settledReviews.title: Abort FUSE requests under the connection mutex
settledReviews.summary: Open this single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
Both FUSE transports hold connection.mu when INIT updates the background request limits. Abort takes asyncMu under the same lock without accessing those limits. It then releases connection.mu between marking the connection disconnected and canceling outstanding requests. A host reply can claim a pending request in that interval.

Guard the background fields with connection.mu and keep it held through Abort. Wake callers waiting for INIT, cancel each pending request in place, then close the full-queue channel after its last notification.

The saved fields and their order stay the same. Removing the nosave mutex changes the graph checkpoint layout fingerprint.

git range-diff a412fc982^! 4b33ee009^!
settledReviews.body:
451b92800 added two shutdown tests that depend on /bin/cat and /bin/sleep. If either program is missing, its test fails before stopNetgofer runs. A PID check alone also accepts a force-killed child in the graceful case.

nodes.head: 5bc25951220fabd92bee33b5862da3271391ada8
nodes.title: Run dependency checks without Bash
nodes.summary:
The netstack, runsc and Sentry dependency tests traverse the configured dependency graph in an aspect. Their generated executables use Bash even for a passing graph, and the shell expands dollar signs in forbidden labels. Using Bazel’s AnalysisTestResultInfo still requires /bin/sh. It also drops transitive validation outputs: on both CPU configurations, the original netstack, runsc and Sentry owners exposed zero, one and two validation artifacts respectively. The runsc and Sentry validations cover prebuilt Protobuf tools. With an intentionally failing validation action, the original rule failed and the analysis-test replacement passed without running that action.

The single-commit change keeps the ordinary test rule and includes its diagnostic in the test runfiles. All three real TestRunners passed uncached on native AMD64 with /bin and /usr/bin masked for the test child. A forbidden edge printed the literal label price$usd and exited 1. The AMD64 and ARM64 executables also returned the expected statuses in empty roots, with ARM64 executed under QEMU on AMD64. With the executable and test label unchanged, a fresh pass was followed by a cached pass. Changing just the generated report produced a fresh failure. The deliberate transitive validation still failed.

The same patch on the compiler integration at 08ca50082 passed all three tests on each of the native AMD64 and ARM64 remote workers. Both Bazel invocations exited 0. The original receipt records six uncached remote TestResults and their XML and log digests. It binds the requested worker image and runtime wrapper to the netstack owner on both architectures. The reporter subsequently failed when it looked for private _validation outputs in ordinary target-completion events. The separate native/QEMU qualification verified validation propagation and the failing action directly.

evidence.label: Single-commit dependency checker
Stock, standard analysis test and native control. All 18 original log/XML pairs
Exact-source native AMD64 tests, direct AMD64 and ARM64 QEMU execution, cache and validation controls
Same source patch on the compiler integration
Six remote TestResults and their original log and XML digests
Published pull request

nodes.summary:
Guard the endpoint’s port reservation flag with its mutex. Record all four reservation details after ephemeral port selection succeeds. The synchronous callback returns success only after it registers the endpoint. Restore clears the flag and restores the closed state in one critical section before stack cleanup.

The TCP analyzer reported zero findings on AMD64 and ARM64. Restoring the previous callback or the unlocked restore assignment independently produced diagnostics at the corresponding statement on both architectures. All 93 named native AMD64 XML cases passed across seven selected Go tests. A saved closed endpoint restored to StateClose and its port could be rebound. settledReviews.head: cc9a10f3a7e2a8bdb971fd984da42ba941993062
settledReviews.title: Guard TCP port reservation ownership
settledReviews.summary: Open the single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
Bind, accept and cleanup hold the endpoint mutex when they record or release a port. Restore cleared the reservation flag without that mutex when returning a saved endpoint to StateClose.

Mark isPortReserved as guarded by the endpoint mutex. Record the port's reservation details after PickEphemeralPort returns successfully. Its callback accepts a port only after registering the endpoint.

Clear the flag and restore StateClose in the same critical section. Release the endpoint mutex before removing the endpoint from the stack's cleanup list.

settledReviews.head: ba00452d5ef8966fb8ee9df0de6330abb45e344f
settledReviews.title: Restart TCP keepalive after a disabled timer fires
settledReviews.summary: Open the single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
Disabling SO_KEEPALIVE leaves the clock timer running. If it fires while keepalive is disabled, the callback returns before consuming the orphaned timer. Re-enabling keepalive then records a new deadline but leaves an idle connection without a scheduled probe.

Consume the clock wakeup before checking SO_KEEPALIVE. Check that an idle connection stays quiet while keepalive is disabled and resumes probing when the option is enabled again.

settledReviews.head: 59a8c8cc138ea704a5e635b794a9e76197faa744
settledReviews.title: Consume TCP timer wakeups before handling expiry
settledReviews.summary:
Open this revised timer PR? It moves wakeup consumption into the timer API. All three packet tests, both owning suites, and both analyzers passed. The proposed description reports the two increases in bytes allocated per operation.

git -C ~/code/gvisor range-diff ba00452d5^! 59a8c8cc1^!
settledReviews.body:
Turning SO_KEEPALIVE off while a probe is pending leaves a clock
callback scheduled. If the callback runs while keepalive is off, the
next enable can mistake the spent callback for one that will still
fire. The connection then sends no more probes.

Have the timer consume each clock wake under the endpoint mutex
before calling the protocol handler. A canceled arm becomes idle,
an early wake rearms the clock for the current deadline, and only a
due arm reaches the handler. This also lets cleanup discard a
callback that was already waiting for the mutex.

nodes.head: 0235b052b4ea92fb70e12b0eb58f576d2688463a
nodes.title: Honor SO_BINDTODEVICE when choosing a TCP connect route
nodes.summary:
A wildcard-bound TCP socket could select a source address on a device other than the one named by SO_BINDTODEVICE. The fix uses the live option for outgoing route selection and preserves the device saved with the port reservation.

Two isolated Linux syscall tests and the stock and fixed systrap runs used identical C++ fixture bytes. Stock chose 192.0.2.129 for both bound devices. Linux and fixed gVisor chose 192.0.2.1 on veth1 and 192.0.2.129 on veth2, whether the application set the device before or after wildcard bind. For an IPv6 destination scope that conflicted with the device, Linux and the fix returned EINVAL. Stock returned ENETUNREACH.

All three changed-device checkpoint controls and all three endpoint device cases passed on both gVisor revisions. The fixed TCP analyzer passed on AMD64 and ARM64. The original ordinary Linux runner skipped the syscall tests for lack of CAP_NET_ADMIN. Both tests executed uncached in the isolated Linux recovery. The IPv4 observations come from getsockname during a nonblocking connect.

evidence.label: Original report: TCP connect can ignore the selected device
Stock and fixed systrap syscall results, checkpoint and endpoint cases, and both Nogo architectures
Exact C++ fixture on isolated Linux with both syscall cases executed
Approved change published as #17278

followup.nextAction: Follow #17278 for maintainer review and import.

settledReviews.head: 0235b052b4ea92fb70e12b0eb58f576d2688463a
settledReviews.title: Honor SO_BINDTODEVICE when choosing a TCP connect route
settledReviews.summary: Open the single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
A wildcard bind reserves a port without selecting a source address. When two interfaces have routes to the peer, connect can then send its SYN through the other interface because it looks up the route without the device selected by SO_BINDTODEVICE.

Use the socket's current device for the route lookup, as Linux does [1]. Reject a conflicting destination scope [2]. Keep the saved device used by the port reservation and endpoint registration. Restore an established connection with the NIC selected for its saved route.

Check the selected source address on two interfaces with overlapping prefixes. Both can reach the peer, so failure to honor the socket's device is visible before the handshake completes.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/e8f897f4a/net/ipv4/tcp_ipv4.c#L233-L235
[2]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/e8f897f4a/net/ipv6/tcp_ipv6.c#L188-L197

Fixes #8276

nodes.title: Resume TCP keepalive at its saved deadline
nodes.summary:
A restored TCP socket could have SO_KEEPALIVE enabled and never send its next probe. On the send-deadline prerequisite, the idle and between-probe tests both failed. The proposed change passed both packet tests and kept a disabled timer quiet. The failed-route test passed on the proposal and failed when terminal timer cleanup was removed.

The first Linux run also exposed a separate reset-socket fixture error. After the fixture deregistered the closed endpoint, changing TCP_KEEPIDLE queued one timer on the previous draft and zero on the proposal. The corrected run exercised only that terminal case.

Reset-socket correction and independent final-versus-previous timer control

contributorReview.head: 38b1dd1dac75b1fcbbe718d33db05237ce849182
contributorReview.title: Resume TCP keepalive at its saved deadline
contributorReview.summary: Open this gVisor PR after the send-deadline prerequisite lands?
contributorReview.body:
An idle TCP connection can resume from a checkpoint with SO_KEEPALIVE enabled and never send another probe. Restoring the endpoint initialized a disabled timer. Setting TCP_KEEPIDLE again restarted it.

Save the active timer's stack-clock deadline and bind its callback after the connected endpoint has a route. This preserves both the remaining idle period and the shorter interval between unanswered probes. Clear the saved timer state if the connection closes before it can be armed.

Check the remaining time and packets across a stack save and restore. Also cover a disabled timer and the configured probe count.

nodes.summary: A FUSE server can reject regular file OPEN and still return a directory handle from OPENDIR. On close, native Linux sent RELEASEDIR for handle 305419896. settledReviews.head: beaf6a3627f81fa6a8575f33c3c12f7d09598b3f
settledReviews.title: Release FUSE directory handles after unsupported file opens
settledReviews.body:
A server can return ENOSYS for OPEN and still implement OPENDIR. The
regular-file fallback then suppresses RELEASEDIR when the directory
closes, leaving the server with an open directory handle.

returned to the server in RELEASEDIR.

nodes.head: a4ca95b85a9a770e6e01852c30da57ae94f89b52
nodes.title: Reserve TCP experiment headers on first use
nodes.summary: With a 1,200-byte peer MSS, both address families sent all 1,200 bytes untagged before the first socket option request. Enabling the option on a capable NIC with the first packet still in flight produced a 1,196-byte IPv4 payload or a 1,192-byte IPv6 payload. Each socket retained the correct limit after two restores. All 11 selected cases passed in Netstack channel-link and host-GSO tests. The TCP/IP, stack and TCP analyzers passed for AMD64 and ARM64. The published message-only revision has the exact tested tree. On a 1,500-byte IPv6 veth, the peer read all 10,153 bytes in eight correctly sized frames. Four multi-segment sends returned ENOMEM before delivery completed. A separate queue-splitting prototype sent eight tagged IPv6 packets without a rejection. Untagged IPv6 and tagged IPv4 still submitted one aggregate each.

contributorReview.head: a4ca95b85a9a770e6e01852c30da57ae94f89b52
contributorReview.title: Reserve TCP experiment headers on first use
contributorReview.body:
A full-size TCP write with the IPv6 experiment header produced a
1,508-byte packet that the 1,500-byte path rejected. TCP had chosen its
segment size before the socket enabled the option.

Reserve header space on the outgoing route before storing the first
nonzero option value. Update the TCP and GSO segment sizes together so
the next send fits, even with earlier packets still in flight. Sockets
that never enable the option keep their full payload.

Retain the smaller of the peer MSS and the path payload limit before
deducting option bytes, as specified in RFC 9293 section 3.7.1 [1].
Use that limit after restore so a newly capable route gets the required
header space and repeated restores deduct it only once.

Test first use with data in flight on IPv4 and IPv6, then restore each
connection twice and check the next segment on the wire.

[1]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html#section-3.7.1
contributorReview.summary: Open this one-commit TCP change after the checksum and ordinary ACK-accounting fixes land?

evidence.label: Original MTU and peer-read evidence
First-use frames, GSO controls and analyzer outputs
Transmitted packet credit across IPv4 and IPv6 restore
Full IPv6 peer read and the eight captured data frames
Parent/candidate sendmmsg results with IPv4 and untagged IPv6 controls
Fork prototype selecting MSS-sized tagged IPv6 writes

nodes.head: 67f8866474c0fb1644927618a9cf20ee71ba441d
nodes.title: Remove the PacketImpact runner's host tool calls
nodes.summary:
Stock failed on the Ubuntu AMD64 worker when it tried to start iptables-nft. With the proposed runner, the native Linux and Netstack handshake targets passed uncached on both AMD64 and ARM64. On fork integration 43fdbb717, LLVM compiled and linked the AArch64 POSIX server on an AMD64 OCI worker. Both AArch64 test executables ran on ARM64 Firecracker workers with root and IPv6 requested. Each IPv4 capture showed the receive window open from 0 to 32,768 and all 11 bytes of Sample Data. Bazel retained both raw captures. The native manifest recorded 611 bytes without a MIME type. The Netstack wrapper reported three printf warnings and omitted the 505-byte capture from its manifest.

Six hosted targets passed with host binaries masked. The development-only dependencies preserve the consuming module’s Netlink version, and all 225 license records passed. The first ARM64 attempt timed out during the build. It reached 7,685 of 10,907 actions, with 803 remote actions completing in the last five minutes. Neither TestRunner had started.

evidence.label: ARM64 Linux and Netstack handshakes, LLVM actions and both packet captures
Stock failure, both remote TestResults and raw packet captures
Six hosted owners and ten verified captures
Development-only modules and the downstream Netlink version

settledReviews.head: 67f8866474c0fb1644927618a9cf20ee71ba441d
settledReviews.title: Remove the PacketImpact runner's host tool calls
settledReviews.body:
PacketImpact builds its runner, DUT and testbench with Bazel, but starts
them through a Bash script that calls find and chmod. Both Linux DUTs
invoke uname for their identity. The runner also requires iptables-nft
and ip6tables-nft at fixed host paths, so a worker without those tools
fails before the first packet exchange.

Run the Go runner as the Bazel test and obtain DUT identity from
uname(2). Install the TCP input filters through nftables in the
testbench network namespace. Packet sockets still see incoming frames
before the input hook drops TCP on the DUT-facing interfaces.

Declare the firewall modules as development dependencies to preserve
downstream Bazel modules' existing Netlink version selection.

nodes.head: be0aab89c556c459e8e110c517ea7e1011d24ce4
nodes.title: Store a single graph waiter without a callback record
nodes.summary: On a 50,000-file checkpoint, the first guest command took 200.2 ms versus 243.2 ms on #16860. Decoding allocated 99.27 MiB versus 121.84 MiB per checkpoint. Both comparisons have 16 pairs. Separate cold and pooled callback, pointer-chain, and map benchmarks detected no timing change. Package and race checks passed.

Six ordinary loads, each measured in 16 alternating pairs

settledReviews.head: be0aab89c556c459e8e110c517ea7e1011d24ce4
settledReviews.title: Store a single graph waiter without a callback record
settledReviews.body:
A graph decoder wait with no callback only needs the ID of the object to
wake. The decoder appends a 72-byte callback record for each such wait.
A checkpoint with 50,000 tmpfs files contained 50,364 objects with
exactly one plain waiter. [1]

Keep that ID in the incoming queue. If another waiter arrives, append
the first waiter to the callback list before adding the second. The
object's own callbacks run before it wakes its waiter.

On Linux AMD64, all 34 checkpoints restored with every file verified.
The first guest command was measured from container creation through a
successful /bin/true. Both decoders also read the same checkpoint in
fresh processes. [2]

                  │   before    │               after                │
                  │   sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base               │
Guest/restore       233.2m ± 1%   184.1m ± 1%  -21.05% (p=0.000 n=16)
Guest/new-to-guest  243.2m ± 1%   200.2m ± 5%  -17.69% (p=0.000 n=16)

                              │    before     │               after                 │
                              │     B/op      │    B/op       vs base               │
CheckpointFile/DecodeStatefile  121.84Mi ± 0%   99.27Mi ± 0%  -18.53% (p=0.000 n=16)

Direct decode time was inconclusive (p=0.305). Cold and pooled tests
of a single AfterLoad, a pointer chain and a shared map also showed no
significant difference in time or allocated bytes across 16 pairs. [3]

[1]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42530264849/artifacts/13637437535
[2]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42537752922/artifacts/13640319931
[3]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42544593510/artifacts/13643640390

nodes.head: 4b987cc5bff6ad50d7926db63a7c62625735e9b8
nodes.title: Split tagged TCPv6 sends before host offload
nodes.summary: On a private Linux veth with a 1,500-byte MTU, four TCPv6 GSO sends carrying gVisor’s experimental IPv6 header returned ENOMEM. Splitting before host offload delivered the same 10,153 bytes in eight packets with no rejected aggregate. Tagged IPv4 and untagged IPv6 still aggregated. The permanent two-MSS test observed a 1,056-byte payload on the parent where it expected 528 bytes. All six cases and the AMD64 and ARM64 TCP Nogo checks passed on the proposed tree.

contributorReview.head: 4b987cc5bff6ad50d7926db63a7c62625735e9b8
contributorReview.title: Split tagged TCPv6 sends before host offload
contributorReview.body:
On a Linux veth with a 1,500-byte MTU, sendmmsg rejected four TCPv6 GSO writes carrying gVisor's experimental IPv6 header with ENOMEM. Individual segments reached the peer after retries. Tagged IPv4 and untagged IPv6 aggregates succeeded on the same link.

Linux finds TCP for IPv6 GSO by walking registered next-header handlers [1]. gVisor cannot rely on a host handler for its experimental next-header value 253. On a noqueue device, a segmentation error can surface as ENOMEM [2].

Limit a tagged host-GSO IPv6 write to one MSS before TCP accounts for it in the send queue. Use the same socket option value to choose the segment size and build its IP header. The host still completes the TCP checksum on each packet.

Exercise a two-MSS write in the existing experiment option tests. Check the payload and sequence range of each segment and retain host aggregation for tagged IPv4 and untagged IPv6.

[1]: https://git.launchpad.net/~canonical-kernel/ubuntu/+source/linux-azure/+git/jammy/tree/net/ipv6/ip6_offload.c?id=41da417a5#n137
[2]: https://git.launchpad.net/~canonical-kernel/ubuntu/+source/linux-azure/+git/jammy/tree/net/core/dev.c?id=41da417a5#n4472

settledReviews.head: 4dad1e4b9741b815b3332d75994ee01224602912
settledReviews.title: Fix PacketImpact runsc debug log filenames

nodes.head: e18f42092698397c1d1ca248b6bc95bec1c910a2
nodes.title: Retry interrupted PacketImpact address dumps
nodes.summary: An interrupted IPv6 address dump stopped an upstream PacketImpact DUT before its testbench started. The fix discards the partial reply and retries only that address family, up to ten attempts. All seven focused Linux controls passed in a private namespace. Two genuine kernel interruptions occurred during 16 successful lookups. An uninstrumented build on the standalone fork timed out after 22 minutes with no TestResult. A separate replay used the exact revised lookup file and unchanged SYN-SENT test on the previously verified ARM64 Firecracker runner integration. All four cases passed without skips. Same upstream Netstack test passed on retry

Uninstrumented Netstack target timed out before a TestResult

settledReviews.head: e18f42092698397c1d1ca248b6bc95bec1c910a2
settledReviews.title: Retry interrupted PacketImpact address dumps
settledReviews.body:
A PacketImpact DUT stopped during bootstrap when the kernel marked its IPv6 address dump as interrupted [1]. Such a dump may contain one address for the requested link even when another address is missing.

Discard the incomplete result and retry only the affected family. Bound the number of attempts at ten, as in the netlink library’s opt-in retry [2], and propagate the last error if the dump remains interrupted.

settledReviews.body:
[endpoint_state.go, line 277](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/17264/files#diff-5701ff02ce1d54c6aa9e84d99c60583cd27dec8b7a85efa2abd098f69c32f1e7R277)

nodes.head: cc9a10f3a7e2a8bdb971fd984da42ba941993062
nodes.title: Guard TCP port reservation ownership
nodes.summary:
Guard the endpoint’s port reservation flag with its mutex. Record all four reservation details after ephemeral port selection succeeds. The synchronous callback returns success only after it registers the endpoint. Restore clears the flag and restores the closed state in one critical section before stack cleanup.

The TCP analyzer reported zero findings on AMD64 and ARM64. Restoring the previous callback or the unlocked restore assignment independently produced diagnostics at the corresponding statement on both architectures. All 93 named native AMD64 XML cases passed across seven selected Go tests. A saved closed endpoint restored to StateClose and its port could be rebound. The evidence establishes the lock precondition and the observed runtime behavior.

evidence.label: Guarded source, two independent analyzer negatives and 93 native runtime cases
Earlier restore-only change exposed the callback access
Approved change published as #17277

settledReviews.head: cc9a10f3a7e2a8bdb971fd984da42ba941993062
settledReviews.title: Guard TCP port reservation ownership
settledReviews.summary: Open the single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
Bind, accept and cleanup hold the endpoint mutex when they record or release a port. Restore cleared the reservation flag without that mutex when returning a saved endpoint to StateClose.

Mark isPortReserved as guarded by the endpoint mutex. Record the port's reservation details after PickEphemeralPort returns successfully. Its callback accepts a port only after registering the endpoint.

Clear the flag and restore StateClose in the same critical section. Release the endpoint mutex before removing the endpoint from the stack's cleanup list.

nodes.head: 0235b052b4ea92fb70e12b0eb58f576d2688463a
nodes.title: Honor SO_BINDTODEVICE when choosing a TCP connect route
nodes.summary:
A wildcard-bound TCP socket could select a source address on a device other than the one named by SO_BINDTODEVICE. The fix uses the live option for outgoing route selection and preserves the device saved with the port reservation.

Two isolated Linux syscall tests and the stock and fixed systrap runs used identical C++ fixture bytes. Stock chose 192.0.2.129 for both bound devices. Linux and fixed gVisor chose 192.0.2.1 on veth1 and 192.0.2.129 on veth2, whether the application set the device before or after wildcard bind. For an IPv6 destination scope that conflicted with the device, Linux and the fix returned EINVAL. Stock returned ENETUNREACH.

All three changed-device checkpoint controls and all three endpoint device cases passed on both gVisor revisions. The fixed TCP analyzer passed on AMD64 and ARM64. The original ordinary Linux runner skipped the syscall tests for lack of CAP_NET_ADMIN. Both tests executed uncached in the isolated Linux recovery. The IPv4 observations come from getsockname during a nonblocking connect.

evidence.label: Original report: TCP connect can ignore the selected device
Stock and fixed systrap syscall results, checkpoint and endpoint cases, and both Nogo architectures
Exact C++ fixture on isolated Linux with both syscall cases executed
Approved change published as #17278

settledReviews.head: 0235b052b4ea92fb70e12b0eb58f576d2688463a
settledReviews.title: Honor SO_BINDTODEVICE when choosing a TCP connect route
settledReviews.summary: Open the single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
A wildcard bind reserves a port without selecting a source address. When two interfaces have routes to the peer, connect can then send its SYN through the other interface because it looks up the route without the device selected by SO_BINDTODEVICE.

Use the socket's current device for the route lookup, as Linux does [1]. Reject a conflicting destination scope [2]. Keep the saved device used by the port reservation and endpoint registration. Restore an established connection with the NIC selected for its saved route.

Check the selected source address on two interfaces with overlapping prefixes. Both can reach the peer, so failure to honor the socket's device is visible before the handshake completes.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/e8f897f4a/net/ipv4/tcp_ipv4.c#L233-L235
[2]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/e8f897f4a/net/ipv6/tcp_ipv6.c#L188-L197

Fixes #8276

nodes.title: Release FUSE directory handles after unsupported file opens
nodes.summary: A FUSE server can reject regular file OPEN and still return a directory handle from OPENDIR. On close, native Linux sent RELEASEDIR for handle 305419896. Both stock gVisor configurations timed out waiting for it. With the fix, ptrace and systrap returned the same handle. The syscall ran on AMD64. The FUSE analyzer passed for AMD64 and ARM64.

Proposed implementation and permanent syscall test

settledReviews.head: beaf6a3627f81fa6a8575f33c3c12f7d09598b3f
settledReviews.title: Release FUSE directory handles after unsupported file opens
settledReviews.body:
A server can return ENOSYS for OPEN and still implement OPENDIR. The
regular-file fallback then suppresses RELEASEDIR when the directory
closes, leaving the server with an open directory handle.

Apply that fallback only to regular-file releases. Record the OPEN
capability atomically since file descriptions on different inodes
share the connection. Exercise the fallback and check the handle
returned to the server in RELEASEDIR.

nodes.head: 5bc25951220fabd92bee33b5862da3271391ada8
nodes.title: Run dependency checks without Bash
nodes.summary:
The netstack, runsc and Sentry dependency tests traverse the configured dependency graph in an aspect. Their generated executables use Bash even for a passing graph, and the shell expands dollar signs in forbidden labels. Using Bazel’s AnalysisTestResultInfo still requires /bin/sh. It also drops transitive validation outputs: on both CPU configurations, the original netstack, runsc and Sentry owners exposed zero, one and two validation artifacts respectively. The runsc and Sentry validations cover prebuilt Protobuf tools. With an intentionally failing validation action, the original rule failed and the analysis-test replacement passed without running that action.

The single-commit change keeps the ordinary test rule and includes its diagnostic in the test runfiles. All three real TestRunners passed uncached on native AMD64 with /bin and /usr/bin masked for the test child. A forbidden edge printed the literal label price$usd and exited 1. The AMD64 and ARM64 executables also returned the expected statuses in empty roots, with ARM64 executed under QEMU on AMD64. With the executable and test label unchanged, a fresh pass was followed by a cached pass. Changing just the generated report produced a fresh failure. The deliberate transitive validation still failed.

The same patch on the compiler integration at 08ca50082 passed all three tests on each of the native AMD64 and ARM64 remote workers. Both Bazel invocations exited 0. The original receipt records six uncached remote TestResults and their XML and log digests. It binds the requested worker image and runtime wrapper to the netstack owner on both architectures. The reporter subsequently failed when it looked for private _validation outputs in ordinary target-completion events. The separate native/QEMU qualification verified validation propagation and the failing action directly.

evidence.label: Single-commit dependency checker
Stock, standard analysis test and native control. All 18 original log/XML pairs
Exact-source native AMD64 tests, direct AMD64 and ARM64 QEMU execution, cache and validation controls
Same source patch on the compiler integration
Six remote TestResults and their original log and XML digests
Published pull request

followup.nextAction: Follow #17284 for maintainer review and import.

settledReviews.head: 5bc25951220fabd92bee33b5862da3271391ada8
settledReviews.title: Run dependency checks without Bash
settledReviews.summary: Open the single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
The netstack, runsc and Sentry dependency tests cannot report a passing graph on a worker without /bin/bash. When a check fails, the generated script expands dollar signs in dependency labels.

Write the diagnostic next to the test executable and include it in the runfiles. Link each test to one target-native program that reads its own report, prints any forbidden edges and exits with failure. Keep the ordinary test rule so Bazel forwards the dependencies’ validation actions, including the prebuilt Protobuf compiler check.

nodes.head: 59a8c8cc138ea704a5e635b794a9e76197faa744
nodes.title: Consume TCP timer wakeups before handling expiry
nodes.summary:
The timer now consumes each clock wake under the endpoint lock before calling a TCP handler. It discards canceled wakes, rearms early ones, and invokes the handler only for a due timer. This replaces the old handler-side predicate that also changed timer state.

Three packet tests observed one, one, and two probes. All 60 package records, eight selected end-to-end records, and both architecture analyzers passed on ad55e4137. The proposed source differs by two comment lines. The median allocation counts were 26, 168, and 171 in both arms.

Allocation size in six paired AMD64 samples:
                                   │    stock     │               fixed                │
                                   │     B/op     │     B/op      vs base              │
WildcardBindClose-2                  4.844Ki ± 0%   4.852Ki ± 0%  +0.16% (p=0.002 n=6)
KeepaliveHandshake/enabled=false-2   18.03Ki ± 1%   18.12Ki ± 1%  +0.49% (p=0.041 n=6)

evidence.label: Published TCP timer wakeup fix
Packet captures, package and analyzer records, and paired benchstat
Exact source changes since the previous proposal
Native Linux, stock gVisor and corrected gVisor: original logs, XML and packet captures

followup.disposition: Published the approved timer wakeup fix as #17286.

settledReviews.head: ba00452d5ef8966fb8ee9df0de6330abb45e344f
settledReviews.title: Restart TCP keepalive after a disabled timer fires
settledReviews.summary: Open the single-commit gVisor PR?
settledReviews.body:
Disabling SO_KEEPALIVE leaves the clock timer running. If it fires while keepalive is disabled, the callback returns before consuming the orphaned timer. Re-enabling keepalive then records a new deadline but leaves an idle connection without a scheduled probe.

Consume the clock wakeup before checking SO_KEEPALIVE. Check that an idle connection stays quiet while keepalive is disabled and resumes probing when the option is enabled again.

settledReviews.head: 59a8c8cc138ea704a5e635b794a9e76197faa744
settledReviews.title: Consume TCP timer wakeups before handling expiry
settledReviews.summary:
Open this revised timer PR? It moves wakeup consumption into the timer API. All three packet tests, both owning suites, and both analyzers passed. The proposed description reports the two increases in bytes allocated per operation.

git -C ~/code/gvisor range-diff ba00452d5^! 59a8c8cc1^!
settledReviews.body:
Turning SO_KEEPALIVE off while a probe is pending leaves a clock
callback scheduled. If the callback runs while keepalive is off, the
next enable can mistake the spent callback for one that will still
fire. The connection then sends no more probes.

Have the timer consume each clock wake under the endpoint mutex
before calling the protocol handler. A canceled arm becomes idle,
an early wake rearms the clock for the current deadline, and only a
due arm reaches the handler. This also lets cleanup discard a
callback that was already waiting for the mutex.

Exercise disabling keepalive, waiting past the old deadline, and
enabling it again on an idle connection.

Binding and closing a socket, or completing a handshake with keepalive
disabled, allocated slightly more memory in six paired runs [1].

                                   │    stock     │               fixed                │
                                   │     B/op     │     B/op      vs base              │
WildcardBindClose-2                  4.844Ki ± 0%   4.852Ki ± 0%  +0.16% (p=0.002 n=6)
KeepaliveHandshake/enabled=false-2   18.03Ki ± 1%   18.12Ki ± 1%  +0.49% (p=0.041 n=6)

[1]: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/42654872005/artifacts/13694980473
settledReviews.note: Published as the reviewed single commit. Benchstat and qualification are retained on this card.

nodes.head: e18f42092698397c1d1ca248b6bc95bec1c910a2
nodes.title: Retry interrupted PacketImpact address dumps
nodes.summary: An interrupted IPv6 address dump stopped an upstream PacketImpact DUT before its testbench started. The fix discards the partial reply and retries only that address family, up to ten attempts. All seven focused Linux controls passed in a private namespace. Two genuine kernel interruptions occurred during 16 successful lookups. An uninstrumented build on the standalone fork timed out after 22 minutes with no TestResult. A separate replay used the exact revised lookup file and unchanged SYN-SENT test on the previously verified ARM64 Firecracker runner integration. All four cases passed without skips. evidence.label: Published pull request
Upstream Buildkite failure during DUT address discovery
Same upstream Netstack test passed on retry
Native namespace controls, two observed kernel interruptions, original logs and XML
Uninstrumented Netstack target timed out before a TestResult
Original ARM64 Netstack test log, four passing XML cases and IPv4 capture

settledReviews.head: e18f42092698397c1d1ca248b6bc95bec1c910a2
settledReviews.title: Retry interrupted PacketImpact address dumps
settledReviews.body:
A PacketImpact DUT stopped during bootstrap when the kernel marked its IPv6 address dump as interrupted [1]. Such a dump may contain one address for the requested link even when another address is missing.

Discard the incomplete result and retry only the affected family. Bound the number of attempts at ten, as in the netlink library’s opt-in retry [2], and propagate the last error if the dump remains interrupted.

[1]: https://buildkite.com/gvisor/pipeline/builds/53930#01a1bb4a-013c-4f0a-aea4-1e82a1d51acf/208978 [2]: https://github.com/vishvananda/netlink/blob/188504cbe/nl/nl_linux.go#L518

nodes.title: Remove the PacketImpact runner's host tool calls
nodes.head: 67f8866474c0fb1644927618a9cf20ee71ba441d
nodes.summary:
Stock failed on the Ubuntu AMD64 worker when it tried to start iptables-nft. With the proposed runner, the native Linux and Netstack handshake targets passed uncached on both AMD64 and ARM64. On fork integration 43fdbb717, LLVM compiled and linked the AArch64 POSIX server on an AMD64 OCI worker. Both AArch64 test executables ran on ARM64 Firecracker workers with root and IPv6 requested. Each IPv4 capture showed the receive window open from 0 to 32,768 and all 11 bytes of Sample Data. Bazel retained both raw captures. The native manifest recorded 611 bytes without a MIME type. The Netstack wrapper reported three printf warnings and omitted the 505-byte capture from its manifest.

Six hosted targets passed with host binaries masked. The development-only dependencies preserve the consuming module’s Netlink version, and all 225 license records passed. The first ARM64 attempt timed out during the build. It reached 7,685 of 10,907 actions, with 803 remote actions completing in the last five minutes. Neither TestRunner had started.

evidence.label: ARM64 Linux and Netstack handshakes, LLVM actions and both packet captures
Stock failure, both remote TestResults and raw packet captures
Six hosted owners and ten verified captures
Development-only modules and the downstream Netlink version
Canonical license catalog and both scoped source fetches
First ARM64 attempt: build time limit, zero TestResults

settledReviews.head: 67f8866474c0fb1644927618a9cf20ee71ba441d
settledReviews.title: Remove the PacketImpact runner's host tool calls
settledReviews.body:
PacketImpact builds its runner, DUT and testbench with Bazel, but starts
them through a Bash script that calls find and chmod. Both Linux DUTs
invoke uname for their identity. The runner also requires iptables-nft
and ip6tables-nft at fixed host paths, so a worker without those tools
fails before the first packet exchange.

Run the Go runner as the Bazel test and obtain DUT identity from
uname(2). Install the TCP input filters through nftables in the
testbench network namespace. Packet sockets still see incoming frames
before the input hook drops TCP on the DUT-facing interfaces.

Declare the firewall modules as development dependencies to preserve
downstream Bazel modules' existing Netlink version selection.
settledReviews.summary: Open the standalone PacketImpact runner PR?

nodes.title: Fix PacketImpact runsc debug log filenames
nodes.head: 4dad1e4b9741b815b3332d75994ee01224602912
nodes.summary: The Netstack PacketImpact runner left literal percent signs in three debug filenames. Bazel interpreted them while writing the undeclared-output manifest and folded the packet capture into a malformed row. Using runsc’s single percent delimiters produced four distinct rows for boot, gofer, run and the capture. Both uncached ARM64 Firecracker handshake tests passed. The native control had one capture row. Both manifests still reported that the worker lacked the file utility for MIME detection.

evidence.label: Original malformed Netstack row and intact packet capture
Corrected native and Netstack manifests, logs, XML and captures
Bazel 9.3.1 manifest formatter

settledReviews.head: 4dad1e4b9741b815b3332d75994ee01224602912
settledReviews.title: Fix PacketImpact runsc debug log filenames
settledReviews.body:
The Dockerless PacketImpact runner introduced in b318556f8 passes its debug log template directly to runsc. Doubling the percent signs leaves literal percent signs around the expanded timestamp and command.

Bazel 9.3.1 uses each output record as a printf format [1]. On a Netstack handshake, the three log names corrupted the manifest entry for the packet capture.

Use the single percent delimiters expected by runsc.

settledReviews.title: Build one marshal test binary per Go library
settledReviews.body:
A two-architecture presubmit ran 92 generated marshal test binaries. Of those, 58 ran no test cases. Each still needed a linked Go executable and a test action on a remote worker. [1]

For example, on AMD64 the pkg/abi/linux tests for common types and AMD64 types run in separate binaries. Bazel also links and runs a 4.2 MiB binary for the ARM64 types, even though Go excludes every one of its tests. [2]

nodes.title: Allow build_test to run without a shell
nodes.head: b2d9986a40604f82df42c322122ad61313104cfa
nodes.summary:
Skylib’s build_test can use a declared marker tool on the execution platform and a declared runner on the target platform. Callers can supply either independently. Omitted tools retain their existing defaults. The private Linux consumer exposed 16 empty markers and one runner in its runfiles while building all 17 checked files.

On the earlier supplier revision, each real gVisor build_test built 16 manual binaries and passed: AMD64 natively and ARM64 through QEMU on the same AMD64 host. The receipt retains both test results and 32 link-output/marker-input pairs. The collector failed while reading the action graph, so those two runs do not establish the physical consumer runfiles or payload digests. Both ran through Bazel’s standard POSIX test harness. Replacing Bazel’s own shell wrapper is tracked separately in #30837.

The final revision keeps the same marker, runner and permanent test. All ten queried labels had the expected effective sizes on the final source. The checked-in reference matches the canonical Stardoc output.

settledReviews.head: b2d9986a40604f82df42c322122ad61313104cfa
settledReviews.title: Allow build_test to run without a shell
settledReviews.body:
build_test uses a genrule to create a marker for each batch of checked targets. Its test executable is also a shell script on POSIX. Both steps require a shell on the machine that runs them.

Let callers provide a tool that creates an empty file on the execution platform and an executable that runs on the test’s target platform. Pass the marker path as a single argument, including when the target name contains shell metacharacters. The markers keep the checked targets in the build graph when another test inherits only the runfiles, without adding their binaries to that test’s runfiles.

In gVisor, both the AMD64 and ARM64 tests built all 16 selected binaries. The AMD64 test ran natively and the ARM64 test ran under QEMU on the same worker. [1]

nodes.summary: On master, poll called EventUnregister once after the file rejected the waiter with EIO. The proposed change returned EIO, made zero unregister calls and left the file’s reference count unchanged. The permanent regression runs pollBlock in the gVisor Linux syscall package.

evidence.label: Merged Unix socket waiter rollback (#16739)
Earlier standalone poll correction
Native AMD64 poll regression on master and on this revision; Linux syscall package Nogo passed for AMD64 and ARM64
Konstantin on the similar failed-registration fixture
Fork-only regression: stock called cleanup once, the fix zero times

settledReviews.head: e39e7d78ecf48665d720b4cd64fea5e888753b9f
settledReviews.title: Unregister only successful poll waiters
settledReviews.body:
poll defers cleanup of each registered waiter. It records the file before EventRegister returns, so a failure causes cleanup to call EventUnregister on the entry that was just rejected. Unix sockets already undo their own registration on a host error (ed3929b26).

Keep the file reference in pollState only after registration succeeds. On failure, release the reference and return the registration error.

nodes.head: cf2a26737bd6a255ef74c136a3c6fd06f5a5ab30
nodes.title: Wake blocked socket receives on pending errors
nodes.summary: A blocked recv slept until timeout even though poll showed a pending error. Listening for EventErr makes recv return ECONNREFUSED as Linux does. Linux and corrected gVisor each passed all 22 UDP records and eight focused reruns. Withholding ICMP hit the intended failure on both. The native AMD64 comparison used the exact two changed files on the RBE integration tree.

evidence.label: Published gVisor PR #17312
Full results, repetitions and missing-ICMP controls
Same-socket POLLERR and recv comparison
Investigation and four upstream CI failures

followup.nextAction: Follow review on #17312.

settledReviews.head: cf2a26737bd6a255ef74c136a3c6fd06f5a5ab30
settledReviews.title: Wake blocked socket receives on pending errors
settledReviews.body:
A connected UDP socket can receive an ICMP port-unreachable error while recv is blocked. The UDP endpoint records ECONNREFUSED and notifies EventErr, but RecvMsg waits only for readable data. Poll then reports POLLERR while recv continues sleeping. With a receive timeout, recv returns EAGAIN even though SO_ERROR still reports ECONNREFUSED.

Subscribe to EventErr when a receive blocks so it retries the read. In the PacketImpact test, wait for the first recv to report the error before sending the datagram for the next recv. That datagram could otherwise wake the reader and hide the missed notification. Bound the first read so a missing ICMP error fails the test.
settledReviews.summary: May I open the UDP receive wakeup fix found in four failing CI builds?

investigations.title: CUBIC recovery and congestion-control testing
investigations.summary: The reporter’s original stall has a tested repair. Separately, gVisor enlarged its post-loss congestion window on writes that never filled it. The candidate keeps its window stable across three write schedules; Linux kept its window stable in all four sparse-write flows.

findings.text: A fork-only endpoint test on master 9ee2906f5 exercised the CUBIC restart callback through the real sender. After 30 seconds with no outstanding data and a 3-second RTO, cwnd fell from 11 to 10. The first ACK for two segments kept it at 10. Removing only the call to HandleWindowRestart still reduced cwnd to 10, then the same ACK raised it to 11. Both 1 ms idle controls held at 11.

evidence.label: Actual sender traces and XML for the normal and callback-omitted cases
Fork-only end-to-end sender fixture

findings.text: The author’s Eifel fix passed all 11 packet cases with #17022 and #17023 together. Adding the published #16081 left five passing. Restricting its recovery guard so Eifel may resume loss recovery restored all 11. All four genuine-timeout controls passed with either version of the guard.

evidence.label: Matched packet cases and genuine-timeout controls for all three changes
TCP reviewer guide and landing order

findings.text: With a 200 ms timeout, the baseline sender retransmitted its oldest repair after 93–98 ms. When an ACK came about 125 ms after repair, #16624 avoided the extra packet in eight of eight pairs. With the ACK 355–360 ms after repair, the corrected sender timed out after 200–201 ms in all eight pairs. All 34 transfers delivered 512 KiB. The two policies used identical loss ranges.

evidence.label: 34 transfers, packet copies, sender timers and test XML
Review order and downstream LAN reordering measurements

findings.text: On the CUBIC sender series, two 512 KiB transfers timed out 93–94 ms after repairing the oldest segment, with a 200 ms RTO. Delaying a new SACK until after the timeout produced no second RACK recovery. The sender had repaired all three holes first. Both transfers delivered the full payload. The four policy comparisons were skipped because this workload exercised just the deadline change.

evidence.label: Two original packet traces, sender events and test XML
Reviewer guide and individual controls

findings.text: On a 20 Mb/s, 100 ms path with a 100-packet queue, counting the original packets and their retransmissions separately increased CUBIC’s share against Linux in both pairs, from 33–36% to 41–44% and from 30–33% to 37–40%. Reno’s ranges overlapped. Neither controller consistently reduced the longest stall. The ranges bound bytes delivered at the edges of the observation window.

evidence.label: Eight competing transfers with verified packet captures

findings.text: gVisor with #15634 received less than 44% of the common-interval bytes in all 16 mixed-stack trials against Linux. Eight same-stack controls ranged from 41% to 60% for the first lane. Increasing the queue to 256 packets did not close the gap. The cause remains open.

evidence.label: 24 receiver comparisons, both lane orders, two queue depths

findings.text: With RACK disabled, the peer reported packet 3, cumulatively ACKed 100 bytes, then also reported packets 6–8 to enter SACK recovery, then acknowledged the whole flight. Linux counted 1,1,4,0; stock gVisor 0,0,0,−3. A fork prototype counted 1,1,6,0 and is not ready: splitting the transmit queue can credit a wire packet twice. This counter discrepancy does not establish a bandwidth effect.

evidence.label: Linux TCP_INFO vs stock and experimental gVisor through RFC 6675 recovery

findings.text: Linux kept one previously SACKed 1,460-byte packet counted as one when ICMP lowered its MSS to 1,160 and it retransmitted the preceding hole at the new size. Stock gVisor reported a negative SACK count on final ACK. A fork candidate removes the negative count, counts overlapping/reversed SACK blocks correctly in the measured cases, and retains a packet boundary after a partial cumulative ACK on a real 4,000-byte GSO buffer. Its duplicate ACK cost fell, but new SACK handling cost 6–15% more in the checked cases. No measured bandwidth effect; still investigating RFC 6675 queue splits before proposing a fix.

evidence.label: Matched gVisor packet controls and accepted/duplicate SACK processing costs
Linux TCP_INFO and 1,160-byte repair following a real path MTU decrease

findings.text: At 20 Mbit/s, 100 ms and a 100-packet queue, Linux took the larger share with both assignments of the two senders. With no TCP probe installed, gVisor received 27–30% of common-interval bytes under Reno and 21–31% under CUBIC. One host, one trial per controller/assignment; sampled senders were backlogged, and the 250 ms snapshots do not distinguish which ACK or loss caused the gap.

evidence.label: Twelve current-source Linux/gVisor shared-flow trials

findings.text: Four shorter trials compare packet headers on both sides of the bottleneck with a matched uninstrumented control. This is investigation work, with no recommendation to change the default controller.

findings.text: The initial common-source trial stopped at setup because two helper binaries were not in the resolved runfiles; it produced no throughput measurement.

Common production source

findings.text: Older tcp_proxy runs without a trace file still assembled TCP endpoint state on every incoming segment and passed it to an empty callback. Those runs measured throughput with that instrumentation; they do not establish uninstrumented throughput.

findings.text: A fork prototype for retrying locally rejected writes suppressed the first window probe when the peer subsequently advertised zero. A peer that closed its window without the prior refusal did receive the probe. Clearing the local retry when the persist timer takes over restored the probe in both cases. All four connections sent the original 536 bytes when the peer reopened the window. This result is about the prototype, not stock gVisor or a public PR.

This timer bug does not account for the previously measured queue delay in the sparse-loss Reno run.

findings.text: After dropping the second of five 1,420-byte segments, the virtual link recorded three acknowledgments with growing SACK blocks. Reno and CUBIC each retransmitted just the missing segment after 20 ms, before the 200 ms retransmission timer. The receiver delivered all 7,100 bytes exactly once; each sender counted one fast retransmit, one SACK recovery and zero timeouts. All eight runs (two algorithms, one or two processors, two trials) reproduced the same 14 packets. During recovery Reno’s window fell from 10 segments to 5; CUBIC’s stayed at 10 at that sample. This measures a single connection recovering from one loss. The trace does not establish a throughput advantage or distinguish the effect of the SACK information from that of duplicate ACKs.

evidence.label: Original packet traces and TCP counters
Two-stack link, deliberate loss and assertions

findings.text: Two real gVisor TCP stacks reproduced the same packet schedule for one connection over a link with a 10 ms delay each way. The client sent 33 bytes at virtual time 30 ms. With no loss, the server acknowledged them at 40 ms; the sender recorded no timeout or retransmission. When the fixture dropped that segment, no packet or data appeared one nanosecond before the 200 ms timeout. At 230 ms the sender retransmitted the same sequence and payload; at 240 ms the server acknowledged all 33 bytes. The sender counted one timeout and one retransmission, and the receiver read the data only once. Both modes produced identical TCP headers, payloads and times across two trials each at GOMAXPROCS=1 and 2. The fixture pauses dispatchers and checks each expected packet before advancing time. This covers a single flow with tail-loss probes disabled; it does not establish that several flows drain in a deterministic order. An earlier fixture sent an already-parsed buffer to the receiver and stopped before the handshake completed.

evidence.label: Two-stack wire and retransmission traces on Linux AMD64
Fork fixture with the link, timeout and delivery checks
Earlier fixture stopped after the initial SYN

findings.text: A real TCP endpoint retransmitted an unanswered SYN after 1.0003 seconds on the Linux worker. Under plain Go 1.27.3 synctest, the SYN was sent but Wait stayed blocked until the five-second watchdog: the idle TCP processor was parked in Sleeper.Fetch. Pausing the single stack once let Wait return without advancing time. No retransmission was queued one nanosecond before the RTO; the same SYN appeared at exactly one virtual second (4.1 ms wall time for the child). This proves a handshake timer can run while the dispatcher is paused. It does not establish a deterministic two-stack link simulator.

evidence.label: Real SYN, plain bubble and paused stack: native worker result

findings.text:
The sustained two-sender FIFO experiment confirms the earlier first-write sensitivity over longer virtual-time windows. With CUBIC writing first, Reno delivered 82,360 bytes on the control versus 8,686,004 with #16495 during seconds 5–20; during seconds 15–20 it delivered 25,560 versus 2,714,048 bytes. Both connection setup orders reproduced this result, and lifetime retransmission timeouts fell from 36 to one. Reno/Reno also improved for the weaker peer with either write order. CUBIC/CUBIC and Reno-writes-first traces were unchanged between sources; both finite payloads completed in every source/schedule.

These are deterministic shared-FIFO observations, not independent live-network samples, pristine-master throughput, general CUBIC superiority or a fairness guarantee. findings.text: A receiver SACK armed the timer at 224 ms. The retransmission timeout interrupted recovery at 225.2912 ms; the timer fired at 226 ms. Stock Reno halved its threshold from four segments to two again and retransmitted the oldest segment twice. The fix marked three segments lost without cutting the window again. Disabling the scan missed a genuinely dropped segment, but under both schedules the two treatments had identical 752-record wire traces, including delivery times. Both repaired the missing bytes at 248.12 ms on the post-timeout schedule. The corrected transfer took 769.032 ms versus stock’s 767.8672 ms; stock sent 15 retransmissions rather than nine. findings.text: Reno and CUBIC saw the same timeout 225.2912 ms after first data, and the same partial cumulative ACK 2,848 with a fresh SACK block [11,392, 14,240) at 245.9648 ms. The ACK covering the original flight was 17,088. On stock gVisor each controller received three premature loss callbacks before that covering ACK. Reno’s threshold fell from 5 to 2 on the first, and CUBIC’s from 4 to 2. Some later callbacks left the threshold unchanged at the two-segment minimum. With the fix neither controller received an early callback. Two repetitions per source delivered the same payload digest, EOF and FIN ACK. The fix keeps the original recovery point even through another timeout, while continuing to use new SACKs to repair losses. After the cumulative ACK covers the original flight, the peer induces a new hole and observes its retransmission. The exact test passed normally and under race. A trace from #16393 is still missing.

Stock TCP enters SACK recovery a second time

findings.text:
The complete approved RACK patch comparison now finishes the original finite-FIFO transfer. The #15634 prerequisite alone completed all 16 MiB in 15.663 modeled seconds with zero retransmission timeouts. Adding the already-approved 83ab4392c2 change reduced completion time to 14.305 seconds and queue drops from 2,201 to 459. Independent retained verification confirmed the two executed source identities and uncached attempts, complete payload and EOF/FIN observations, both counter sets, the classic control, and original bundle/receipt source hashes. These are measurements of real netstack execution on the modeled manual-clock path. They are not a child-alone test, a general performance guarantee or an explanation of the customer outage. findings.text:
A separate open Reno report, #16393, describes no-timestamp burst-loss recovery on gVisor 7bffefa, Windows/AMD64 and Go 1.27.3. Markus reports that three of five 512 KiB Reno transfers remained incomplete after 35 seconds, while all four stock-CUBIC transfers completed. These are the reporter's small-sample observations, not results of the independent FIFO experiments above. The report itself does not establish the cause of the original network stalls or validate its diagnostic patch.

Ayush directly mentioned Tamir and suggested changing the default to CUBIC. That suggestion is recorded as external feedback; no default-congestion-control decision has been made. A separate controlled Linux/netstack fixture has now completed; its limited diagnostic result is recorded below. The approved reply is now posted: it requests the standalone reproducer and a stalled-run seed or drop sequence, separates the ACK-path and reorder-timer guards, and keeps the Reno bug open independently of any default-controller discussion. No verified causal link to the existing FIFO results or a customer outage is established.

evidence.label: Open external report: slow Reno recovery without TCP timestamps
Ayush directly mentions Tamir and suggests CUBIC as the default
Posted approved reply: request reproducer and separate the two recovery guards

findings.text:
The separate #16393 diagnostic completed on Linux/AMD64 with two real netstack endpoints and a fixed 512 KiB transfer. In the deliberate first-flight blackout, stock Reno completed in 2.126752 modeled seconds with three retransmission timeouts; the ACK-path-only diagnostic completed in 0.7878112 seconds with one timeout. Each retransmitted eleven segments. The control therefore did not reproduce the reporter's 35-second Windows stall.

The trace associates the extra recovery entries with positive RACK scans on cumulative ACKs. The reorder-timer treatment was never enrolled, so this does not establish or test the proposed timer predicate. The reporter's seed and packet schedule remain unavailable. No production repair, shared outage cause or default-controller decision follows.

evidence.label: Separate no-timestamp Reno diagnostic: stock versus ACK-path-only treatment

findings.text: A separate Linux TCP reference run passed all 22 independently recomputed calibration gates, covering capacity, offered and delivered traffic, overload drops, clocks, headroom and host throttling. The native result is PASS and the reference is usable for its declared controlled measurements. This establishes the experiment's calibration, not a Reno/CUBIC ranking or a production-throughput result, and it does not reproduce the Windows report.

evidence.label: Separate Linux TCP reference: all 22 calibration gates pass

findings.text:
A separate matched Reno/SACK comparison without TCP timestamps now tests stock netstack, the #15634 prerequisite, and that prerequisite plus the already-approved flight-counting change 83ab4392c2. Six uncached attempts completed all 18 transfers with 512 KiB delivered and FIN observed. These are modeled-time Linux/netstack measurements, not a reproduction of the reporter's 35-second Windows stall.

In the full first-flight blackout, stock and #15634 had the same trace: 2.126752 seconds, three retransmission timeouts and eleven retransmissions. Adding flight counting completed in 0.8225728 seconds with one timeout and the same eleven retransmissions. When the fixture also deliberately dropped a retransmission, stock and #15634 fell back to four timeouts and completed in 3.7273376 seconds; the combined change completed in 0.8237536 seconds with one timeout. Each recorded twelve retransmissions. The combined trace marks the newly lost retransmission during active SACK recovery, sends the next copy immediately, and receives an advancing ACK. It does not start another recovery episode or invoke a separate congestion-control callback; a callback-specific interpretation remains unresolved.

The partial-loss case was slower with the child: 0.5354304 seconds versus 0.5092176 seconds, a 26.2128 ms difference; both had seven retransmissions and no timeout. Independent terminal interpretation confirmed the native evidence and these limits. This is neither a uniform speed improvement nor a child-alone comparison. It does not establish a new ACK or timer guard, a customer-stall cause, or a default-controller change. The existing contributor approval and #15634 delivery gate for 83ab4392c2 are unchanged.

evidence.label: Matched no-timestamp Reno loss comparison: all 18 transfers complete; outcomes vary by loss case
Existing approved flight-counting proposal and its #15634 gate
SACK-accounting prerequisite #15634

findings.text:
The controlled single-loss experiment used a fixed 4 MiB transfer, a modeled 10 Mbit/s forward link and 100 Mbit/s reverse link, 100 ms round-trip delay, and a 100-packet limit. Both loss arms had identical observed events through the first congestion-control callback, with congestion window and flight count both 109 segments. CUBIC set the slow-start threshold to 76 segments; Reno set it to 54. Each repaired the same original segment once without a retransmission timeout, and every transfer delivered the complete payload and FIN. Two deterministic repetitions matched; they are not independent network samples.

The no-injected-loss Reno mirror overflowed its queue 221 times. Its elapsed time therefore does not isolate the cost of the injected loss. Because congestion window and flight count were equal at the callback, this experiment also cannot distinguish which quantity supplied Reno’s denominator. No isolated goodput effect, default-controller recommendation or customer-outage attribution follows.

evidence.label: Controlled gVisor single loss: exact 109/109 callback input and thresholds 76/54

findings.text:
A separate Linux 6.18.57 reference measured the corresponding single-loss response in one TCG boot. All 32 path, overload, clock and headroom gates passed; four shaped 4 MiB transfers and the unshaped control delivered exact receiver bytes and EOF. Each loss arm dropped one original covering the named application byte, allowed one identical retransmission, and had no retransmission timeout or spontaneous forward-qdisc drop.

investigations.summary: Restoring 50,000 tmpfs files allocated a temporary pointer cell almost every time the decoder queued a parent pointer. The queue already held a copy of the pointer. Reusing that cell reduced total allocations per decode from 155,164 to 105,078.

findings.text: Across 300,736 LoadValueTo calls, the decoder needed 50,130 temporary cells on stock and 43 with direct-value reuse. Total allocations fell 32.3%, about 401 kB per decode. Live heap remained 67.04 MiB. Eight paired restores of the same 50,000-file checkpoint put the first guest command at 251.1 ms on stock and 245.0 ms with reuse (p=.721).

findings.text: Keeping the first scan in wire order lets the 50,000-file checkpoint resolve its three deferred frames without creating an index. Across 16 pairs, ordinary decode was 190.4 vs 188.4 ms (p=.926); both used 65.50 MiB live and 131.5 MiB peak heap. Eight native pairs verified every file after restore and showed no clear change to first guest readiness. An index for rows still unresolved after the first scan reduced a legal 1,024-cell chain from 3.554 to 0.814 ms (77.1%). The 16- and 64-cell cases showed no clear difference. The implementation adds 85 net lines for this worst case. Hold it while profiling ordinary restore.

investigations.title: Scheduled tracker refresh reliability
investigations.summary: The default-branch workflow requests a refresh at minutes 7, 17, 27, 37, 47 and 57. On November 8 GitHub recorded five scheduled runs, at 01:32, 07:52, 14:34, 19:01 and 22:45 UTC. All five succeeded. These timestamps establish gaps between scheduled runs. The cause of the missing events is unknown. An explicit dispatch at 00:03 UTC on November 9 succeeded, and the active owner’s next collection checked GitHub at 00:14 UTC.

findings.text: At the 11 October schedule audit, the default-branch workflow was configured for minutes 18 and 48 of each UTC hour. The latest scheduled run observed by that audit was created at 01:01:30 UTC on 11 October and completed the 01:03:14 snapshot in status-only commit 560dd0edb. That newer automated snapshot was preserved before the curated update. Five earlier scheduled runs succeeded on 10 October, created at 01:18, 07:45, 13:59, 18:39 and 22:00 UTC. Successful execution is established, but the observed multi-hour gaps before event creation do not demonstrate regular 30-minute cadence. Their cause remains unexplained.
