investigations.summary:
The Debian Ruby candidate builds on both architectures, but its package layer would replace the base image’s fixed OpenSSL with a vulnerable version and overwrite its package inventory. Keep the existing Ruby fixture in service. The corrected public catalog audit on bccbb767a9 passed canonical Fetch and Verify for all 212 dependency records, including the 12 artifact-pinned manual Ruby entries. All complete Entry values remained unchanged. Six native phases exited zero; no tests, HTTP consumers or image assemblies were rerun. This validates the candidate catalog against the existing policy, without adopting the candidate records or changing policy.

The original public audit 289a3144 remains FAIL: eight preparation/build phases passed, including both CPU native-gem outputs and both image archives, but Fetch and Verify each rejected ten singleton license lists before doing their work. The correction changed those lists to the scalar form required by the public checker. Its focused recovery d321c46b was verified 3.98 seconds after native completion. The original public archive and native tar/profile identities matched the earlier qualified outputs; their source-specific image evidence remains valid independently of the original catalog failure.

The source-bound fork experiment on 86b8d128d5d5 passed the unchanged TestRuby HTTP consumer under AMD64 runc and systrap, plus the inspector for both CPU archives and native-extension ABI. The earlier repeatability result covers the two architecture-specific gem payloads. ARM64 Docker execution remains unqualified.

Portability still requires a complete declared C compiler, make, sysroot, target Ruby ABI and matching execution-CPU contract. The examined portable Ruby headers match 190 non-generated headers per CPU, but its static Ruby/OpenSSL configuration differs from the qualified official image; header similarity alone does not establish extension compatibility. Keep the working public Dockerfile and do not present a Ruby contributor proposal yet.

Earlier source-specific Ruby consumer and supplier assessment:

The existing Ruby HTTP consumer now passes on remote AMD64 workers under both native runc and gVisor systrap. On source 6e2a86620241, both TestRuby cases loaded the same archive (2d55be5414b2) and image config (4af0598eae31), then passed the HTTP 200 and Hello World assertions. Authenticated source, conversion, TestRunner inputs, loaded-image logs and distinct daemon configurations connect the image to each runtime.

The original 71f63a5a invocation remains FAIL because buildifier rejected two BUILD layouts; neither Ruby case failed or skipped. Source 7ff366cdbb0a applies only that emitted formatting, and the separate 8befae51 singleton buildifier run passes. The consumers were not rerun. This closes the existing Ruby image consumer gap, not an image migration, ARM runtime, performance or reproducible-image claim; the recipe still installs unpinned Sinatra, rackup and Puma dependencies.

A source-only assessment of rules_img packaging for the unchanged Ruby HTTP server found no small drop-in native-gem supplier. rules_ruby v1.0.0-rc2 supplies pinned gem fetching, offline bundle installation and exportable gem files, but native extension compilation inherits its compiler from PATH and does not bind the native-extension outputs to the image’s Ruby ABI and target CPU. The inspected current Puma 8.0.2 and nio4r 2.7.5 gem archives contain extconf.rb and no prebuilt shared objects; these inspected versions are not asserted to be the historical image’s installed versions. A usable supplier must declare the native compiler, target Ruby ABI and AMD64/ARM64 outputs. No migration source, dependency change or new runtime qualification follows from this assessment.

Earlier source-specific image evidence:

Source-image export, archive verification and actual load are qualified for the retained Stable Diffusion and Triton paths. Stable source 5ba04f3e2 completes Dockerfile export through stock archive conversion and the named Docker-load case; Triton source/archive run 743979bb and fresh-load run 05df74e5 also pass on their recorded sources. These results close those source/export/load obligations, without GPU inference or general throughput claims.

The durable source-image verifier was qualified at 474d330d26 by its full 108-method reporter suite and lint, plus a separate retained nine-image/seven-consumer audit. The accepted 24-owner local benchmark union and source-bound consumer results remain recorded below. Original failed attempts, the separate hosted VFS limitation and unqualified GPU execution are preserved.

Retained consumer-policy evidence:

The full PHP 8.5.11 run c7ffc9ac on source 537a323d selected all 21,872 direct PHPT names in each AMD64 filesystem mode. After the retained suite-name correction, each mode has 15,691 PASSED, 6,297 SKIPPED, 9 XFAILED and one WARNED native body result; redirect children are counted separately from direct selection. The ten reporting-group errors and 500 missing results were resolved from the original artifacts without rerunning PHP. All 16 Bazel wrappers exited zero, satisfying the public process-exit policy on this retained source. PHP excludes WARNED from its failing exit states, and the public gVisor make/proctor/runner chain preserves that process result; the relevant current bf84 execution paths match the retained source. The stricter qualification still records watch_006.phpt as WARNED and keeps aggregate FAIL in both modes. A separate one-case native runc control a4f8a5ba used the exact original image archive, proctor and runner and produced the same WARNED result: its XFAIL marker was present although the expected output passed. This discrepancy does not support a gVisor runtime or exit-rule fix, a PHP backport or another full run. Exact-image parity and public process-exit success remain distinct from the preserved strict failure; neither is a new Buildkite result, a whole-matrix pass at bf84, full native parity or ARM runtime evidence.

investigations.title: Runtime startup performance
investigations.summary:
Sandbox creation can return before the Sentry serves control RPCs. For a new startup comparison, put both arms on the same boot implementation and measure through a successful Start or control RPC.

The retired integrated state proposal 3a38641f0 has a matched startup comparison against its prerequisite base. CLI medians are 2.380 versus 2.397 ms (p=.410), and StartupEmpty medians are 283.7 versus 265.8 ms (p=.198); neither establishes a timing difference or equivalence. State initialization remains 3,032 bytes and 13 allocations in both runsc and Sentry. Production file growth is 98,304 bytes for AMD64 runsc, 253,952 for AMD64 Sentry, 131,072 for ARM64 runsc and 262,144 for ARM64 Sentry. This source-specific comparison is separate from the earlier scalar and rewrite measurements below; samples are not pooled.

Earlier scalar-source record:

The scalar-store candidate 0fb39effd has verified matched CLI and StartupEmpty comparisons against original baseline 685d734a5: 6.104 to 6.113 ms (p=.887) and 479.1 to 476.5 ms (p=.551). Both are inconclusive, with unchanged pkg/state initialization allocations. The separate checkpoint/restore run failed and is under diagnosis. The earlier immediate-pair comparison against e0e088476 also found all ten package timing differences inconclusive; those samples are not pooled with the original-baseline startup comparisons. The candidate retains its verified code-size reduction, but remains 245,760 bytes larger per AMD64 binary and 196,608 bytes larger per ARM64 binary than the original implementation. It is not ready for contributor review.

Earlier source-specific startup evidence:

The earlier state rewrite at 91323cf62 completed matched Linux AMD64 CLI and sandbox startup comparisons: 5.868 to 6.054 ms (p=.143) and 251.116 to 254.198 ms (p=.932). Both are inconclusive. Each current AMD64 runsc/Sentry file grows by 2,351,104 bytes and each ARM64 file by 2,293,760 bytes; this is not measured RSS.

Fixed Linux AMD64 CLI comparisons for netip, the earlier state design, the owned-Value successor and the compiler-only change found no statistically significant timing difference. The compiler-only comparison also found no statistically significant sandbox-start difference (346.079 to 341.365 ms, p=.977, twelve batch means per version). It uses matched Go 1.26.3 sources. The owned-Value state CLI result remains 6.814 to 6.973 ms (p=.478), with production-file growth of about 4.01 MB on AMD64 and 3.74 MB on ARM64. The matched netip sandbox comparison also found no statistically significant difference: 288.4 to 296.1 ms (p=.590), with twelve batch means of eight starts per arm. It uses frozen Go 1.27.0 sources 6212e4f7b and 86ea1d1f3, not current upstream. Earlier state sandbox results concern their then-current source. These measurements do not establish equal startup cost or qualify the owned-Value successor for sandbox startup. The independently approved gofer initialization correction merged in #15859 as d5b092c05.

The build then stopped on 211 GoImports actions that tried to start a generated /bin/sh wrapper.

Integration 24d291a8f adds the approved stateify change from #16710. Stateify now selects and formats its own imports. The production build ran 211 of the 212 configured GoStateify actions. All 211 succeeded, and the build configured and ran zero GoImports actions. A separate generated file contained the time import under its cross-file alias, the aliased type, and both save and load calls.

The same strict AMD64 runsc build recorded 785 successful uncached linux-sandbox spawns. Six configurations of //tools/nogo:stdlib failed before execution: each GoStandardLibraryAnalysis action declares no-sandbox, and Bazel reported NO_USABLE_STRATEGY_FOUND. The diagnostic reader missed the wording in the console and marked its verification incomplete; all six action records retain the structured error. Make exited 2 and Bazel exited 1. The release did not link, and no tests ran.

On fork integration 1668d83dc, both native Linux workers built //runsc:runsc with Make and Bazel under the strict sandbox strategy. The fork integrates the Nogo producer change in 4b4839487 with the SDK tool from rules_go #4772. Each worker built objdump once for its execution architecture. Six standard-library and six gohacks configurations consumed that executable across AMD64 and ARM64 archive configurations. The same tool disassembled the Noescape function in an archive passed to the analyzer. On ARM64, the separate version check rejected protoc 36.2 when it required 35.1.

Make and Bazel both exited zero on each worker. The 13,103,264-byte AMD64 and 12,255,392-byte ARM64 runsc binaries both reported the runtime and OCI specification versions with --version. Neither production build had failed actions or TestRunner invocations. These were native workers; the evidence does not establish remote worker placement, the other eight programs in //:release, or a full-graph build.

investigations.title: Verify locking contracts with checklocks
investigations.summary: Add annotations where actual callers establish a locking invariant. Check analyzer coverage and any effect on lock order or runtime behavior rather than adding locks solely to silence a diagnostic.

findings.text: The POSIX timer proposal guards both the table of timers and the next timer ID. Its checkpoint control identified the unguarded pause read on AMD64 and ARM64.

evidence.label: Signed timer-lock proposal
Original lock analysis, Linux syscall and lockdep systrap save/restore results

findings.text: VFSPipe.newFD still required callers to hold a mutex removed when FIFO opens switched to waiter queues. The batch cleanup removes that precondition and the unused vfs and inode mutex declarations. The lockdep runtime suite and both pipe Nogo owners passed on 0bae5ce4b.

evidence.label: Pipe mutex declarations and newFD precondition cleanup
Pipe runtime suite with lockdep
Both Nogo owners executed successfully on the 16 GB worker

findings.text: Put the mutex on ipc.Object so Nogo can check permission reads through an object pointer. Registration initializes and indexes the key before publishing it. This removes six lock wrappers and introduces no additional lock acquisitions. Removing the lookup lock now fails analysis on AMD64 and ARM64. The integrated change passed the four owning analyzers, 97 unit and syscall cases, and 18 restores covering message queues, semaphores and shared memory.

evidence.label: Patch above both parents
Combined tests, restores and negative controls
Original missing-lock comparison

findings.text: With two waiters asleep on a futex, Linux returned 2 for a request to requeue up to seven of them on the same word. Stock gVisor returned 0. Counting instead of removing and reinserting the same waiters fixes both the return value and the queue used by the next requeue. A change that only increments the count returned 7 for the same two threads. Both FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG settings reproduced the difference.

evidence.label: Linux, stock, count-only and corrected syscall results
Six named syscall cases on Linux and gVisor, 13 package cases and both architecture analyzers

findings.text: An ordinary futex wake let a thread return successfully from a priority-inheritance lock while the futex word still named the old owner. In the reverse case, a PI unlock assigned ownership to a thread that had only asked to wait. Linux rejected both operations with EINVAL. The correction preserved ownership for private and shared futexes and distinguished an ordinary requeue from a PI requeue.

evidence.label: PI waiter first, original native, stock and corrected runs
Ordinary waiter first and same-key requeue on all three implementations
67 Linux and 67 gVisor syscall cases, both analyzer reports
13 named Go package tests

findings.text: A successful semop on semaphore 1 overwrote GETPID on untouched semaphore 0. Stock returned PID 1. Linux and corrected gVisor returned zero and passed all six cases. A separate test found that gVisor loses the writer’s PID after the writer is reaped because GETPID looks up a live thread group. Linux retains the PID.

evidence.label: Original comparison after the child was reaped
Linux semaphore PID lookup
Linux, stock and corrected gVisor on the same six syscall cases

findings.text: The timekeeper starts and stops its update goroutine under its lifecycle mutex. Nogo accepted the normal callers on AMD64 and ARM64. Moving start in Resume and stop in Destroy just before locking produced both expected diagnostics on each architecture. These annotations enforce the existing protocol without changing the runtime code.

evidence.label: Three timekeeper mutex annotations
Both architectures: guarded and deliberately unguarded callers

findings.text: Timekeeper.update reuses the vDSO write buffer under updateMu. The annotation passes Nogo on AMD64 and ARM64; moving the periodic call past Unlock produces one distinct missing-lock diagnostic, printed four times on each architecture. The original wrapper rejected those repeats. Replaying the same logs confirmed the result without another Bazel run. The change documents existing locking; it does not fix a production race.

evidence.label: Reconciled receipt from the original logs
Both normal and intentionally unlocked analyzer runs
Lock annotation

findings.text: Annotate copiedUp, cachedFD and cachedFlags with their existing mutex. Only final release has exclusive ownership without that mutex. Removing the existing EventUnregister lock produces a missing-lock diagnostic on each architecture.

evidence.label: Positive checks on AMD64 and ARM64
Removing the EventUnregister lock triggers both architecture analyzers

findings.text: Blocking flock and fcntl requests now register directly with the wait queue under the mutex before releasing it. findings.text: Use runsc statefile -checkpoint FILE (or -checkpoint -html FILE) to inspect existing Sentry memory checkpoints. The option is listed by runsc help statefile. Historical images have no unambiguous format marker, so the default generic command can still print incomplete output. On native ARM64, two original images had 64 and 62 regions. The generic text and HTML commands each reported 3 regions in the wire image and 4 in the graph image. Their output stayed byte-identical before and after the change. The two printers share graph traversal and use pgalloc’s format definitions to find the owner graph and consume one private MemoryFile per owner. The earlier draft added 407 non-test lines, compared with 348 here. EOF just after the first two graphs is valid for a split checkpoint and cannot identify an entirely missing inline tail without external context. The earlier split-page and filesystem-only checks passed. That run exposed the generic short-frame difference that the final native run verifies on stock, the intermediate reader and the corrected reader.

investigations.title: Interrupted IPv6 address dumps stop PacketImpact before the TCP test starts
investigations.summary: Four builds stopped while the test DUT was retrieving IPv6 addresses. Each affected TCP target ran and passed uncached in the same-head retry.

findings.text: The affected TCP tests were unaccepted sequence numbers (#53950), handshake window size (#53959), TCP_INFO (#53965) and TIME_WAIT reset (#53975). Their retries took 7.3, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.5 seconds respectively. #53975 separately reproduced the connected UDP receive failure.
